concept-2-what-living-things-need.explanation:
Every living thing needs the same four things to stay alive: food, water, air and warmth. A tiny chick needs them. A big camel needs them. A tall mango tree needs them. You need them too.

Think about your own body. When you feel hungry, that is your body asking for food. You are a living thing, and living things need food. When you feel thirsty, your body is asking for water.

Food gives living things the energy to move and grow. A goat eats grass. A chicken pecks seeds. A cat eats food and drinks water. A mango plant makes its own food in the sunshine.

Water matters just as much. You drink from a cup. The goat drinks from the well. The banana plant drinks water from the soil through its roots. No living thing can live without water.

Air is all around you, even though you cannot see it. Take a slow breath in, then out. You just used air. Living things need gases from the air for essential life processes.

Warmth is the last one. Living things need to be warm enough, not too cold. That is why a hen sits on her eggs, and why seeds wake up and grow in the warm season.

concept-1-all-living-things-have-needs.explanation:
Let us begin with the most important idea of the whole unit. Every living thing has needs. A need is something you must have to stay alive. If you do not get it, you cannot survive. This is true for you, for animals, and for plants.

Think about a young goat, a waxar, on a farm near Baidoa. What does it need every day? It needs food — the fresh grass and leaves it chews. It needs water — a drink from the trough or a puddle. It needs air — the breath it takes in and out without even thinking. And it needs shelter — a shady spot or a pen to keep it safe from the hot sun and from danger. These four needs — food, water, air, and shelter — are the needs of every animal on Earth.

Let us look at each need more closely, one at a time, so you understand it well.

Food is like fuel. When you eat bariis (rice) with a little goat meat, or drink warm camel milk in the morning, your body turns that food into energy. Energy lets you run, play, think, and grow. Animals are the same. A lion eats meat to get its energy. A giraffe stretches its long neck to eat leaves from the tall acacia tree. A little sunbird sips sweet nectar from flowers. Different animals eat different foods, but they all need food to live.

Here is something special about plants. Plants do not eat food the way animals do. Instead, plants make their own food inside their leaves, using sunlight, water, and air. This is one of the most amazing things in all of nature. Because plants can make their own food, they are like the great cooks of the world — and almost every animal depends on the food that plants make.

Water is precious, and in dry lands we know this better than anyone. Every living thing needs water. Your body is mostly made of water, and so is the body of a goat, a beetle, and a blade of grass. Animals drink water to stay alive. A camel is famous because it can go many days without drinking — but even a camel must drink in the end, and it can gulp down a huge amount of water very quickly when it finds a well.

Plants need water too. The roots of the mango tree drink water from the soil and carry it all the way up to the leaves. When the rains come in the Gu season, you can almost see the land turn green as thirsty plants drink deeply. When there is no rain for a long time, the plants dry out and turn brown. This shows us just how important water is.

Air is all around you, even though you cannot see it. Inside the air is a special gas called oxygen. Animals breathe in air to take oxygen into their bodies. You breathe through your nose and mouth. A goat, a lion, and a bird breathe too. Even a fish respires — it uses gills to take in oxygen dissolved in the water.

Plants also use air. They take in a gas from the air called carbon dioxide, and they use it to make their food. Then plants give out oxygen — the very gas that animals and people need to breathe. So plants and animals help each other. This is one of the beautiful ways that Allah has made the living world fit together.

Shelter and space keep living things safe

Every animal needs a safe place — a shelter. Shelter protects an animal from the hot sun, from cold nights, from rain, from strong wind, and from other animals that might harm it. A bird builds a nest. A spider makes a web in a quiet corner. A crab digs a hole in the sand at Lamu beach. A family of goats rests inside a pen at night. Even you have a shelter — your home, where you feel safe and warm.

concept-2-environments-and-habitats.explanation:
Now that you know what living things need, let us talk about where they live. The place where a living thing makes its home is called its habitat. All the things around it — the air, the soil, the water, the weather, and the other living things — make up its environment.

Not all places are the same. Some places are wet and some are dry. Some places are sunny and some are shady. Some are hot and some are cool. Each kind of place is home to different living things, because different living things need different conditions. Let us take a journey across the land you know and see how the environments change.

Dry places: the savanna and semi-arid land

Much of East Africa is warm and dry, with wide open grasslands called the savanna and drier land called semi-arid land. Here the Sun is strong and rain comes only in certain seasons. The plants that live here are tough. The acacia tree has tiny leaves and sharp thorns to protect its precious water. The baobab tree stores water in its huge, fat trunk. Aloe vera keeps water inside its thick leaves.

The animals here are adapted to the dry land. Camels can walk far to find water and food. Goats nibble on thorny bushes that other animals cannot eat. Giraffes reach the high leaves. Ostriches run fast across the open ground. Every one of these living things is suited to its dry home.

Now imagine a very different place — the edge of the Jubba River, or a green mangrove swamp along the coast. Here there is plenty of water. Frogs and toads live near the water. Fish such as tilapia swim in the river. Dragonflies dart above the surface. Reeds and water plants grow in the soft, wet mud. This wet environment is full of life that could never survive out on the dry savanna.

The coast: the Indian Ocean and coral reefs

Along the Indian Ocean coast, from Mombasa to Kismaayo, there is yet another kind of environment — the sea. Under the waves grow coral reefs, which are like busy underwater cities. Thousands of colourful fish, crabs, sea stars, and other creatures make their homes there. On the sandy beach, tiny crabs scuttle and dig. This salty, watery environment has its own special animals and plants.

Sunny and shady, wet and dry — even at home

You do not have to travel far to find different environments. You can find them in your own home and yard! A sunny windowsill is warm and bright. A shady corner under a table is cool and dim. The ground near a dripping tap is damp, while a shelf indoors is dry. If you look carefully, you will notice that little plants and minibeasts choose different spots. Some like the damp shade, and some like the warm sunshine. Later in this unit you will explore these tiny environments yourself.

Did You Know? A single acacia tree on the savanna can be a habitat for hundreds of creatures at once — ants living in its thorns, birds nesting in its branches, beetles under its bark, and giraffes feeding on its leaves. One tree can be like a whole busy town for living things!

concept-4-caring-for-our-environment.explanation:
The earth is a gift, and Allah has made people the khalifah — the carers and guardians of the earth. This means it is our job to look after the land, the water, the plants, and the animals. In this part of the unit you will learn how people can harm the environment, and, more importantly, how we can protect it.

Sometimes people harm nature without meaning to. Litter is rubbish that is dropped on the ground instead of being thrown away properly. A plastic bag blowing across the market in Eastleigh, a bottle left on Lamu beach, or a pile of rubbish by the road can all harm animals. A goat might swallow a plastic bag and become sick. A sea turtle might eat a floating plastic bag, thinking it is a jellyfish.

Pollution is when harmful things get into the air, the water, or the soil. Dirty water can make fish sick and can make people sick too if they drink it. Smoke can dirty the air we breathe. When too many trees are cut down, animals lose the shelter of their habitat, and the soil can blow away. These are the kinds of problems that a good scientist learns to notice and to help solve.

The good news is that everyone, even a young student like you, can help care for the earth. Here are some things you can do:

Do not drop litter. Put your rubbish in a bin, and pick up litter you find (when it is safe and clean to do so).

Reuse and recycle. An old tin can become a plant pot. A jar can be washed and used again instead of thrown away.

Save water. Turn off the tap while you wash, and do not waste this precious gift, especially in the dry season.

Plant and protect trees. Trees give shelter, shade, and clean air, and they hold the soil in place. Planting a mango or acacia tree is a gift to the future.

Be kind to animals. Give water to a thirsty animal, and never harm creatures just for fun.

Keep water clean. Do not throw rubbish into rivers, wells, or the sea.

When you do these things, you are being a good khalifah. You are caring for the world that Allah has trusted to us, and you are helping animals and plants get the things they need to live. Even small good actions add up to make a big difference.

concept-5-watching-the-weather.example: A real weather scientist is called a meteorologist. You can be one too! Each day, look outside and describe the weather. Is it sunny, cloudy, rainy, or windy? Is it hot or cool? Write it down in a weather chart. If you do this every day for a week or two, you will have a set of data. Then you can look at your data and notice patterns — for example, you might see that most days that week were sunny, or that the wind blew hardest in the afternoon. Noticing patterns is what scientists love to do.

steps: Choose a safe spot outdoors — a corner of the yard, near a wall, or under a stone or leaf.
Look quietly for 10 minutes. Move slowly so you do not scare the minibeasts.
Each time you see a minibeast, make a tally mark next to its name in your table.
Gently look at one or two closely in your clear jar, then let them go back where you found them.

we01.solution:
Step 1 — Ask a question. Amina asked: Which minibeast will I see most in my yard in ten minutes?

Step 2 — Make a plan. She decided to watch for ten minutes and make a tally mark for every minibeast she saw.

Step 3 — Collect the data. She saw 6 ants, 3 beetles, 2 butterflies, and 1 spider. She made a tally mark for each one as she saw it.

outcomes: By the end of this unit, you will be able to:
Identify and describe different rocks using their properties, such as colour, texture, hardness, and weight.
Explain how people use rocks to build houses, roads, and beautiful things.
Describe what soil is made of and how broken rock slowly becomes soil.
Sort materials into natural (made by nature) and man-made (made by people).
Observe and record the properties of materials carefully, the way a real scientist does.
Use what you know about rock properties to choose the best material for a job.

concept-1-what-is-a-rock.explanation:
A rock is a hard, solid material that is made by nature and found in the Earth. Let us think about what makes something a rock. First, a rock is hard and solid — it is not like water that pours or air that you cannot hold. Second, a rock is natural, which means nature made it, not people in a factory. Third, rocks come in many colours, sizes, and shapes. And fourth, rocks are made of tiny pieces called minerals that fit together like the pieces of a puzzle.

Imagine you are walking along the beach at Kismaayo. You bend down and pick up a small stone. It is grey, it is smooth, and it feels a little heavy in your hand. That little stone is a rock. Now imagine you are up in the volcanic highlands near the Rift Valley, and you see a huge dark cliff taller than a house. That giant cliff is also rock — the very same kind of material, just a great deal bigger. Rocks can be as tiny as a grain of sand or as huge as a mountain.

When scientists want to describe a rock, they look at its properties. A property is simply a word that tells us what the rock is like. Here are the properties you will learn to observe:

Colour: Rocks can be black, white, grey, red, brown, green, and many colours mixed together. Some have stripes or spots.

Size: A rock can be a tiny pebble or a huge boulder.

Shape: Some rocks are round and smooth; others are jagged and sharp.

Texture: This is how the rock feels — smooth, rough, bumpy, or grainy.

Weight: Some rocks feel surprisingly heavy; others feel light for their size.

Hardness: Some rocks are so hard you cannot scratch them; others are soft and crumble easily.

A good scientist uses all of these words together. Instead of just saying 'this is a rock', you can say something like: 'This rock is grey, smooth, round, and heavy for its size.' That is real scientific describing, and you can do it!

Here is a helpful way to picture what rocks are made of. Think about canjeero (the soft flat bread) made from many tiny grains of flour pressed together. In a similar way, a rock is made of many tiny minerals pressed and joined together. Some minerals are shiny and catch the light, some are dull, and some have beautiful colours. When you see sparkly bits inside a grey rock, you are looking at its minerals. Different rocks have different minerals inside them, and that is one big reason why no two rocks are exactly the same. When you learn to notice these tiny parts, you are seeing the rock the way a real geologist does.

It is also useful to know that some rock properties can only be seen when you look very closely, and others you can feel straight away. Colour and shape you can see from far away. Texture and weight you must feel with your hands. Hardness you have to test by trying to scratch the rock. This is why scientists use their eyes, their hands, and simple tools all together. The more of your senses you use, the more you will discover. So when you study a rock, do not just glance at it — hold it, turn it over, run your fingers across it, and take your time.

Rocks are found in many different places, and the place where a rock lives often changes how it looks. Near water — on the beaches of the Indian Ocean coast or in the Jubba and Shabelle rivers — rocks are usually smooth and round. Why? Because the moving water rolls them over and over for years and years, slowly wearing away their rough edges. Think of the water like a giant, gentle rock tumbler that polishes stones over a very long time.

Up in the mountains and hills, like the highlands around Hargeisa or the volcanic land near the Rift Valley, rocks are often rough and sharp. There is less water rolling them smooth, so when the hot days and cool nights crack them apart, they stay jagged. In your garden or farm, you might find a mix of sizes, from tiny pebbles to bigger stones, all buried in the soil. And in special places like old volcanoes, rocks were once so hot they melted into liquid, then cooled and became solid again.
concept-1-what-is-a-rock.example: Did You Know? The waves of the Indian Ocean never stop moving the stones on the beach. A rough, sharp rock that falls into the sea can slowly become a smooth, round pebble — but it takes many, many years.

concept-2-how-people-use-rocks.explanation:
People have used rocks for thousands of years, all over the world and right here in East Africa. Rocks are useful because of their properties. Let us see how the very same properties you learned to observe are exactly what make rocks so helpful.

Why are rocks so good for building houses, walls, and roads? Think about their properties:

Hard rocks last a long time. They do not break easily in the sun, the rain, or the wind.

Heavy rocks stay in place. The wind cannot blow them away, and floods struggle to move them.

Rocks do not rot. Unlike wood, a rock will not decay or be eaten by insects.

Most rocks do not burn, which helps keep a house safe from fire.

In the old town of Lamu and along the Swahili coast, people have built beautiful houses for hundreds of years using coral stone — a natural rock that comes from the sea. In Berbera and other coastal towns, thick stone walls keep the inside of a house cool even when the sun is very hot outside. Far away in Egypt, the ancient pyramids were built from huge blocks of a rock called limestone, and they are still standing after thousands of years. That is the power of choosing a hard, strong rock for building.

People also crush rocks into small pieces to make new building materials. Concrete, which is used for floors, bridges, and modern buildings, is made by mixing crushed rock and sand with cement (which itself is made from ground-up limestone) and water. When it dries, it becomes as hard as stone. Gravel — small crushed stones — is spread under roads and buildings to help water drain away. So even when a rock does not look like a rock anymore, it may still be doing an important job.

How do people get these rocks ready for building? They dig them from big pits in the ground called quarries. First they find a place with useful rock. Then, with strong tools and machines, they cut and break the rock into pieces of the right size. Some rock is crushed small to make concrete; some is cut into flat blocks for walls; and some is polished smooth and shiny for floors and countertops. Finally, trucks carry the rock to where it is needed. Different jobs need different rocks: a very hard rock like granite is chosen for parts that must be strong, while a rock that splits into flat sheets, like slate, is perfect for roofs. This is a wonderful lesson — people choose each rock because of its properties, exactly the properties you are learning to observe.

Rocks are not only useful — they can be beautiful too! People polish special rocks until they shine and use them to make necklaces, rings, and bracelets. These beautiful, hard, colourful stones are called gemstones. Because they are so hard, they last for a very long time, which is one reason people treasure them. Artists also carve big rocks into statues, and gardeners arrange smooth stones to make peaceful, pretty spaces. Maybe you have kept a special stone yourself because you liked its colour or its shape. If you have, then you already understand why people have loved rocks for thousands of years.

Here is something surprising: many things you use every day are made from rocks, even though they do not look like rocks at all! Let us become detectives and find the hidden rocks:

Toothpaste contains tiny bits of ground rock (like limestone) that gently help clean your teeth.

Glass — in windows and cups — is made from sand, which is really just tiny pieces of rock, melted at a very high heat.

Salt for your food is a rock! It is dug from the ground or dried out from seawater.

Pencils write with a soft mineral called graphite.

Chalk is made from a soft rock, and metal spoons and pans come from rock ores dug out of the Earth.

So when you help set the table for bariis (rice) at dinner, remember that the glass cup, the metal spoon, and even the salt all began their lives as rocks inside the Earth. Rocks really are all around us and inside so many things we use.

concept-3-the-story-of-soil.explanation:
Now let us dig into one of the most important materials on the whole Earth: soil. Without soil, farmers near the Jubba River could not grow bariis, maize, or vegetables, the acacia and baobab trees could not stand tall, and there would be almost no food for people or animals. Soil is precious, and it has an amazing story.

If you look very closely at a handful of soil, perhaps with a magnifying glass, you will see that it is not just one thing — it is a mixture of several things all together:

Tiny rock pieces: The biggest part of most soil. Big rocks slowly break into sand, then even smaller silt, then the tiniest pieces of all, called clay.

Dead plant and animal matter: Old leaves, roots, and other once-living things that have rotted down. The dark, rich part is called humus.

Air: There are tiny gaps between the soil pieces, and these gaps hold air that roots need to breathe.

Water: Soil also holds water in its gaps, which plant roots drink.

Living things: Earthworms, insects, and tiny living things too small to see all live in healthy soil and help keep it healthy.

Where does soil come from? It begins as solid rock. Over a very long time, weathering breaks the rock apart. The hot sun and cool night make rocks crack. Rain and wind wear them down. Even plant roots pushing into cracks help break rocks into smaller pieces. As the rock pieces get smaller and smaller, dead leaves and plants mix in, worms and insects tunnel through, and slowly — after hundreds or even thousands of years — rich soil is made. This is why we must take great care of soil: it takes a very, very long time to make, but it can be washed away in a single heavy rainy-season storm.

Did You Know? It can take more than five hundred years for nature to make just a thin layer of new soil. The soil in your garden may be older than the oldest building in your town.

Not all soil is the same. The kind of soil depends on the sizes of the rock pieces inside it:

Sandy soil is made mostly of large sand grains. It feels gritty, and water drains through it very fast. It is common near beaches and in dry, semi-arid land.

Clay soil is made of the tiniest pieces. It feels smooth and sticky when wet and holds water for a long time — sometimes too long for plants.

Loamy soil is a good mix of sand, silt, and clay. It is soft and crumbly and holds just the right amount of water. This is the best soil for most plants and for farming.

The colour of soil tells a story too. Dark brown or black soil is usually rich in humus and very good for growing food. Reddish soil often has iron in it and is common in warm places like much of East Africa. Pale, sandy soil usually has fewer nutrients for plants. When farmers look at the colour and feel of their soil, they are already learning a great deal about how well their crops will grow.

Soil is not still and quiet — it is full of busy life! The most helpful of all is the earthworm. As a worm tunnels through the soil, it makes little passages that let air and water travel down to plant roots. The worm also eats old dead leaves and turns them into rich food for plants. Ants, beetles, and tiny living things too small to see all work together, mixing the soil and breaking down what has died. In a way, all these creatures are little farmers of the underground world, keeping the soil healthy so that plants can grow. When you see a worm in the garden, do not be afraid of it — it is one of the soil's best friends.

Because soil takes so long to form, we must protect it. The biggest danger is erosion — when wind or water carries the soil away. In the dry season, strong winds can blow away loose, bare soil. In the rainy season, heavy rain can wash soil down slopes into the rivers. You may have seen brown, muddy water rushing along after a big storm — that brown colour is precious soil being carried away and lost. Once it is gone, it takes hundreds of years to make again.

The good news is that there are simple ways to protect soil, and nature shows us how. Plant roots hold soil in place like many tiny hands gripping the ground, so keeping the land covered with grass, trees, and crops stops the soil washing away. Farmers can add compost and animal manure to keep the soil rich, spread mulch (a cover of dead leaves or straw) to shield it from heavy rain, and build low walls or steps on slopes so the water slows down instead of rushing. As a khalifah of the Earth, even you can help by not wasting, by helping plants grow, and by keeping your soil covered and healthy.
concept-3-the-story-of-soil.example: Soil is like a life-support system for plants. It does four big jobs. First, it holds water like a sponge so that roots can drink. Second, it gives plants nutrients — the goodness from rotted plants and minerals that helps them grow strong, green, and healthy. Third, it gives support, holding the plant up straight against the wind so it does not fall over. And fourth, it holds air in its tiny gaps, because roots need to breathe just like you do. Good soil has the right balance of all four: water, nutrients, support, and air.

concept-6-man-made-materials.explanation:
A man-made material is made by people using tools, machines, and heat. People often make these materials because they can give them exactly the properties they want — very strong, very light, waterproof, or the same shape every single time. Here are some examples:

Plastic is made from oil. It is light, waterproof, and can be shaped into anything — bottles, buckets, and toys.

Glass is made by melting sand at a very high heat until it turns clear and hard.

Steel is a very strong metal made by people from iron that comes from rock.

Concrete and bricks are made by people from rock, sand, and clay to build strong walls.

Here is a clever secret that good detectives notice: even man-made materials start as something natural! A plastic bucket began as oil deep in the Earth. A glass cup began as natural sand. A steel knife began as iron rock. People just changed these natural things a great deal to make something new. This means the line between natural and man-made is really about how much people have changed the material. Some things, like a plain stone, are barely changed at all. Some things, like cut wood or clean cotton, are only shaped a little. And some things, like plastic and glass, are changed so much that you cannot recognise where they came from. A good scientist learns to trace any material back to its natural beginning.

explore-3.prompt: What do you think you will see inside the soil when it settles in water? Write your guess. What You Need A clear jar with a lid (a clean jam jar works well) Soil from a garden, farm, or pot — about one cup Water A ruler What To Do Put the soil into the jar until it is about one-third full. Pour in water until the jar is about two-thirds full. Screw the lid on tightly. Check it is closed, then shake hard for 30 seconds. Put the jar down and do not touch it. Let it settle for 15 minutes. Watch the layers form. The heaviest pieces (sand) sink first to the bottom, then silt, then the lightest clay on top. Bits of dead plants may float. Measure each layer with your ruler and record it.

explore-4.prompt: Which do you think lets water through faster — sandy soil or sticky clay soil? Write your guess. What You Need 2 clear plastic bottles cut in half by an adult (use the top halves as funnels, turned upside down) 2 clean cups or jars to catch the water Two different soils — one sandy, one more clay-like or from a garden A coffee filter, paper towel, or thin cloth A measuring cup of water A clock or timer What To Do Put a filter or cloth inside each upside-down bottle top so soil does not fall through. Fill each funnel with the same amount of a different soil. Rest each funnel on top of a catching cup. Pour the same amount of water onto each soil at the same time. Watch and time how fast the water drips into each cup. After 5 minutes, compare how much water is in each cup.

concept-1-solids-liquids-and-gases.explanation:
Before we watch materials change, we need to know what they can change *into*. Every material around you is usually in one of three forms. Scientists call these forms the states of matter. The three states are solid, liquid, and gas. Let us meet each one.

A solid keeps its own shape. If you put a solid on the table, it just sits there and stays the same shape. Think of a date stone, a stone from the ground, a wooden spoon, or a cube of ice. You can pick a solid up and it will not run through your fingers. Solids are firm because the tiny parts inside them are holding on to each other tightly, like children in a line all holding hands and standing still.

A liquid flows. It does not keep its own shape — instead it takes the shape of whatever container you pour it into. Pour water into a round cup and it becomes round. Pour it into a tall bottle and it becomes tall. Water, camel milk, cooking oil, and tea are all liquids. In a liquid, the tiny parts are still close together, but now they can slide past each other, like children walking slowly in a crowd, gently bumping and moving around.

A gas spreads out to fill all the space it can find. Most gases are so spread out that you cannot even see them. The air all around you right now is made of gases. When water boils on the stove, some of it turns into a gas we call steam, and it floats up into the air and disappears. In a gas, the tiny parts are far apart and zooming around quickly, like children running freely all over a big open field, never holding hands at all.

Did You Know? The very same material can be a solid, a liquid, AND a gas! Water is a solid when it is ice, a liquid when you drink it, and a gas when it becomes steam. It is still water the whole time — only its state has changed.

This last fact is one of the most important ideas in the whole unit. A material can change from one state to another, but it is still the same material. Ice, water, and steam are all just water wearing different clothes. What makes it change its 'clothes'? The answer is heat. When we add heat or take heat away, materials move between solid, liquid, and gas. Let us find out how.
concept-1-solids-liquids-and-gases.example: Here is a helpful way to picture it. Imagine the tiny parts inside a material are like children in a classroom. In a solid, the children are sitting very still in their places, packed close together — nobody moves, so the shape stays firm. In a liquid, the children stand up and walk slowly around the room, still close but able to slide past one another — so a liquid can flow. In a gas, the children run out into a big open field and dash around freely, far apart — so a gas spreads out everywhere. When you add heat, you give the children more energy to move, so a solid can become a liquid and a liquid can become a gas. When you take heat away, the children calm down and settle, so a gas can become a liquid and a liquid can become a solid. Hold this picture in your mind and the whole unit will make sense.

concept-2-what-heating-does.explanation:
Heating means adding heat to make something warmer. In your home, heat comes from the sun, from a charcoal stove, from a fire, or from an oven. When you add heat to a material, the tiny parts inside it start to move faster and spread out a little. This simple idea explains so many things you see every day.

The most exciting thing heat can do is turn a solid into a liquid. We call this melting. Think about butter or ghee. When it is cool, it is a firm, yellow solid you can hold. But when your mother puts it in a warm pan to cook, it becomes soft, then shiny, then runny. The solid butter has melted into liquid butter. The heat made the tiny parts inside the butter move faster until they could slide around, and a flowing liquid is exactly what you get when the parts can slide.

You have seen melting many, many times, even if you never gave it a name. On a hot afternoon, a piece of ice left on a plate slowly turns into a puddle of water. That is melting. A bar of chocolate carried in your pocket on a warm day becomes soft and messy. That is melting. A candle burning gives a small pool of melted wax around the flame. That is melting too. Every time a solid gets hot enough and turns into a liquid, that is melting.

Here is something clever to notice: not all solids melt at the same temperature. Ice melts when it is only a little bit warm — even the warmth of your hand can melt it. Butter needs to be warmer than that before it melts. A metal spoon needs to be extremely, dangerously hot before it would melt, far hotter than anything in your kitchen. That is why we can safely stir hot food with a metal spoon — the spoon stays solid because the stove is nowhere near hot enough to melt metal.

If you keep heating a liquid, something else amazing happens. It gets so hot that it starts to bubble and turn into a gas. When water does this, we say it is boiling, and the gas it turns into is called steam. Many families boil water on a charcoal stove to make it clean and safe to drink, because boiling kills the tiny germs that can make people sick. When you watch that pot, you can see white steam rising up and floating away. The water is changing from a liquid into a gas.

Boiling water and steam are very, very hot and can burn your skin badly. Steam can burn you even when you cannot see it clearly. This is why you must always let an adult handle boiling water, and why you should never lean your face over a boiling pot. We will talk more about staying safe very soon.

Safety First Boiling water and steam are HOT enough to burn your skin. Never touch them. Always ask an adult to handle anything on a stove or fire. For your own experiments, you will only use WARM water, never boiling water.

Heat does one more thing that is easy to miss. When many materials are heated, they get a tiny bit bigger. We call this expanding. Air expands when it is warmed. If you put a soft, half-blown balloon in the warm sun, the air inside gets warm, spreads out, and the balloon grows a little bigger. The material did not turn into a puddle, and it is still a balloon — but the warmth made it expand. This is a gentle change, but it is real, and clever builders remember it when they build roads and bridges that sit in the hot sun all day.

concept-3-what-cooling-does.explanation:
Cooling is the opposite of heating. Cooling means taking heat away so a material becomes colder. When you take heat away, the tiny parts inside a material slow down and move closer together. If heating spreads things out, cooling brings them back in. And just as heating can turn a solid into a liquid, cooling can turn a liquid back into a solid.

When a liquid gets cold enough, it turns into a solid. We call this freezing. The clearest example is water. If you pour water into a small cup and put it in a freezer, and then come back later, the water will have turned into hard, solid ice. The liquid has frozen. The cold took heat away from the water until the tiny parts slowed right down, moved close together, and locked into a firm shape — and a firm shape is exactly what a solid is.

Freezing and melting are like two doors that lead the same way. Melting takes a solid and warms it into a liquid. Freezing takes a liquid and cools it back into a solid. If you melt an ice cube into water and then freeze that water, you get ice again. You have gone all the way there and all the way back. That is a very special kind of change, and it has its own name, which we will learn in the next big idea.

concept-4-changes-you-can-undo-and-chang.explanation:
Now we come to one of the most useful ideas in all of science. Some changes can be undone, and some cannot. Learning to tell the difference will make you a very sharp scientist.

A reversible change is a change you can undo. After the change, you can get back exactly what you started with. Melting and freezing are the perfect example. If you melt ice into water, you can freeze the water and get ice again. Nothing was lost. You can go forwards (melt) and backwards (freeze) as many times as you like. Because you can reverse it — go back the way you came — we call it a reversible change.

Dissolving is usually reversible too. If you dissolve salt into water, the salt seems to disappear. But it is not gone! If you leave that salty water in a warm, sunny place, the water slowly floats away as a gas (this is called evaporation), and the salt is left behind as tiny white crystals. In fact, this is one of the oldest ways in the world to make salt: people let sea water from the Indian Ocean dry up in the sun, and the salt stays behind. The salt was hidden, not destroyed, so dissolving can be reversed.

An irreversible change is a change you CANNOT undo. Once it happens, there is no going back to what you started with. Cooking is the best example. When your family cooks an egg, the runny, clear liquid inside turns white and firm. Now try to imagine turning that cooked egg back into a raw, runny egg. You cannot do it — not by cooling it, not by any trick at all. The egg has changed forever. That is an irreversible change.

There are many irreversible changes in your kitchen and community. Baking flour and water into canjeero or bread is irreversible — you can never turn the bread back into raw batter. Burning charcoal or wood is irreversible — the wood turns into ash and smoke, and ash can never become wood again. Frying meat, roasting coffee beans, and mixing certain things together can all cause changes that cannot be undone. In an irreversible change, a brand new material is made, and the old material is gone for good.

Did You Know? When bread bakes, tiny bubbles of gas puff it up and the outside turns brown and firm. This is irreversible — no baker in the world can turn a loaf of bread back into flour and water!

concept-6-when-a-material-dissolves.explanation: When you stir sugar into a cup of tea, the sugar seems to vanish. You stir and stir, and soon you cannot see a single grain. But the sugar is not gone — taste the tea and it is sweet! The sugar has broken into pieces far too tiny to see, and those pieces have spread all through the water. This is called dissolving. The sweet, clear tea you are left with is called a solution. Materials that can dissolve, like sugar and salt, are called soluble.

outcomes: By the end of this unit, you will be able to reach these learning goals. Read them now, and read them again at the end to see how much you have grown as a scientist.
Name many light sources around you and say whether each one is natural or made by people.
Explain that we need light to see objects, and that in complete darkness we cannot see at all.
Describe what darkness is — it is not a thing by itself, it is simply what happens when light is missing or blocked.
Show how a shadow forms when an object blocks light, and explain what makes a shadow bigger, smaller, or point in a different direction.
Explain reflection — how light bounces off smooth, shiny surfaces such as mirrors and calm water.
Explain day and night as the result of the sun lighting one side of the spinning Earth.
Follow light safety rules, especially the golden rule of never looking straight at the sun.
Carry out simple, safe investigations about light using things from your own home.

Here are the important words for this unit. A good scientist learns to use the right words, just as a good carpenter learns the names of every tool. Read each word, its meaning, and the example. You will meet all of these words again inside the lesson.

concept-1-what-is-light-and-where-does-i.explanation:
Let us start with a big and simple idea. Light is a kind of energy that lets us see. Without light, the world would be completely dark and we would not be able to see anything at all — not our mothers, not our food, not even our own hands. Light is so ordinary that we often forget how special it is. But stop and think: every colour you have ever seen, every face you love, every beautiful sunset over the Indian Ocean, reached your eyes because of light.

Some objects make their own light. We call these objects light sources. A light source is special because the light comes out of it. The most important light source of all is the sun. The sun is a giant ball of hot, glowing gas in the sky. It is really a star, the closest star to us. The sun gives light to the whole Earth. It lights up the savanna, the coral reefs, the busy streets of Nairobi and Mogadishu, and the quiet villages by the Jubba River. Without the sun, there would be no daytime, no warmth, and no plants growing for the goats and cattle to eat.

Light sources can be sorted into two groups. Natural light sources are made by nature. The sun is a natural light source. So are the stars that sparkle over the desert at night, the bright flash of lightning during the wet season, and the orange flames of a fire. Artificial light sources are made by people. When you switch on an electric light bulb, shine a torch, or light a candle, you are using artificial light. People invented artificial light so they could see at night and in dark places where sunlight cannot reach, such as inside a room with the curtains closed.

Here is a tricky question that fools many people. Is the moon a light source? It looks so bright in the night sky! But the answer is no. The moon does not make its own light. Instead, sunlight travels to the moon, and the moon reflects that light back to us, like a giant mirror in the sky. This is why the moon seems to change shape through the lunar month, growing from a thin curve to a full round circle and back again. The Islamic calendar follows these moon shapes, which is how your family knows when the blessed month of Ramadan begins and ends. So the moon is not a light source, even though it lights up the night. It is a reflector, and you will learn much more about reflection later in this lesson.
concept-1-what-is-light-and-where-does-i.example: Light has one more secret you should know. Light travels in straight lines, and it travels very, very fast — faster than anything else in the whole universe. When you shine a torch across a dusty room, you can sometimes see the beam going in a straight path. When sunlight comes through a small gap in the clouds, it makes straight golden rays reaching down to the ground. Because light moves in straight lines, it cannot bend around corners on its own. This one idea will help you understand shadows and reflection, so keep it in your mind like a treasure.

concept-3-how-we-see-objects.example: This explains something you already know from your own life. In a bright room you can see everything clearly. As the room gets dimmer, you can see less and less. In complete darkness you cannot see at all, no matter how hard you try or how wide you open your eyes. This is not because your eyes stopped working. It is because there is no light bouncing off the objects into your eyes. Your eyes need light the same way a well needs water — without it, they simply cannot do their job.

concept-4-shadows-and-how-they-form.explanation:
Shadows are one of the most fun parts of studying light, and you can play with them almost anywhere. A shadow is a dark shape that appears when an object blocks the light. Remember that light travels in straight lines. When something solid stands in the way, the light cannot pass through it or bend around it. So behind the object there is a patch where the light did not reach, and that patch is the shadow.

To make a shadow, you always need three things working together. First, you need a light source, such as the sun or a torch. Second, you need an opaque object — opaque means something that blocks light, like your hand, a book, or the trunk of an acacia tree. Third, you need a surface for the shadow to fall on, such as the ground, a wall, or the floor. If any one of these three is missing, there can be no shadow. Take away the light and everything is dark with no shadow. Take away the object and the light reaches the surface with nothing to block it. Take away the surface and there is nowhere for the shadow to land.

Not every material makes a strong shadow. Opaque materials, like wood, stone, metal, and your own body, block light completely and make dark, clear shadows. Transparent materials, like clean glass or clear water, let light pass straight through, so they make almost no shadow at all. That is why you can see through a glass of water but not through a wooden door. When you hold a thin cloth up to the light, some light gets through and some is blocked, so it makes a faint, soft shadow — materials like this are called translucent, which means they let a little light through.

Shadows also change their size and shape, and you can control this. When you move a torch closer to an object, the shadow grows bigger. When you move the torch farther away, the shadow gets smaller. You can test this yourself with a torch and a toy. The position of the light also decides where the shadow points. The shadow always falls on the opposite side of the object from the light. If the light is on the left, the shadow stretches to the right. This is why your own shadow outside changes through the day as the sun moves across the sky.

In the early morning, when the sun is low in the eastern sky, your shadow is very long and stretches far across the ground. At midday, when the sun is high overhead, your shadow becomes short and hides almost under your feet. In the evening, as the sun sinks low in the west, your shadow grows long again but points the other way. Long ago, before clocks and phones, clever people used these changing shadows to tell the time of day. They built simple shadow clocks called sundials, and you could make one too.

concept-5-reflection-and-mirrors.example: People use reflection in many clever and helpful ways. A car has mirrors so the driver can see what is behind without turning around. A dentist uses a tiny mirror to see the hidden back of your teeth. A periscope uses two mirrors so a person can see over a tall wall or fence. People even use shiny mirrors to flash sunlight and signal for help when they are lost. Understanding reflection is not only interesting — it can also keep people safe.

concept-6-day-and-night.explanation:
Now let us put our light knowledge together to understand something that happens every single day of your life: day and night. During the day it is bright and we can see easily. During the night it is dark and we often need a lamp or torch. Why does this happen? It is all because of the sun and the spinning Earth.

The Earth is shaped like a giant ball, and it is always slowly spinning, like a top. The sun can only light up one half of the ball at a time — the half that is facing it. When your part of the Earth is turned toward the sun, sunlight reaches you and it is day. As the Earth keeps spinning, your part slowly turns away from the sun. The sunlight can no longer reach you, and so it becomes night. The Earth takes one whole day and night to spin around once, which is why we get one daytime and one night-time every single day.

This is why the sun seems to rise in the east each morning and set in the west each evening. The sun is not really travelling across the sky. It is the Earth that is turning, carrying you around with it. When Khadija in Hargeisa is enjoying bright afternoon sunshine, children on the other side of the world are fast asleep in the dark of night. When it becomes night for you, it is becoming day for them. Understanding this helps you see that day and night are simply about which side of our spinning Earth is facing our great light source, the sun.

we01.solution:
The question: What happens to the shadow when the torch moves closer to the toy camel?

Step 1 — Set up carefully. Farah stands the toy camel on the table near a wall. He holds the torch far away at first and shines it at the camel so a shadow appears on the wall.

Step 2 — Measure the first shadow. With the torch far away, Farah measures the shadow with a ruler. The shadow is 10 centimetres long. He writes this down. Writing down what you see is an important part of doing science.

Step 3 — Change one thing. Farah moves the torch closer to the camel. He keeps the camel and the wall in the same place — he only moves the torch. Changing just one thing at a time is a smart scientist trick, because then you know exactly what caused the change.

sci-g02-u05.unitOverview: Assalaamu alaykum, young scientist! In this unit you are going to explore one of the most useful and most exciting things in the whole world — electricity. Electricity is a kind of energy that helps us in ways we sometimes forget to notice. When you switch on a light in the evening, when your family listens to the radio, when a phone is charging in the corner, or when a fan pushes cool air across the room on a hot Mogadishu afternoon, electricity is quietly doing its work.

concept-4-making-movement.example: Electricity has to be made somewhere before it can help us. There are two main ways the electricity in your home might arrive: from batteries or from the mains. Let us look at both, and then at the special way many East African homes get their power — from the sun.

concept-5-batteries-electricity-you-can-.explanation:
A battery is a small store of electricity that you can carry around. Inside a battery there are special chemicals that hold energy. When you put the battery into a torch or a radio and switch it on, the battery lets its energy flow out as electricity. Batteries are wonderful because they are small and safe to hold, and you can take them anywhere — to the farm, on a journey, or out with the animals.

Batteries come in different sizes. A small AA battery is the kind we use for our science experiments. It gives out only a gentle, safe amount of electricity — 1.5 volts. Bigger devices sometimes use bigger batteries, and a phone has a flat battery hidden inside that can be charged again and again. But all batteries have one thing in common: after a while their energy runs out, and they must be recharged or replaced.

concept-6-mains-electricity-strong-power.explanation:
Mains electricity is the electricity that comes out of the sockets in the wall. It is very strong — much, much stronger than a battery. Big devices like fridges, televisions, and electric cookers plug into the mains because they need a lot of power. Mains electricity travels to houses through thick wires and cables, sometimes from a large power station far away, and sometimes from a town generator.

Because mains electricity is so strong, it is also very dangerous. It is strong enough to hurt a person very badly, or even worse. This is the most important thing to remember in this whole unit: you must never, ever put anything into a wall socket, and you must never use mains electricity for experiments. Only grown-ups should plug things in and unplug them. We will talk much more about safety very soon.

we01.solution:
Worked Example 1. Idris has one AA battery. How many volts does it give? We know one AA battery gives 1.5 volts. So the answer is 1.5 volts. That was an easy one, but every good scientist starts with the simple case first.

Worked Example 2. Now Idris joins two AA batteries end to end, the bump of one touching the flat of the next. When we join batteries this way, their pushes add together. So we work it out step by step: one battery gives 1.5 volts, and a second battery adds another 1.5 volts. We add them: 1.5 + 1.5 = 3 volts. Two batteries together push harder than one, which is why the bulb often shines brighter with two batteries.

Worked Example 3. Halima wants to know how many volts three AA batteries give when joined end to end. We add one more 1.5 to our answer above: 1.5 + 1.5 + 1.5 = 4.5 volts. Notice the pattern — each battery we add gives another 1.5 volts. Counting in steps of 1.5 is good maths practice and good science at the same time.

Worked Example 4. Omar has a torch that needs 3 volts to work. How many AA batteries does he need? Since one battery gives 1.5 volts, and 1.5 + 1.5 = 3, he needs two AA batteries. Working backwards like this — starting from the answer we want and finding the batteries we need — is exactly how grown-up engineers plan real devices.

outcomes: Explain that Earth spins (rotates) on its axis, and that this spinning gives us day and night.
Describe how the Sun appears to move across the sky from east to west, and explain why it only *appears* to move.
Tell the story of a day: sunrise in the east, the high midday sun, and sunset in the west.
Observe and describe how shadows change in length and direction through the day.

Understand that when it is day where you live, it is night on the other side of Earth.

Use the Sun and shadows to help you find direction and guess the time.

concept-1-earth-is-a-giant-spinning-ball.explanation:
Let us start with something surprising. When you stand still in your yard, it feels like you are not moving at all. The ground feels solid and steady under your feet. But the truth is amazing: you are moving right now, very fast, because the whole Earth is spinning. Earth is a giant ball, and it turns around and around, like a football spinning on the tip of a finger, or like a spinning top that a child sets going.

Earth is so enormous, and it spins so smoothly, that you cannot feel it moving at all. Think of riding in a smooth car or a boat on calm water. If you close your eyes, you can hardly tell you are moving. Earth is like that, but much, much bigger and smoother. It takes Earth one whole day — 24 hours — to spin around one time.

Now here is the important part. The Sun shines its light on Earth from one side, like a very bright lamp. But a ball can only be lit on one side at a time. The side of Earth that faces the Sun is bright — that side is having day. The side that faces away from the Sun is dark — that side is having night. As Earth keeps spinning, your town is carried around from the dark side into the light, and then later back into the dark again.

So when the sun rises in the morning, the Sun is not really climbing up into the sky. Instead, your part of Earth is turning to face the Sun. And when the sun sets in the evening, the Sun is not really going down. Instead, your part of Earth is turning away from the Sun. This is the big secret of day and night. Read it one more time slowly, because it is the most important idea in the whole unit: day and night happen because Earth spins.

It is easy to believe the Sun is the thing that moves, because that is exactly how it looks from where you stand. For a very long time, wise people everywhere believed the Sun travelled around the Earth. But good scientists learned to look more carefully, to test their ideas, and to change their minds when they found the truth. This is a wonderful lesson for you as a young scientist: the way something *looks* is not always the way it really *is*. That is why we do experiments and think hard, instead of just believing the first thing we see. In this unit you will practise looking beyond what your eyes tell you, to understand what is truly happening in the sky above your town.

Did You Know? Earth is spinning so fast that a town near the middle of Earth, like Mogadishu or Nairobi, is carried along at over 1,600 kilometres every hour — faster than an aeroplane! You do not feel it because everything around you is moving smoothly together.

concept-2-why-the-sun-seems-to-travel-ac.explanation:
Go outside in the morning (but remember — never look straight at the Sun!). Notice where the Sun is. In the early morning, the Sun is low in the sky in the east. That is the direction of the sunrise, out over the Indian Ocean if you live on the coast. Later, in the middle of the day, the Sun is high up, almost straight above your head. By the evening, the Sun is low again, but now in the west, and it slowly sinks until it is gone.

It really does look like the Sun is walking across the sky, from east to west, every single day. People long ago believed the Sun truly moved around the Earth. But now we know the real answer, and it is even more wonderful: the Sun stays still, and it is Earth that is turning. Because you are standing on spinning Earth, the Sun only *appears* to move. We call this the Sun's apparent movement — apparent means 'how it looks', not 'what is really happening'.

Here is a way to feel this for yourself. Sit on a chair that can turn around, in the middle of a room. Look at a lamp or a window. Now slowly turn the chair around. What happens? The lamp seems to slide across in front of you and move around the room — but you know the lamp did not move at all. You moved. The Sun in the sky is just like that lamp. It looks like it moves, but really you and all of Earth are turning.

Did You Know? The Sun always rises in the east and sets in the west, everywhere on Earth — in Hargeisa, in Dar es Salaam, in Kampala, and in every country in the world. Travellers and sailors have used this for thousands of years to find their way.

concept-3-the-story-of-shadows.explanation:
A shadow is a dark shape that appears when something blocks the light. Light from the Sun travels in straight lines. When your body, or a tree, or a house stands in the way, the light cannot pass through you, so a dark shape falls on the ground behind you. That dark shape is your shadow. You need three things to make a shadow: a light source (the Sun), an object to block the light (like you), and a surface for the shadow to fall on (like the ground or a wall).

The most exciting thing about shadows is that they change through the day, and they change in a pattern you can predict. Let us follow a shadow from morning to evening. Imagine Amina places a straight stick in the sand in her yard in Garissa and watches its shadow all day.

In the early morning, the Sun is low in the east. When the Sun is low, shadows are very long. Amina's stick makes a long shadow that stretches far across the ground, pointing toward the west, away from the Sun. At midday, the Sun is high overhead. When the Sun is high, shadows are very short. Now the stick's shadow is tiny, just a small dark patch at its feet. In the late afternoon, the Sun is low again in the west, and the shadow grows long again, but now it points toward the east.

Can you see the pattern? Shadows are long in the morning, short at midday, and long again in the evening. And shadows always point away from the Sun. In the morning the Sun is in the east, so shadows point west. In the evening the Sun is in the west, so shadows point east. Once you know this pattern, a shadow can tell you roughly what time of day it is — it is like a clock made of sunlight.

Did You Know? Long ago, people built clever shadow clocks called sundials. A sundial is just a stick that casts a shadow onto marked lines. As the Sun moves across the sky, the shadow moves across the lines and shows the time. You will build your very own sundial in the Experiments book!

concept-4-the-sun-is-a-star.explanation:
When you look up on a clear night, far from the town lights, you can see thousands of tiny points of light. Those are stars. A star is a huge ball of hot, glowing gas that makes its own light. The stars look tiny to us only because they are unbelievably far away.

Here is a surprise: our Sun is a star too! The Sun does not look like the tiny stars of the night. It looks big and bright and warm. Why? Because the Sun is the closest star to Earth. All the other stars are so far away that they shrink to little dots, but the Sun is our neighbour, so we can feel its heat and see its bright light filling the whole sky.

The Sun is far bigger than Earth — so big that more than a million Earths could fit inside it. And it is very, very far away, so far that even the fastest aeroplane could never reach it. Yet its light and warmth cross all that space to reach us. Every plant that grows — the mango trees, the maize, the grass the cattle eat — uses the Sun's light to make its food. Without the Sun there would be no light, no warmth, no plants, and no life. The Sun is the most important thing in our sky.

concept-6-hot-days-cool-nights-and-the-s.explanation:
You have surely noticed that the middle of the day is hot, but the night can feel surprisingly cool, especially in the dry, semi-arid land away from the coast. Why? During the day, the Sun pours its warmth onto the ground and heats it up. At night, your part of Earth is turned away from the Sun, so no new warmth arrives, and the heat slowly escapes into the sky. That is why nights in the desert can feel cold even after a very hot day. A wise family keeps a blanket ready even in a hot land.

Over a whole year, the weather also changes in a pattern we call the seasons. In East Africa we do not have deep snow and ice like some cold countries. Instead we have times of rain and times of dryness — the long rains, the short rains, and the dry season. These seasons come because Earth travels all the way around the Sun once each year, and this long journey slowly changes the weather and the length of the daylight. Farmers watch the seasons closely to know when to plant their crops, and herders move their animals to find fresh grass and water. You will learn much more about seasons and Earth's yearly journey when you are a little older.

Near the middle of Earth, close to the imaginary line called the equator, the Sun climbs very high and its light is strong and direct. This is why the sun in East Africa feels so powerful, and why it is so important to wear a hat, stay in the shade during the hottest hours, and drink plenty of clean, safe water. The same strong sun that can tire you out is also a gift: it can be used to dry clothes and food quickly, and special solar panels can catch its energy to make electricity, even in a village far from any power line.
concept-6-hot-days-cool-nights-and-the-s.example: Did You Know? Muslims all over the world use the Moon and the Sun to keep time for worship. The five daily prayers follow the Sun's position — Fajr near sunrise, Dhuhr after midday, and Maghrib right at sunset. And the month of Ramadan is found by watching for the thin crescent Moon. Watching the sky has always helped people order their days.

concept-1-everything-is-made-from-materi.explanation:
Before we can mix materials, we must know what a material is. A material is simply what an object is made from. Your spoon is made from metal. Your cup might be made from plastic or clay. The canjeero on your plate is made from flour, water, and a little salt. Water itself is a material. Sand is a material. Sugar and salt are materials. When we talk about mixing, we are talking about putting two or more materials together.

Every material has properties. Properties are the things you notice about a material — its colour, whether it is hard or soft, rough or smooth, whether you can pour it, and whether it dissolves in water. When Amina looks at a handful of dry rice, she notices it is hard, small, and pale. When she looks at cooking oil, she notices it is yellow, slippery, and can be poured. Noticing properties carefully is the first skill of a good scientist.
concept-1-everything-is-made-from-materi.example: Materials come in different states. A solid like a stone or a grain of rice holds its own shape. A liquid like water or camel milk flows and takes the shape of whatever container you pour it into. There are also gases, like the air all around us, which spread out to fill any space. In this unit we will mostly mix solids into liquids — like stirring sugar (a solid) into tea (a liquid) — so keep these two states firmly in your mind.

concept-2-what-is-a-mixture.explanation:
A mixture is what you get when two or more materials are put together but each material still keeps its own properties. This is a very important idea, so read it again slowly. In a mixture, nothing is destroyed. The materials are simply sitting together, and if you are clever, you can take them apart again.

Imagine Hassan pours a cup of dry bariis (rice) onto a tray and finds some small stones hidden in it. The rice and the stones are now a mixture. The rice is still rice — it has not turned into stone. The stones are still stones. They are just mixed up together. Because each one keeps its own properties (the stones are hard and heavy, the rice is light and edible), Hassan can separate them again by picking the stones out, one by one, the way his grandmother does before every meal.

Here are more mixtures from daily life in East Africa. Sand and small shells on the beach at Lamu are a mixture. Tea leaves floating in hot water are a mixture. A handful of mixed beans and lentils is a mixture. Muddy water from the well, where dust and soil float in the water, is a mixture. Even the air you breathe is a mixture of different gases! Once you understand mixtures, you start to see them everywhere.

Some mixtures are easy to see, and some are harder. In a mixture of rice and beans, you can clearly see the two different materials sitting side by side. We call this a mixture you can see the parts of. But when Khadija stirs salt into water, the salt seems to disappear, and the water still looks clear. You cannot see the separate parts any more — yet the salt is still there, hiding in the water. This special kind of mixture, where a solid disappears into a liquid, has its own name, and that is our next big idea.
concept-2-what-is-a-mixture.example: Did You Know? The Indian Ocean water at Kismaayo and Mombasa is a giant salty mixture. Sea water is a solution of salt and other minerals in water. If you left a shallow dish of sea water in the hot sun, the water would evaporate and leave real salt crystals behind — the same way sea salt is made!

concept-3-dissolving-and-solutions.explanation:
When you stir a spoon of sugar into a hot cup of shaah, something wonderful happens. At first you can see the white grains sitting at the bottom. But as you stir, the grains get smaller and smaller until — they are gone! The sugar has dissolved. Dissolving is when a solid breaks up into pieces so tiny that you cannot see them any more, and they spread evenly all through the liquid.

It is very important to understand this: the sugar has not disappeared from the world. It has not been destroyed. It is still there, floating in tiny hidden pieces throughout the tea. How do we know? Because the whole cup of tea now tastes sweet, from the top to the bottom. Your tongue is the proof that the sugar is still there. When a solid dissolves completely in a liquid like this, the clear mixture we are left with is called a solution. Sweet tea is a solution of sugar in water.

A material that can dissolve is called soluble. Sugar is soluble in water. Salt is soluble in water. A material that does not dissolve is called insoluble. Sand is insoluble — stir it into water as long as you like and it will always sink back to the bottom, still as sand. Cooking oil is insoluble too — it floats on top of water in a separate yellow layer and never mixes in. Flour is only partly soluble; it makes the water go cloudy and slowly sinks, which is why canjeero batter must be stirred and is thick and cloudy, not clear.

So, why do some things dissolve and others do not? At the tiniest level, water is very good at pulling apart the pieces of sugar and salt and surrounding each tiny piece. But water cannot pull apart the pieces of sand or oil, so those materials stay whole and separate. You do not need to remember all the tiny details yet — just remember the pattern: sugar and salt dissolve, sand and oil do not.

Sometimes a solid dissolves quickly, and sometimes it takes a long time. Three things change the speed of dissolving, and you can test each one at home:

Heat. Sugar dissolves much faster in hot tea than in cold water. The warmer the liquid, the faster the dissolving. This is why your mother adds sugar while the tea is still hot.

Stirring. When you stir with a spoon, the solid dissolves faster. Stirring moves the tiny pieces away and lets fresh water reach the solid. If you never stir, dissolving takes much longer.

Grain size. A spoon of fine, powdery sugar dissolves faster than one big lump of sugar. Smaller pieces have more surface touching the water, so they break apart more quickly.
concept-3-dissolving-and-solutions.example: Understanding these three helpers — heat, stirring, and small grains — lets you dissolve things quickly when you want to, and it also teaches you how to plan a careful fair test, which you will learn about soon.

concept-4-separating-mixtures.explanation:
Because a mixture is only materials sitting together, we can nearly always pull them apart again. This is called separating a mixture. The clever part of science is choosing the right method for each mixture. The method you choose depends on how the materials are different from each other — are they different sizes? Is one a solid floating in a liquid? Is one dissolved? Let us look at four important methods, all of which you can try safely at home.

A sieve is a tool with many small holes, like the kitchen sieve your family uses for flour. Small pieces fall through the holes, while big pieces are too large and stay behind. Sieving works when the materials in your mixture are different sizes.

For example, imagine Maryam has a bowl of flour with hard lumps in it. She pours it through a sieve. The fine, soft flour falls through the little holes into the bowl below, but the big lumps cannot fit through the holes, so they are left behind in the sieve. Now she has smooth flour ready for baking. Farmers use giant sieves to separate grain from bits of stalk, and builders sieve sand to remove pebbles before mixing cement.

Method 2: Filtering (Solid Out of a Liquid)

Filtering means pouring a mixture through a cloth or paper that has holes far too small to see. The liquid trickles through the tiny holes, but solid pieces that are floating in the liquid are caught and left behind. Filtering is perfect for taking solid bits out of a liquid.

Think about muddy water carried up from the well. It is a mixture of water and tiny bits of soil. If Yusuf pours this muddy water slowly through a clean, folded cloth, the water passes through and comes out much clearer, while the mud and dirt stay trapped in the cloth. Filtering does not make water safe to drink all by itself — the water must still be boiled to kill germs — but filtering is an important first step to remove the dirt you can see. This is real, life-saving science used across East Africa.

Method 3: Evaporation (Getting a Dissolved Solid Back)

What if a solid has dissolved and you cannot see it any more? A sieve is useless — the salt in salty water is far too small to catch. A filter is useless too — the dissolved salt slips straight through with the water. To get a dissolved solid back, we use evaporation.

When a liquid is left in a warm, sunny place, it slowly turns into a gas (water vapour) and floats away into the air. This is called evaporating. But here is the clever part: the dissolved solid cannot evaporate. It is left behind! So if Zahra leaves a shallow dish of salty water in the hot sun, day after day the water evaporates until, at last, only dry salt crystals remain in the dish. The water has gone into the air, but the salt could not follow it, so it stayed. This is exactly how people have made salt from sea water for thousands of years along the coasts of the Indian Ocean.

Some heavy solids do not dissolve and simply sink to the bottom if you leave the mixture still. This is called settling. When Idris brings home a bucket of muddy water and lets it stand quietly for a few hours, the heavy soil slowly sinks and gathers at the bottom, while cleaner water rises to the top. Then he can carefully pour off the clear water on top into another container, leaving the mud behind. Pouring off the clear liquid gently like this is called decanting. Settling and decanting are often used before filtering, to remove the heaviest dirt first.

Now you know four methods. The secret to being a good materials detective is asking: How are these materials different? If they are different sizes, sieve them. If a solid is floating in a liquid, filter it. If a solid is dissolved, evaporate the liquid. If a heavy solid can sink, let it settle and decant. Match the method to the mixture, and you can separate almost anything.
concept-4-separating-mixtures.example: Did You Know? The way you clean muddy well water at home — settle, then filter, then boil — is a small version of what huge water-treatment plants do for whole cities. Engineers use the very same ideas of settling, filtering, and cleaning, just with enormous tanks. The science you learn in your kitchen is the same science that keeps a city healthy.

concept-5-being-a-fair-scientist-fair-te.explanation:
When scientists want to find something out, they do a fair test. A fair test is an investigation where you change only one thing and keep everything else exactly the same. This is the only way to be sure what caused your result. If you change many things at once, you can never be certain which change made the difference.

Imagine Sahra wants to find out whether sugar dissolves faster in hot water or cold water. To be fair, she must use the same amount of sugar in each cup, the same amount of water in each cup, and stir the same number of times. The only thing she is allowed to change is the temperature of the water — hot in one cup, cold in the other. Now, if the sugar dissolves faster in the hot cup, she knows for certain that the heat made the difference, because heat was the only thing she changed.
concept-5-being-a-fair-scientist-fair-te.example: In a fair test there are three kinds of things to think about. The thing you change on purpose (here, the temperature). The thing you measure or watch (here, how long the sugar takes to dissolve). And the things you keep the same to be fair (the amount of sugar, the amount of water, and the stirring). Good scientists plan all three before they begin. Doing this makes your discoveries trustworthy — and being truthful and careful is a value that Islam praises highly.

concept-6-some-changes-can-be-undone.explanation:
Here is a thought that surprises many young scientists. When you mix materials or dissolve them, you have not made a brand-new substance. You have only put things together, and most of the time you can take them apart again and get the very same materials back. A change that you can undo like this is called a reversible change. Mixing and dissolving are both reversible changes, and this is exactly why separating works so well.

Think about the salt experiment. When Zahra dissolves salt in water, she seems to lose the salt. But by evaporating the water, she gets her salt back, exactly as it was. Nothing was destroyed and nothing new was made. The change was reversed. In the same way, when Grandmother mixes rice and beans, she can un-mix them; when Yusuf muddies water with soil, he can settle and filter it clean again. Because these changes are reversible, the materials never lose their own properties.

Not every change in the world is reversible, though. When bread dough is baked into canjeero over the fire, or when an egg is cooked, you cannot turn it back into the runny batter or the raw egg again. Those are irreversible changes, and they make a truly new material. But in this unit, the mixing, dissolving, and separating you study are all reversible — and that is the good news that makes a materials detective's job possible. If mixing destroyed materials forever, no one could ever separate them.
