outcomes: By the end of this unit, you will be able to:
Name and point to the major organs of your body: the brain, heart, lungs, stomach, intestines, and skeleton.
Explain the main job of each of these organs in simple, clear words.
Describe how organs work together as teams, or systems, to keep you alive.
Find and measure your own pulse and count your breathing rate at rest and after moving.
Explain how exercise changes your heartbeat and your breathing, and why this happens.
Name several healthy habits — good food, exercise, clean water, cleanliness, and rest — that keep your organs strong.
Use the correct science words such as organ, pulse, oxygen, nutrients, and digest when you talk about your body.
Here are the important words for this unit. You will meet them again and again, so learn them well. Try using each one in a sentence with your family.
A special part of your body that has its own important job.

concept-1-the-brain-the-control-center.explanation:
Your brain sits inside your head, protected by the hard bone of your skull like a precious egg inside a strong shell. The brain is the boss of your whole body. It is the control center, a little like the person who directs everything at a busy port in Berbera, telling every ship where to go. Everything you think, remember, feel, and decide happens in your brain. When you remember the way from your home to the mosque, that is your brain. When you feel happy hearing your mother's voice, that is your brain. When you solve a hard sum, that is your brain working.

Your brain does something even more amazing: it sends and receives messages to every other part of your body, faster than you can blink. When you decide to kick a football, your brain sends a message down to your leg muscles telling them to move. When you touch something hot, your skin sends a message racing up to your brain, and your brain quickly tells your hand to pull away. These messages travel along thin threads called nerves, which spread through your whole body like the branches of a great acacia tree. Your brain never truly switches off. Even while you are fast asleep, it keeps your heart beating and your lungs breathing.

Your brain is soft, a little like a firm jelly, so it needs to be kept very safe. That is why it sits inside the hard bone of your skull. When you climb, run, or play, your skull protects your precious brain from bumps. This is one reason why we are taught to be careful and to look after our heads. Your brain is also greedy for two things: oxygen from the air you breathe and nutrients from the food you eat. If your brain does not get enough of these, you feel dizzy or find it hard to think clearly. This is why eating a good breakfast, such as anjero with a little honey, or drinking camel milk in the morning, helps you concentrate at your lessons.

How can you keep your brain healthy and strong? You exercise it just like a muscle. Every time you read, solve a puzzle, memorise a verse, or learn something new, your brain grows stronger and cleverer. Sleep is also very important, because while you sleep your brain tidies up everything you learned during the day and stores your memories safely. Boys and girls your age need plenty of sleep each night so their brains can grow well. Curiosity and wondering about the world — asking how and why things work — is exactly what your brain loves most, and it is also a beautiful way to reflect on the wonders of creation.
concept-1-the-brain-the-control-center.example: Did You Know? Your brain uses more energy than any other organ in your body, even though it is not very big. It uses about one fifth of all the energy your food gives you — just for thinking, remembering, and controlling your body!

concept-2-the-heart-the-tireless-pump.explanation:
Make a fist with your hand and look at it. Your heart is about the same size as your own fist, and it sits in the middle of your chest, tilted a little to the left. Your heart is a strong muscle, and its job is to pump blood all around your body, day and night, without ever taking a rest. It works like a hard-working water pump at a village well, pushing water through pipes to everyone who needs it. Instead of water, your heart pushes blood through tiny tubes that reach every corner of your body.

Why is blood so important? Because your blood is like a delivery truck driving on the roads between Nairobi and Mombasa. It carries oxygen from your lungs and nutrients from your food, and it delivers them to every part of you — your muscles, your bones, even the tips of your toes. On the way back, it collects the waste your body does not need and carries it away to be cleaned out. Every part of you needs this delivery to stay alive, and that is why your heart can never stop, not even for one moment. Each thump of your heart is one delivery of fresh blood pushed out to your body.

The blood travels along tubes called blood vessels, which are like the roads and paths that carry the delivery trucks. Some blood vessels are wide, like the big road into Mombasa, and some are thinner than a hair. Together they make a huge network that reaches every single corner of you. When you press two fingers on your wrist and feel a soft tapping, you are feeling your blood being pushed along by each heartbeat. We call this tapping your pulse, and every time you feel one tap, your heart has just squeezed once.

concept-3-the-lungs-the-air-balloons.explanation:
You have two lungs, one on each side of your chest, and they feel soft and spongy like two big balloons. Their job is to help you breathe. When you breathe in, air rushes down your throat and fills your lungs, and they get bigger. When you breathe out, the air leaves and your lungs get smaller. Put your hands on the sides of your chest and take a deep breath — can you feel your chest grow bigger as your lungs fill with air?

But why do we breathe at all? The air around us contains a special gas called oxygen. Every tiny part of your body needs oxygen to live and work, just as a fire needs air to keep burning. Your lungs are clever: they take the oxygen out of the air you breathe in and pass it into your blood. Then your heart pumps that oxygen-rich blood all around your body. At the same time, your lungs do the opposite job too. Your body makes a waste gas called carbon dioxide, and your blood carries it back to your lungs so you can push it out when you breathe out. So every breath is really two jobs at once: bringing in the good gas, oxygen, and getting rid of the waste gas, carbon dioxide.

Your lungs and your heart are the very best of friends, and they work side by side in your chest. The lungs collect the oxygen, and the heart delivers it. One cannot do its job without the other. This is why, when you run fast, both your breathing and your heartbeat speed up together — your body is calling for more oxygen, so your lungs pull in more air and your heart pumps faster to deliver it. When you rest, they both slow down again, calm and steady.

Because your lungs breathe in the air around you, the kind of air you breathe really matters. Clean, fresh air keeps your lungs pink and healthy. Smoky air from fires, dusty air, or the smoke from cigarettes can harm your lungs and make it harder to breathe. This is why we should sit away from smoke and enjoy fresh air whenever we can — a walk by the sea, a morning breeze, or the clean air after the rains. Taking slow, deep breaths of fresh air is a lovely way to help your lungs and to feel calm.
concept-3-the-lungs-the-air-balloons.example: Did You Know? You breathe in and out about 20,000 times every single day, and you almost never have to think about it. This is why clean, fresh air matters so much — the coastal wind by the Indian Ocean is lovely and fresh for your lungs.

concept-4-the-stomach-and-intestines-the.example: Next, the mushy food moves into your intestines, which are very long tubes coiled up neatly inside your tummy. The intestines have a very important job: they soak up the nutrients — the goodness and energy from the food — and pass them into your blood, so your heart can deliver them everywhere. Nutrients from healthy foods like fish, dates, fruit, and milk give you the energy to run, learn, and grow strong. Whatever your body cannot use becomes waste, and it leaves your body when you go to the toilet. The small intestine is surprisingly long — if you stretched it out straight, it would be several times taller than you are!

concept-6-your-senses-how-you-know-the-w.explanation:
How do you know that the sea is blue, that anjero smells delicious, or that a goat's fur is soft? You know because of your five senses: sight, hearing, smell, taste, and touch. Your senses are the way your body gathers information about the world and sends it to your brain. Your eyes let you see, your ears let you hear, your nose lets you smell, your tongue lets you taste, and your skin lets you feel touch.

Each sense sends its messages racing along nerves to your brain, and your brain makes sense of them all. When you smell your favourite food cooking, your nose sends a message to your brain, and your brain tells you what it is and might even make your stomach feel hungry. Your senses work together to keep you safe and to help you enjoy the wonderful world around you — the call to prayer you hear, the warm sun you feel, and the sweet taste of ripe mango.

steps: Sit quietly and rest for two minutes so your heart is calm.
Turn one hand palm up. Place two fingers of your other hand gently on your wrist below your thumb. Feel the soft tapping — that is your pulse.
Count the taps for 15 seconds while watching the clock. Multiply your count by 4 to get beats per minute. Write it in the table as your resting rate.
Now march in place quickly for two minutes, lifting your knees high.
Straight away, find your pulse again and count for 15 seconds. Multiply by 4 and write it as your after exercise rate.

Put one hand on your chest. Each time your chest rises and falls counts as one breath.
Count your breaths for 30 seconds, then multiply by 2 to get breaths per minute. Write it as your resting rate.
March in place or do gentle star jumps for two minutes.
Straight away, count your breaths for 30 seconds again. Multiply by 2 and write it as your after exercise rate.

Notice how the ribs curve around from your front to your back, making a cage shape.
Take a deep breath in and feel how your ribs move outward to make room for your lungs.

we01.solution:
The idea: There are 60 seconds in one minute. Instead of counting for all 60 seconds, we count for 15 seconds. Because 15 seconds is one quarter of a minute, we multiply what we counted by 4 to find the whole minute.

Worked Example: Amina wanted to find her resting heart rate. She sat quietly, found her pulse, and counted the beats for 15 seconds using a clock. She counted 22 beats.

Step 1 — Write down what you counted. Amina counted 22 beats in 15 seconds.

Step 2 — Remember the rule. 15 seconds fits into 1 minute exactly 4 times, so we multiply by 4.

we02.prompt: Step 1 — Write down what you counted. Amina counted 22 beats in 15 seconds.
we02.solution:
Step 2 — Remember the rule. 15 seconds fits into 1 minute exactly 4 times, so we multiply by 4.

Step 3 — Do the sum. 22 x 4 = 88.

Step 4 — Write the answer with the units. Amina's heart rate is 88 beats per minute.

Now try one yourself. Hassan counted 20 beats in 15 seconds. What is his heart rate? Do the sum: 20 x 4 = 80 beats per minute. Well done! A resting heart rate for a child your age is usually somewhere between 70 and 110 beats per minute, so both Amina and Hassan are perfectly healthy.

concept-1-what-is-a-force.explanation:
A force is a push or a pull. That is the whole idea, and it is worth saying again: every force is either a push or a pull. You cannot see a force by itself, but you can always see what a force *does*. When Yusuf pushes open the wooden door of his home, you see the door swing. When Halima pulls the rope of the well, you see the bucket rise. The push and the pull are the forces; the moving door and rising bucket are what the forces do.

Forces need two objects. One object gives the force, and another object receives it. When you kick a ball, your foot is one object and the ball is the other. Your foot pushes the ball, and the ball flies away. A force is like a message passed between two things that touch or that pull on each other from a distance.

Forces can do four main jobs. First, a force can start something moving — a still ball on the grass stays still until a foot pushes it. Second, a force can stop something moving — the goalkeeper's hands stop the flying ball. Third, a force can change speed or direction — a defender can push the ball sideways so it curves. Fourth, a force can change the shape of something — when you squeeze a ripe mango, your fingers press dents into it, and when you stretch a rubber band it grows longer. Look for these four jobs everywhere and you will start to see forces you never noticed before.

Let us collect some examples from an ordinary day. Notice how each one is clearly a push or a pull:

Push: shutting a door, pressing a light switch, kicking a football, sweeping the floor with a broom, pushing a wheelbarrow of sand.

Pull: drawing water up from a well, opening a drawer, a camel pulling a loaded cart, stretching a catapult, tugging your sandal onto your foot.

Both in one action: riding a bicycle — you push the pedals down and the chain pulls the back wheel around.

🧠 Did You Know? When you sit completely still on a chair, forces are still acting on you! Gravity pulls you down, and the chair pushes you up by exactly the same amount. Because the two forces are balanced, you stay perfectly still.

The size of a force matters too. A gentle push moves a ball slowly; a hard kick sends it far. We say a force can be strong or weak. Later in this unit you will use a special spring tool called a forcemeter to measure exactly how strong a force is, in units called Newtons.

Forces also have a direction. A push always moves an object away from the pusher, and a pull always brings it closer. When Sahra sweeps the yard, she pushes the dust away from her body toward the gate. When she pulls the goat toward the shade by its rope, the goat comes closer to her. If you kick a ball to the left, it goes left; if you kick it to the right, it goes right. So every force has both a size (strong or weak) and a direction (which way it goes). Good scientists always notice both.

Sometimes two forces act on the same object at once. When they push in opposite directions and are equal in size, we say the forces are balanced, and the object does not change how it is moving — it stays still, or keeps moving steadily. When one force is bigger than the other, the forces are unbalanced, and the object speeds up, slows down, or changes direction. Think of two children playing tug-of-war with a rope: while they pull equally hard, the rope does not move. The moment one child pulls harder, the rope moves toward the stronger side. That is unbalanced forces in action, and you can see it in many games and daily tasks.

Guided Exploration — Spotting Forces at Home

Let us explore together. Walk slowly through your home in your mind and look for forces. In the kitchen, someone pushes down on dough to flatten it for canjeero, and pulls a pot toward the edge of the stove. At the door, you push it open and pull it shut. Outside, the wind pushes against washing on the line, and a child pulls a toy along on a string.
concept-1-what-is-a-force.example: For each of these, ask yourself three questions: Is it a push or a pull? Is it strong or weak? And what does the force do — does it start something, stop something, change its direction, or change its shape? When you can answer these three questions, you are truly thinking like a scientist. Try it now with five things around you, and then explain your answers to someone else. Talking about your thinking helps it grow stronger, just as walking every day makes your legs stronger.

concept-3-friction-the-force-that-slows-.explanation:
Friction is a contact force. Whenever two surfaces rub against each other, friction appears and works *against* the movement, trying to slow it down or stop it. Friction is caused by the tiny bumps and rough spots on every surface. Even a surface that looks smooth is covered in tiny hills too small for your eyes to see. When two surfaces slide past each other, all those little bumps catch and drag.

The roughness of the surface changes how much friction there is. Imagine Farah kicking a football. On smooth, packed ground the ball rolls a long way, because there is little friction. On loose sand near the coast, the same kick sends the ball only a short distance, because the rough, shifting sand grips the ball and creates a lot of friction. On grass the ball rolls somewhere in between. Same kick, different ground, different friction, different result.

Friction is not our enemy — most of the time it is a great helper. Without friction you could not walk, because your feet would slip like walking on wet soap. Friction between your sandals and the ground is what lets you push off and move forward. Friction lets you hold a cup, grip a pencil, and stop a bicycle with its brakes. The brake pads squeeze the wheel, and friction turns the movement into a stop.

When Friction Is Helpful and When It Is a Problem

Helpful — friction turns motion into a stop

We can reduce friction by making surfaces smoother or by adding a slippery layer like oil or soap — this is why a wet, soapy floor is dangerous and slippery. We can increase friction by making surfaces rougher — this is why footballers wear boots with studs to grip the pitch, and why tyres have deep grooves. A clever scientist knows when to add friction and when to take it away.

Friction also depends on how heavily an object presses down. A light empty box slides easily across the floor, but the same box filled with stones or sacks of rice is much harder to move. The heavier the object, the harder it presses on the ground, and the more the two rough surfaces grip each other. This is why a donkey pulling an empty cart in Kismaayo trots along happily, while a cart loaded with heavy goods makes the same donkey strain and pull hard. More weight means more friction, and more friction means more force is needed to move.

There is one more helpful idea about friction that you can see with your own eyes. When surfaces rub, friction turns some of the movement into heat. Rub your palms together fast and they warm up. Machines that move quickly, like the wheels of a lorry, also grow warm from friction, which is why moving parts are often oiled to keep them cool and smooth. So friction can slow things down, wear them out, and make heat — three effects all from the same simple rubbing.

concept-4-magnets-and-magnetism.explanation:
A magnet is a special object that can attract — that means pull toward itself — certain metals without touching them. This is a non-contact force. Hold a magnet a little above a steel paper clip and, when it is close enough, the clip suddenly jumps up and sticks to the magnet. The invisible pull that reaches across the gap is called magnetism.

Magnets do not attract everything. This is a very important discovery. Only a few materials are magnetic, meaning a magnet can pull them. The main magnetic materials are iron, nickel, cobalt, and steel (steel is mostly iron). Everything else is non-magnetic — a magnet has no effect on it at all. Plastic, wood, paper, glass, cloth, rubber, aluminium and copper are all non-magnetic. This is surprising because aluminium and copper are metals, yet a magnet ignores them! So remember: all magnetic materials are metals, but not all metals are magnetic.

Every magnet has two special ends called poles. One is the north pole and one is the south pole. The pull of a magnet is strongest at its poles. If you sprinkle small iron pins near a bar magnet, most of them will cluster at the two ends, because that is where the magnetism is strongest.

Now here is the most exciting rule in this whole unit. When you bring two magnets close together, something wonderful happens, and it depends on which poles face each other:

Opposite poles attract. A north pole and a south pole pull toward each other. If you let them, they will snap together.

Like poles repel. Two north poles push each other away. Two south poles also push each other away. You can feel this invisible push if you try to press two like poles together — it feels like there is a soft, springy cushion of air between them that will not let them meet.

A short way to remember this is: opposites attract, likes repel. This single rule explains compasses, many toys, and even huge machines.

🧠 Did You Know? The Earth itself is like one giant magnet with a north and a south pole. That is why a compass needle always swings to point north and south. Travellers, sailors and many Muslims use a compass to help find the qibla, the direction of prayer, when they are far from home.

A compass is simply a tiny, light magnet allowed to spin freely. Because the Earth is a giant magnet, the little compass magnet lines up with the Earth and always points the same way, north and south. Long before phones existed, this simple tool guided caravans across the desert and dhows across the Indian Ocean. It is a beautiful example of a small piece of science being useful every day.

The magnetism around a magnet fills the space near it in a shape we call the magnetic field. You cannot see this field with your eyes, but it is really there, like the warmth around a fire that you can feel without seeing. If you place a magnet under a sheet of paper and gently scatter tiny iron pins on top, the pins line up in curved paths that arc from one pole to the other. Those curved paths show you the invisible field. The field is strongest close to the poles, which is exactly where a magnet grips hardest, and it grows weaker as you move away, which is why a magnet can only pick up a pin once the pin is quite near.

concept-5-gravity-and-weight.explanation:
Gravity is a non-contact force that pulls everything toward the centre of the Earth. It is the reason a mango falls *down* from the tree and never floats up into the sky. It is the reason water pours down into your cup, the reason rain falls, and the reason you land back on the ground when you jump. Gravity is always pulling, it always pulls downward, and it never switches off.

Gravity is invisible and it acts at a distance, so it belongs to the non-contact family, just like magnetism. But unlike a magnet, gravity pulls on *everything* — stones, water, camels, people, and even the air. The bigger and heavier an object is, the more strongly gravity pulls on it.

The strength of gravity's pull on an object is called its weight. This is a special science word. Weight is a force, and because it is a force we measure it in Newtons (N), not in the everyday way. A small apple is pulled down with a force of about 1 Newton, so we say it weighs about 1 Newton. A heavier object like a full water bottle is pulled harder, so it has a larger weight.

Because gravity is always pulling down, we have to use forces to work against it every day. When Ibrahim lifts a bucket of water from the well, he is pulling up against gravity, which is pulling the water down. When Zahra carries a basket of mangoes on her head, her neck and back push up to hold the load against gravity's downward pull. Every time you climb stairs, jump, or lift anything, you are winning a small contest against gravity. And the heavier the object, the harder gravity pulls, so the more force you must use — which is why a full water container is so much harder to lift than an empty one.

Here is an idea that even grown-ups sometimes mix up, so read it slowly. Mass is how much *stuff* is inside an object — how much material it is made of. Mass never changes. Weight is how hard gravity *pulls* on that stuff, and weight can change if gravity changes.

On the Moon, gravity is much weaker than on Earth — about six times weaker. So a camel taken to the Moon would have exactly the same mass (the same amount of camel!), but it would weigh much less, because the Moon pulls on it more gently. The amount of stuff stays the same; only the pull changes. On Earth, though, we can happily use a forcemeter to measure weight in Newtons.
concept-5-gravity-and-weight.example: 🧠 Did You Know? A famous story says Sir Isaac Newton began thinking about gravity after he watched an apple fall from a tree. He wondered why it fell straight down instead of sideways or up. The unit of force, the Newton, is named after him. A small apple weighs about one Newton — how fitting!

concept-6-measuring-forces-with-a-forcem.explanation:
A forcemeter (also called a spring scale) is a tool that measures how strong a force is. Inside it there is a spring. When you hang an object on the hook, gravity pulls the object down, the spring stretches, and a pointer moves along a scale. The bigger the force, the more the spring stretches, and the higher the number the pointer shows. The numbers are marked in Newtons.

Reading a forcemeter is like reading a ruler. You look at where the pointer lines up and read the number next to it. Always read at eye level so you do not make a mistake. Let us practise with some worked examples.

Amina hangs four objects on a forcemeter, one at a time, and writes down the weight of each:

Question: Which object is the heaviest, and how much heavier is the book than the apple?

Step 1 — Find the largest number. The largest weight is 8 N, so the book is the heaviest.

Step 2 — Subtract to compare. The book is 8 N and the apple is 2 N. We take away: 8 N minus 2 N equals 6 N. So the book is 6 Newtons heavier than the apple.

Step 3 — Put them in order. From lightest to heaviest: pencil (0.5 N), apple (2 N), water bottle (5 N), book (8 N). Always check that your order goes from the smallest number to the biggest.

Omar measures the force needed to pull different objects across the floor with a forcemeter: a plastic toy needs 2 N, a wooden block needs 5 N, a heavy book needs 8 N, and a metal box needs 12 N.

Question: How much more force is needed for the metal box than for the plastic toy?

Step 1 — Pick the two numbers. Metal box = 12 N, plastic toy = 2 N.
concept-6-measuring-forces-with-a-forcem.example: Step 2 — Subtract. 12 N minus 2 N equals 10 N. So the metal box needs 10 Newtons more force. The metal box is heavier and its surface grips the floor more, so friction is greater and you must pull harder.

concept-1-is-it-living-once-living-or-no.explanation:
Before we can sort living things into groups, we must first answer a simpler question: what makes something alive? This sounds easy, but it can be tricky. A rushing river moves and a flickering fire grows, yet neither is alive. Meanwhile, a seed sitting still in the dry ground looks like it is doing nothing, yet it is very much alive. So how do scientists decide?

Scientists use a checklist of seven signs of life. If something does all seven, it is living. A helpful way to remember them is that all living things move, breathe, sense, grow, feed, get rid of waste, and reproduce (make young). Let us walk through them one by one, using animals and plants you know.

Movement — Living things can move by themselves. A goat walks, a bird flies, and even a sunflower slowly turns to face the sun.

Breathing (respiration) — Living things take in the gases they need to release energy from their food. A camel breathes air; a tilapia takes in oxygen from water through its gills.

Sensing — Living things notice and respond to the world. A gazelle hears a lion and runs; a plant's roots grow toward water.

Growth — Living things grow bigger and change. A tiny acacia seed grows into a huge thorny tree; a calf grows into a full-grown cow.

Feeding (nutrition) — Living things need food for energy. Animals eat other living things; plants make their own food from sunlight.

Getting rid of waste (excretion) — Living things remove the waste their bodies make, just as you do when you breathe out or visit the toilet.

Reproduction — Living things make more of their own kind. Camels have calves, birds lay eggs, and plants make seeds.

Now think about a rock. It never grows on its own, never feeds, never has babies. It is non-living. Think about a wooden stool or a piece of dried frankincense resin. It was once part of a living tree, but it is no longer alive. We call these things once-living. And a leather sandal, made from an animal's skin, is once-living too. Learning to tell these three groups apart is the very first skill of a living things detective.

explore-2.explanation: The Big Groups — Plants and Animals: Once we know something is alive, the next question is: what kind of living thing is it? Scientists sort all living things into large groups called kingdoms. There are several kingdoms, including tiny living things too small to see, but in Year 4 we will focus on the two you know best: the plant…

Step 3 — Feathers? No feathers are described. So it is not a bird.

Step 4 — Gills in water for its whole life? No, it comes onto the sandy bank and suns itself. So it is not a fish.

sci-g04-u03.unitOverview: Look around you right now. The cup you drink from, the sufuria your mother cooks bariis in, the water in the clay pot keeping cool in the shade, the air you are breathing this very moment — every single one of these is made of something we call a material. A material is simply what an object is made from. Your school shoes are made of rubber and cloth. A window is made of glass. A cooking pot might be made of metal or clay. In this unit you will become a materials detective, learning to look closely at the world and ask, 'What is this made of, and why was that material chosen?'
outcomes: Name and describe many properties of materials, such as hardness, flexibility, strength, transparency, whether they are waterproof, and whether they carry heat well.
Explain that every material is made of tiny particles that are too small to see.
Describe the three states of matter — solid, liquid and gas — and tell how the particles are arranged in each one.
Explain how heating and cooling can change a material from one state to another, for example ice melting into water and water boiling into steam.
Use the particle model to explain why solids keep their shape, why liquids flow and pour, and why gases spread out to fill a room.
Sort and group materials into natural materials (from nature) and manufactured materials (made by people).
Choose a suitable material for a job by matching the material's properties to what the job needs, such as choosing metal for a cooking pot or plastic for a rain cover.
Design a fair test to compare materials and record what you find in a clear table.
Here are the important words for this unit. Do not try to memorise them all at once. Come back to this table whenever you meet a word you have forgotten — that is exactly what a good scientist does.
What an object is made from.

concept-1-materials-are-all-around-you.explanation:
Let us start with something simple. Pick up any object near you. Ask yourself two questions: 'What is it made of?' and 'Why was that material chosen?' Try it with a spoon. If it is a metal spoon, it is made of metal because metal is strong, does not break easily, and can be washed again and again. If it is a wooden spoon, it is made of wood because wood does not get too hot to hold when you stir hot food. Already you can see that people choose materials on purpose, matching the material to the job.

Many objects are made from more than one material. Think about a torch. The outside case is plastic, the little window over the bulb is glass or clear plastic, the battery inside has metal ends, and the switch may be rubber. Each part uses the material that suits it best. A pencil is another example: wood on the outside because it is easy to sharpen, and a soft grey material called graphite in the middle that leaves marks on paper. Learning to spot the different materials in one object is an important skill.

Scientists like to sort materials into groups. One useful way is to ask, 'Did this come straight from nature, or did people make it?' Natural materials come from nature. Wood comes from trees such as the acacia or the mango tree. Cotton comes from the cotton plant. Wool comes from sheep. Stone, sand and clay come from the ground. Leather comes from the hide of an animal such as a goat or a cow. These materials have been used by people for thousands of years.

Manufactured materials are made or heavily changed by people, often in factories. Plastic is made from oil in a factory. Glass is made by heating sand until it melts and then letting it cool. Steel is made by heating iron rock and mixing it carefully. Concrete, used for many buildings in Mogadishu and Nairobi, is made by mixing cement, sand, small stones and water. Manufactured materials are useful because people can design them to have exactly the properties they want.

Some materials sit in between. Paper is made by people, but it comes from wood, which is natural. Clay pots are shaped and baked by people, but the clay itself is natural. That is fine — sorting is a tool to help us think, not a strict set of walls. What matters is that you can explain your reasons.

Why does this sorting matter? Because natural and manufactured materials often behave differently and cost different amounts to use. Natural materials such as wood, clay and cotton are usually easy to find nearby and gentle on the earth, but they can wear out or rot over time. Manufactured materials such as plastic and steel can be made very strong and long-lasting and shaped into exactly what is needed, but making them uses a lot of energy, and some, like plastic, take hundreds of years to break down if thrown away. When we choose materials wisely and reuse or recycle them, we are looking after the earth we were trusted to care for.
concept-1-materials-are-all-around-you.example: [*] Did You Know? The clay pot your family may use to keep water cool works because of tiny holes in the clay. A little water seeps through and evaporates on the outside surface. Evaporation takes heat away, so the water left inside stays cool — a natural fridge with no electricity at all!

concept-2-properties-of-materials.explanation:
A property is a feature of a material that you can observe or measure. Properties are the reason we choose one material over another. Let us meet the most important properties one by one, with examples from daily life.

Hardness — how well a material resists being scratched or dented. A stone is hard; a sponge is soft. A metal knife is hard enough to cut, while soft butter is not.

Strength — how much force a material can take before it breaks. A thick rope is strong; a single thread is weak. Builders need strong materials for walls and roofs.

Flexibility — how easily a material bends without breaking. A rubber band is flexible; a glass rod is stiff and will snap. A fishing line must bend, so it is flexible.

Transparency — whether light passes through. Transparent materials like clear glass let you see through them. Opaque materials like wood or metal block light completely. Some, like frosted glass, are in between and are called translucent.

Waterproof or absorbent — a waterproof material keeps water out, like a plastic sheet over goods at the market. An absorbent material soaks water up, like a cotton towel or a piece of canjeero soaking up sauce.

Heat conductor or insulator — a conductor lets heat pass through quickly. Metal is a good conductor, which is why a metal sufuria handle gets hot on the charcoal stove. An insulator does not let heat pass easily. Cloth and wood are insulators, which is why you use a cloth or a wooden handle to lift a hot pot.

Notice how each property matches a job. When your mother lifts a hot sufuria off the charcoal jiko, she wraps a folded cloth around the handle. Why cloth? Because cloth is an insulator — it does not let the heat reach her hand quickly. If she grabbed the bare metal handle, the metal, being a good conductor, would carry the heat straight to her skin. Understanding properties keeps us safe as well as helping us choose materials.

A single material usually has several properties at once. Metal, for example, is hard, strong, waterproof, and a good heat conductor. Glass is hard, transparent, and waterproof, but it is brittle, meaning it breaks easily if dropped. When we choose a material we think about all its properties together and pick the one whose mix of properties best suits the job.
concept-2-properties-of-materials.example: [*] Did You Know? Camel wool and goat hair are natural materials that trap air. Trapped air is an excellent insulator, which is why a woollen blanket keeps you warm on a cold desert night — it slows down heat leaving your body.

concept-3-the-particle-model-the-hidden-.explanation:
Now we come to one of the greatest ideas in science. Every material — solid, liquid or gas — is made of unimaginably tiny pieces called particles. They are so small that millions upon millions of them would fit onto the tip of a needle. You cannot see a single particle even with a school magnifying glass. Yet scientists are completely sure they are there, because thinking about particles explains so much about how materials behave.

Here is a helpful way to picture it. Imagine a big pile of dry rice grains, or a heap of sand from the Indian Ocean beach. From far away the pile looks like one smooth thing. But come close and you see it is made of thousands of separate grains. Particles are like that, except billions of times smaller. A drop of water is not one smooth blob — it is a crowd of countless tiny water particles too small to see, all packed together.
concept-3-the-particle-model-the-hidden-.example: The two big questions the particle model helps us answer are: How closely are the particles packed together? and How much do the particles move? The answers to these two questions are different for solids, liquids and gases — and that is exactly why the three states behave so differently. Let us look at each state in turn.

concept-4-the-three-states-of-matter.explanation:
The three states of matter are solid, liquid and gas. The very same substance can exist in all three states. Water is the perfect example, and you can find all three in your own kitchen: ice is solid water, the water you drink is liquid water, and the steam rising from a boiling sufuria is water as a gas. Let us understand each state using our particle glasses.

In a solid, the particles are packed very closely together, touching each other like people squeezed tightly in a crowded bus. They are held in fixed places and cannot move around — they can only vibrate, which means they wobble a tiny bit on the spot. Because the particles are locked in place, a solid keeps its own shape and does not flow. A stone stays a stone. A metal sufuria keeps its shape. An ice cube stays a cube until something changes it. Solids also keep the same size, or volume — you cannot squeeze a solid into a smaller space.

This is why you cannot pour a stone or a block of wood. The particles are locked together, so the whole object moves as one piece. Examples of solids all around you include wood, metal, glass, rock, ice, plastic, bone and dried beans.

In a liquid, the particles are still close together and still touching, but now they are not locked in place. They can slide and roll around each other, like a bag full of wet, slippery seeds that shift when you tip the bag. Because the particles can move past each other, a liquid can flow and pour, and it takes the shape of whatever container you put it in. Pour water into a round pot and it becomes round; pour it into a tall cup and it becomes tall. But a liquid still keeps the same volume — a litre of milk is a litre whether it is in a bottle or a bowl. Examples of liquids include water, milk, cooking oil, honey and camel milk.

In a gas, the particles are spread far, far apart with lots of empty space between them, and they zoom around freely in every direction, bumping into things. Because the particles fly everywhere, a gas has no fixed shape and no fixed size. A gas spreads out to fill any container it is in, right to the edges. This is why the smell of frankincense or of cooking spreads to fill a whole room — the gas particles carrying the smell fly out in all directions. Air is a gas. Steam is a gas. The gas that burns on a charcoal stove is a gas. Because there is so much empty space between the particles, a gas can also be squeezed into a smaller space, which is how air is packed into a football or a bicycle tyre.

Here is a simple way to remember the three states, using how tightly the particles are held: solid particles are like children holding hands tightly in a fixed ring, liquid particles are like children milling about in a crowd but still touching shoulders, and gas particles are like children running freely all over an open field.
concept-4-the-three-states-of-matter.example: [*] Did You Know? Air feels like nothing, but it is really matter — it has weight and takes up space. A large room full of air holds several kilograms of air, about the weight of a big water container. You do not feel it because it presses on you evenly from all sides.

concept-6-changing-state-heating-and-coo.explanation:
One of the most exciting things about materials is that they can change from one state to another. A solid can become a liquid, a liquid can become a gas, and it can all happen in reverse too. What causes these changes? The answer is heat energy. Heating adds energy and makes particles move faster; cooling removes energy and makes particles slow down. Let us follow water as it changes, because you can watch every step of this in your own home on the charcoal stove.

Take an ice cube out of the freezer and leave it on a plate in the warm air. Soon it turns to a puddle of water. This change from solid to liquid is called melting. What is happening to the particles? The warm air gives the ice particles more energy. They begin to vibrate harder and harder until they break free from their fixed places and start to slide around each other. The solid has become a liquid. Ice melts at zero degrees Celsius. Different solids melt at different temperatures — butter and chocolate melt in gentle warmth, but metal needs to be extremely hot before it melts.

Now do the opposite. Put liquid water into the freezer. As it cools, the particles lose energy and move more slowly, until they can no longer slide around and they lock into fixed places. The liquid has become a solid. This change is called freezing. Freezing is simply the reverse of melting, and for water it happens at the same temperature, zero degrees Celsius. Cooling removes energy; heating adds it. Melting and freezing are two sides of the same coin.

Leave a wet cloth in the hot sun, or a small puddle on the ground after washing, and after a while it dries. Where did the water go? It changed into an invisible gas called water vapour and floated away into the air. This slow change from liquid to gas is called evaporation. Evaporation happens faster when it is hot, windy, or when the water is spread out thinly. When you heat water much more strongly, on the charcoal stove for instance, it boils: bubbles of gas form quickly and you see steam rising. In both cases the fast-moving particles at the surface gain enough energy to escape from the liquid and fly off as a gas.

Hold a cold metal spoon or a cold glass near the steam rising from a boiling pot, and tiny drops of water appear on it. The gas has turned back into a liquid. This change from gas to liquid is called condensation. It happens when a gas is cooled. The steam particles hit the cold surface, lose energy, slow down and join together into liquid drops. You see the same thing when droplets form on the outside of a cold cup of water on a warm day — water vapour from the air condenses on the cold glass.

Notice a wonderful pattern: these changes are reversible. Ice can melt to water, and water can freeze back to ice. Water can evaporate to vapour, and vapour can condense back to water. No new material is made — it is still water all the way through, just wearing a different 'coat'. Heating and cooling are like an on-and-off switch that moves the same particles between being packed, being loose, and being far apart.

The Golden Rule of Changing State Heating adds energy — particles move more and spread out — solid to liquid to gas. Cooling removes energy — particles move less and pack together — gas to liquid to solid.

outcomes: By the end of this unit, you will be able to:
Describe the three main layers of the Earth — the crust, the mantle and the core — and say what each layer is made of.
Explain how scientists use models to understand the inside of the Earth, and why a model is never a perfect copy of the real thing.
Describe how a volcano forms and name its main parts: the vent, the crater, the lava and the ash.
Explain what causes an earthquake and how the shaking travels as waves to the surface.
Describe how earthquakes under the sea can cause a tsunami (a giant sea wave).
Explain how animals and plants are suited to their habitat, using local examples such as the savanna, the coral reef and the mangrove.
Connect the Earth's hot inside layers to the volcanoes and earthquakes we see at the surface.
Here are the important words for this unit. Read them now, and come back to this table whenever you meet a word you have forgotten.
The thin, solid outer layer of the Earth where we live, made of rock.

concept-1-the-structure-of-the-earth.explanation:
You already know quite a lot about the outside of the Earth. It is made of rocks, soil, sand, mountains, and the salty water of the seas and oceans. Scientists call this the Earth's external structure — 'external' just means 'outside'. When you walk across the savanna near Garissa, or feel the sand of the Indian Ocean coast at Kismaayo, you are touching the external structure of the Earth.

But what about the parts we cannot see — the parts deep inside the Earth? These make up the Earth's internal structure ('internal' means 'inside'). Here is a big problem for scientists: nobody can cut the Earth in half to look inside! The deepest hole that humans have ever drilled goes down only about 12 km, and yet the Earth is thousands of kilometres deep. So how can we possibly know what is down there?

The answer is that scientists use a model. A model is a way of showing or explaining something that we cannot easily see. You use models all the time without knowing it. A toy camel is a model of a real camel. A drawing of your house is a model of your house. Models help us understand and picture things — but a model is never a perfect, true copy of the real thing. A toy camel cannot walk, chew or give milk!

To imagine the inside of the Earth, think about a peach (or a mango, which may be easier to find near you). A whole mango has smooth skin on the outside. But if you cut it open, you see it has different layers inside: the soft juicy fruit, and then the hard stone in the very middle. The Earth is a little bit like this. It has a thin skin on the outside and different layers hidden inside, all the way down to a hard centre. Cutting the mango is a model that helps us picture what we would see if we could slice the Earth in half.

Did You Know? The temperature inside the Earth gets hotter and hotter the deeper you go. This is why deep gold mines in Africa are extremely hot to work in — the miners are getting closer to the Earth's burning-hot inside!

Scientists tell us the Earth has three main layers. Let us travel from the top all the way down to the centre.

1. The Crust. This is the thin, solid outer layer where we live. It is made of rock. Even though it feels enormous to us, the crust is really very thin compared to the whole Earth — a bit like the thin skin on the mango. Under the oceans the crust is only about 5 km thick. Under the land it is thicker, about 70 km. At the surface the crust is a comfortable temperature, around 20 degrees Celsius, but deep down at the bottom of the crust it reaches about 400 degrees Celsius.

2. The Mantle. Below the crust is the mantle, and it is very thick — about 3000 km deep. Try to imagine a journey of 3000 km; that is much further than driving from Mogadishu all the way to Cairo! The rocks in the mantle have been heated so much that they have softened and partly melted. This melted rock is called magma, and it can slowly move and flow, almost like very thick honey. Here the temperature rises to about 1000 degrees Celsius.

3. The Core. Right in the centre is the core, about 3400 km thick. The core is not made of rock — it is made of the metals iron and nickel. The core has two parts. The outer core is so hot that the metal is liquid and runny. The inner core is squeezed so tightly by the weight of all the layers pressing down on it that, even though it is unbelievably hot, it stays solid. For a long time scientists thought the inner core was about 5000 degrees Celsius. Then, in 2014, scientists used new equipment in a laboratory and discovered it is closer to 6000 degrees Celsius — that is as hot as the surface of the Sun!

Did You Know? Notice how scientists changed their answer about the core in 2014. This is a wonderful example of how science works. When scientists find better tools and new evidence, they are happy to update what they know. Being ready to learn something new is a sign of a good scientist — and a good student!

You might still be wondering: if nobody can go down to the core, how do scientists feel so sure about these layers? They are like clever detectives. They cannot see the hidden layers, but they can study the clues that the Earth gives them. One important clue comes from earthquakes. When a big earthquake happens, it sends waves of energy right through the whole planet. These waves travel at different speeds through solid rock, softened rock and liquid metal, and they bend and bounce as they pass from one layer to another. By carefully measuring these waves as they come out on the other side of the Earth, scientists can work out what the hidden layers must be made of — just as you might guess what is inside a wrapped gift by shaking it and listening. Another clue is the rock and magma that volcanoes bring up from below, which lets scientists study a real piece of the mantle without digging.
concept-1-the-structure-of-the-earth.example: Here is a way to picture all three layers at once. Imagine the Earth is a hard-boiled egg. The thin, cracked eggshell is the crust. The thick white part is the mantle. And the yellow yolk in the middle is the core. Just like a peach or a mango, this egg is only a model — the real Earth is far more amazing and much, much hotter — but it helps you remember the order of the layers: crust on the outside, mantle in the middle, core at the centre.

concept-2-volcanoes.explanation:
Now that you know there is hot, melted magma inside the mantle, you can understand volcanoes. Sometimes a big crack develops in the Earth's crust. Because the magma below is under great pressure, it pushes its way up through that crack. When the magma finally bursts out onto the surface, we say the volcano erupts. Once the magma has reached the surface and is flowing in the open air, we give it a new name: lava. It is the same red-hot rock, just with a different name depending on whether it is inside the Earth (magma) or outside (lava).

This is the exciting link between Part 1 and Part 2: a volcano is the hot inside of the Earth reaching the surface. When you watch a video of glowing lava, you are actually looking at a piece of the mantle that has escaped from deep inside our planet.

Why does the magma push upwards at all? Think about what happens when you squeeze the bottom of a tube of toothpaste: the paste has nowhere to go but up and out of the opening. In a similar way, the weight of all the rock pressing down on the magma, together with gases trapped inside it, puts the magma under enormous pressure. When a weak crack appears in the crust above, the squeezed magma rushes up through it, just like the toothpaste out of the tube. The trapped gases can make the eruption sudden and explosive, throwing ash and rock high into the sky.

Let us name the main parts of a volcano so you could label a diagram:

Magma chamber — a large pool of magma stored deep underground.

Vent — the central pipe or tube that the magma travels up through to reach the surface.

Crater — the bowl-shaped hole at the very top, where the vent widens and the material bursts out.

Lava — the melted rock flowing down the sides after it erupts.

Ash — tiny bits of burnt lava that shoot into the air like grey powder.

Secondary cone — a small 'baby' volcano on the side, formed when magma pushes out through a crack in the slope.

The most common kind of volcano is a composite volcano. It is built up over many eruptions from layers of ash and layers of lava, one on top of another, like the layers of a canjeero stack. These layers form a tall, cone-shaped mountain with smooth sides. Some volcanoes are different: when very runny lava flows out, cools and hardens over and over, it builds a wide, flat shape called a volcanic plateau rather than a tall cone.

Did You Know? Mount Kilimanjaro in Tanzania, the tallest mountain in all of Africa, is a volcano! It was built up over a very long time by erupting lava and ash. Today it is quiet, and its high top is even covered with ice and snow — a frozen cap sitting on top of a mountain born from fire.

Volcanoes are not spread evenly all over the world. They mostly form where there are many cracks in the Earth's crust. The biggest set of these cracks circles the edge of the Pacific Ocean, and because so many volcanoes erupt there it has earned the name the Pacific Ring of Fire. Countries such as Indonesia, the Philippines and Japan sit along this ring and have many volcanoes.

Here in East Africa we have our own special line of cracks: the Great Rift Valley. This is a giant split in the crust that stretches for thousands of kilometres. The Earth's crust here is slowly being pulled apart, which lets magma rise up. That is why the Rift Valley is dotted with volcanoes and volcanic highlands, including Mount Kilimanjaro, Mount Kenya, and the still-active Ol Doinyo Lengai in Tanzania. Places far from any cracks, like the flat middle of a large continent, almost never have volcanoes.

You might think volcanoes only bring death and destruction. It is true that they can be very dangerous. But millions of people choose to live near volcanoes, because volcanoes also bring good things. Let us look at both sides.

The dangers: People can be injured or killed by hot lava and by hard lumps of flying rock. Lava burns and buries crops, animals and homes. Ash covers everything, and breathing in ash or poisonous volcanic gases can make people very ill.

concept-3-earthquakes.explanation:
The word 'quake' means to shake. So an earthquake is a sudden shaking of the ground. Rub your two hands together quickly right now. Can you feel them getting warm? That warmth is energy made by the two surfaces rubbing. Something similar, but on a giant scale, causes an earthquake.

Two special words help us describe an earthquake. The focus is the exact spot inside the crust where the earthquake begins — where the rocks first slip. The epicentre is the point on the surface directly above the focus. The shaking is usually strongest at the epicentre, so that is where the worst damage happens. Think of dropping a stone into a still pond: the place where the stone hits the water is like the focus, and the ripples spreading out are like the earthquake waves.

Here is another way to picture how the energy stores up and then lets go. Take a fresh green twig from a tree and slowly bend it. At first it just bends and holds, storing up the pushing energy in your hands. But if you keep bending, all of a sudden it snaps — CRACK! — and you feel the shock jump through your fingers. The rocks in the crust are like that twig. They bend and hold under pressure for years, storing energy, until at last they suddenly slip and snap, and all that stored energy shoots out as shaking waves. This is why an earthquake often comes without warning: the rocks were quietly holding their energy until the moment they gave way.

Did You Know? There are about 500,000 earthquakes around the world every single year! Most are so tiny that nobody feels them. Only about 100 each year are strong enough to cause serious damage.

Earthquakes happen in the same places as volcanoes — wherever the rocks of the crust are broken and moving. So the Pacific Ring of Fire has many earthquakes, and so does our own Great Rift Valley. People living in Nairobi, Addis Ababa and other Rift Valley towns sometimes feel small tremors. A large earthquake can also cause a landslide, which is when loose soil and mud slide down a slope and can bury roads, farms or houses below.

What happens if an earthquake occurs under the sea, on the ocean floor? The energy from the shaking passes into the water and can create a tsunami — a huge, powerful sea wave. Out in the deep ocean the wave is not very tall. But as it races toward the shore and the water becomes shallow near the coast, the wave grows taller and taller. When it finally reaches the beach it can be many metres high and floods the coastal land with terrible force.

concept-4-different-habitats.explanation: The Earth is not only rock and fire. Its surface is covered with living things, and every plant and animal lives in the place that suits it best. A habitat is the natural home of a living thing — the place where it finds the food, the water, the shelter and the space it needs to survive. Living things have special features, called adaptations, that make them suited to their own habitat.

Question: The mantle is about 3000 km deep. The ocean crust is about 5 km thick. About how many times thicker is the mantle than the ocean crust?

Step 1 — Write down what we know. Mantle depth = 3000 km. Ocean crust thickness = 5 km.

Step 2 — Decide what to do. To find out 'how many times thicker', we divide the bigger number by the smaller number.

Step 3 — Do the division. 3000 divided by 5 = 600.

concept-2-the-circuit-a-path-for-electri.explanation:
Electricity is a little like water in a pipe: it needs a proper path to flow along. The special path we build for electricity is called a circuit. The word circuit comes from the same idea as a circle, because electricity must travel all the way around a complete loop and return to where it started. If there is even one tiny gap anywhere in the loop, the electricity stops flowing at once, just as water stops if a pipe is cut.

A simple circuit needs three main things. First, a cell (or battery) to push the electricity and give it energy. Second, wires to carry the electricity along the path. Third, a component that does a useful job, such as a bulb that gives light. When you join a cell, two wires, and a bulb into a complete unbroken loop, the electricity flows and the bulb lights up. This is one of the most exciting moments in all of science, and you will make it happen with your own hands.

Imagine electricity leaving one end of the battery, travelling along a wire, passing through the bulb (where it lights up), continuing along the second wire, and returning to the other end of the battery. Round and round it goes, again and again, so quickly that the bulb glows steadily. This continuous flow is called the current. As long as the loop stays complete, the current keeps flowing and the bulb stays lit.

A complete circuit is a loop with no gaps: the bulb lights up. A broken circuit (also called an incomplete circuit) has a gap somewhere: a loose wire, a wire that is not touching the battery, or a switch that is turned off. When the circuit is broken, the current cannot flow and the bulb stays dark. Learning to spot the gap in a broken circuit is a skill electricians and engineers use every day. It is called troubleshooting.

[*] Did You Know? Electricity in a wire flows incredibly fast, close to the speed of light. That is why a lamp lights the instant you flick the switch, even though the power station may be many kilometres away.

Circuit Symbols — The Secret Code of Scientists

Drawing little pictures of batteries and bulbs takes a long time and everyone draws them differently. So scientists all around the world agreed to use the same simple circuit symbols. These symbols are a special code that any scientist, from Kismaayo to Kampala to London, can read. Here are the ones you need to know:

A cell is shown as one long thin line next to one short thick line ( -|i- ). The long line is the positive (+) end.

A battery (two or more cells) is just two or more of these cell symbols in a row.

A wire is shown as a plain straight line joining the parts.

A bulb is shown as a circle with a cross inside it (like a small round window with an X).

An open switch is shown as a line with a small gap and a lever lifted up (off). A closed switch has the lever down, closing the gap (on).

concept-6-where-electricity-comes-from.explanation:
The electricity in your circuits comes from a cell or battery, which stores energy through a safe chemical reaction inside it. But batteries are not the only source of electrical energy. Across East Africa, people use several clever ways to make electricity.

Solar panels are one of the most important. A solar panel catches the strong sunlight, which is plentiful near the equator, and turns light energy directly into electrical energy. Many homes, schools, and clinics that are far from power lines use solar panels on the roof to charge batteries during the day, then use that stored energy to light rooms and charge phones at night. This is clean, renewable energy: the sun keeps shining for free.

A dynamo turns movement energy into electricity. When you wind the handle of a hand-crank torch or radio, a dynamo inside spins and generates electricity to power the light or the sound. Large power stations make electricity for whole cities. Some burn fuel, some use the movement of falling water (hydroelectric), and some use wind turbines that spin in the coastal breeze near Berbera or Mombasa. All of these send electricity along thick cables into homes as mains electricity.

Here is the most important difference of all. The electricity from a battery has a low, safe voltage (a gentle push). The mains electricity in the wall sockets has a high, dangerous voltage (a very strong push). Low-voltage battery electricity is safe for your experiments. High-voltage mains electricity can badly injure or even kill a person. This is why every experiment you do uses only batteries, and never, ever the sockets in the wall.

Electricity and Magnetism — A Surprising Friendship

Here is a wonderful secret that scientists discovered long ago: electricity and magnetism are close friends. When electricity flows through a coiled wire, it makes the wire behave like a magnet. We call this an electromagnet. If you wrap insulated wire many times around an iron nail and connect the ends to a battery, the nail becomes magnetic and can pick up small steel objects like paper clips and pins. The moment you disconnect the battery, the magnetism disappears at once. An electromagnet is a magnet you can switch on and off, which an ordinary magnet cannot do.

This friendship between electricity and magnetism is one of the most useful ideas in all of technology. It is how an electric motor works: electricity makes magnetism, and the pushing and pulling of magnets makes the motor spin. Motors are inside fans, water pumps, toys, and many other machines. The same idea, working the other way round, is how power stations make electricity: spinning magnets create a current in coils of wire. You do not need to master all of this now, but it is exciting to know that the simple circuits you build are the first step towards understanding motors, generators, and the machines that power the modern world.

Problem: Yusuf has built a simple circuit with one 1.5V cell and one small bulb. The bulb glows, but only faintly. He wants it to shine more brightly. What can he do, and what must he be careful about?

Step 1 — Understand the cause. The brightness of a bulb depends on how much current flows through it, and the current depends on the electrical push, the voltage, from the cell. One cell gives a fairly small push, so the bulb is dim.

Step 2 — Choose a change. To increase the push, Yusuf can add a second cell in a line with the first. Two cells together give roughly twice the push of one cell, so more current will flow.

Step 3 — Predict the result. With two cells, the bulb should glow noticeably brighter than it did with one cell. This is his prediction, which he can now test.

concept-1-the-three-states-of-matter.explanation:
Let us begin with what you can see and touch. Take a look at three things you know well: an ice cube, a cup of water, and the air in the room. These are the three states of the very same substance — water — and yet they behave completely differently. Understanding why is the key that unlocks this whole unit.

A solid keeps its own shape. If you place a stone in a bowl, it stays stone-shaped. If you move it to a bucket, it is still the same shape and the same size. A solid has a definite shape and a definite volume, which means it does not spread out or squash down easily. Think of the things around your home that are solids: a metal spoon, a wooden stool, a dried date, a bar of soap, a goat's horn. You can pick them up, and they hold their form. When you press a solid, it does not get smaller — solids are very hard to squeeze, or compress.

A liquid is different. It still takes up a fixed amount of space — it has a definite volume — but it does not have a shape of its own. Instead, a liquid takes the shape of whatever container you pour it into. Pour water into a tall thin glass and it becomes tall and thin. Pour that same water into a wide flat dish and it spreads out wide and flat. But the amount of water does not change — one cup of water is still one cup of water. Liquids can flow and be poured, which is why you can pour camel milk from a jug into a cup. Like solids, liquids are hard to compress.

A gas is the freest of all. A gas has no definite shape and no definite volume. It spreads out to completely fill whatever container it is in, no matter how big. Blow up a balloon and the air fills every part of it. Let the air out and it spreads across the whole room. You often cannot see gases, but they are truly there. When you feel the warm coastal wind on your face, you are feeling moving air, which is a mixture of gases. When steam rises from a pot, that is water in its gas form. Unlike solids and liquids, gases can be squeezed into a smaller space quite easily, because there is a lot of empty space inside a gas.

The wonderful thing is that the same substance can be all three. Water is a solid when it is frozen as ice, a liquid when you drink it, and a gas when it becomes water vapour. It is still water the whole time — only its state has changed. This idea, that one substance can take three different forms, is at the very heart of this unit.

Let us build a habit right now. At your next meal, look at your plate and cup and try to spot all three states. The bariis (rice) and the goat meat are solids. The water or the camel milk is a liquid. The warm air rising above the hot food, carrying its lovely smell to your nose, is a gas mixed with water vapour. When you can point to solids, liquids, and gases without even thinking, you are already beginning to see the world the way a scientist does.
concept-1-the-three-states-of-matter.example: Did You Know? The air around you is not empty — it is a gas, and it has weight! The air in an ordinary classroom weighs about as much as a small child. Even though you cannot see most gases, you breathe in about 20,000 breaths of them every single day.

concept-2-the-particle-model-the-secret-.explanation:
Now we come to one of the biggest ideas in all of science. Why does a solid keep its shape while a gas floats away? To answer that, scientists imagine that all matter is built from unbelievably tiny pieces called particles. These particles are far too small to see, even with a normal magnifying glass. A single drop of water contains billions upon billions of them. The way these particles are arranged, and how they move, explains everything about the three states.

In a solid, the particles are packed very closely together in a neat, regular pattern, like dates stacked tightly in a box or bricks in a wall. Strong forces of attraction hold them firmly in place. The particles are not completely still — they vibrate, or jiggle, on the spot — but they cannot move away from their neighbours. Because the particles are locked in position, a solid keeps its shape and its volume. Because they are already so close together, you cannot squeeze a solid any smaller.

In a liquid, the particles are still close together, but they are no longer locked in a fixed pattern. They can slide and roll past one another, a bit like a bag of small dried beans that shift around when you tip the bag. This is why a liquid can flow and take the shape of its container — the particles move to fill the bottom of whatever holds them. But because they are still close together, a liquid keeps a definite volume and is hard to compress.

In a gas, the particles are spread far, far apart with lots of empty space between them. They move quickly in every direction, bouncing off each other and off the walls of their container. There is almost no force holding them together, so they spread out endlessly to fill any space. This is why a gas has no shape and no fixed volume. And because there is so much empty space between the particles, you can squeeze a gas into a much smaller space — the particles simply move closer together.

Here is a helpful picture. Imagine a class of children. When they line up in neat rows, standing still and shoulder to shoulder, that is like a solid. When the same children mill about the classroom, close together but moving around each other, that is like a liquid. When they run freely all over a wide open field, far apart and moving fast in all directions, that is like a gas. The children are the same children — only their arrangement and movement have changed. That is exactly what happens to particles when matter changes state.

[*] Remember! Solid particles: packed tight, vibrate in place, keep their shape. Liquid particles: close together, slide past each other, take the container's shape. Gas particles: far apart, move fast in all directions, fill all the space. The particles themselves do not change — only how they are arranged and how they move.

concept-3-changing-state-the-power-of-he.explanation:
How does one state turn into another? The answer is energy, and usually that energy comes as heat. When you heat matter, you give its particles more energy, so they move faster and push further apart. When you cool matter, you take energy away, so the particles slow down and move closer together. By adding or removing heat, we can make matter change from solid to liquid to gas, and back again.

When you heat a solid, its particles vibrate faster and faster. At a certain temperature, called the melting point, they gain enough energy to break free from their fixed positions and begin sliding around each other. The solid has become a liquid. This is melting. You see it when an ice cube melts into water in a warm room, or when a piece of ghee (subag) melts in a hot pan. Ice melts at 0 degrees Celsius.

Freezing is the opposite of melting. When you cool a liquid, its particles slow down. At the freezing point, they slow so much that the forces of attraction lock them back into fixed positions, and the liquid becomes a solid. Water freezes into ice at 0 degrees Celsius — the very same temperature at which ice melts. Notice that melting and freezing are simply the same doorway travelled in opposite directions.

When you heat a liquid, some of its particles gain enough energy to escape from the surface and fly off into the air as a gas. This is evaporation, and we will study it closely in the next section. If you heat the liquid strongly enough, it reaches its boiling point and changes to gas very fast, with bubbles forming all through it — this is boiling. Water boils at 100 degrees Celsius. When your family boils water on the charcoal jiko to make it safe to drink, you can watch the bubbles rise and the steam pour out.

Condensation is the reverse of evaporation. When water vapour in the air is cooled, its particles slow down and join together to form liquid water again. You have seen this many times: droplets of water forming on the outside of a cold glass of juice, or a misty film on a cool window in the early morning. The water did not leak through the glass — it condensed out of the air.

All of these changes are physical changes, not chemical ones. That means no new substance is made — water is still water whether it is ice, liquid, or vapour. And every one of these changes can be reversed. Melt an ice cube and you can freeze the water again. Boil water into steam and you can cool the steam back into water. This is why the water on Earth has been recycled over and over for millions of years.

concept-4-evaporation-and-the-factors-th.explanation:
Evaporation deserves special attention because it happens all around you, all the time, and understanding it is genuinely useful. Here is the key idea: evaporation can happen at any temperature, not just at boiling point. A puddle in Garissa dries up on a warm morning long before the water is anywhere near boiling. This is because, even in cool water, a few of the fastest-moving particles at the surface always have enough energy to escape into the air. Slowly, one by one, they leave, and the puddle shrinks until it is gone.

Why does wet washing dry faster on some days than others? Why does seawater left in a shallow pan turn to salt more quickly in the sun? The answer is that four main factors control how fast a liquid evaporates. Let us look at each one.

The hotter the liquid or the air around it, the faster it evaporates. Heat gives the particles more energy, so more of them can escape from the surface. This is why Halima hangs the clothes out in the strong afternoon sun rather than in the cool shade — the warmth speeds up evaporation and the clothes dry much faster.

The larger the surface of the liquid that is exposed to the air, the faster it evaporates, because more particles are near the surface where they can escape. A puddle spread out wide and thin dries much faster than the same amount of water in a deep narrow cup. This is exactly why families collecting salt from seawater use wide, shallow pans — the huge surface lets the water evaporate quickly and leaves the salt behind. It is also why we spread washing out flat on the line instead of leaving it bunched in a ball.

Moving air makes evaporation faster. When particles escape from a liquid, they gather in the air just above it. If that damp air sits still, it becomes crowded and some particles fall back into the liquid. But a breeze carries the damp air away and brings fresh dry air, making room for more particles to escape. This is why clothes dry so quickly on a breezy day near the coast, and why waving a wet hand in the wind makes it feel cold as the water evaporates fast.

Humidity is the amount of water vapour already in the air. When the air is dry, it has plenty of room for more water vapour, so evaporation is fast. When the air is very humid — already full of water vapour, as it often is along the damp Indian Ocean coast — there is little room for more, so evaporation is slow. This is why washing dries more slowly on a humid, cloudy day than on a dry day inland.

[*] Remember! Evaporation is FASTER when it is hot, when the surface is large, when there is wind, and when the air is dry. Evaporation is SLOWER when it is cool, when the surface is small, when the air is still, and when the air is humid.
concept-4-evaporation-and-the-factors-th.example: Did You Know? Sweating cools your body using evaporation. When sweat evaporates from your skin, it carries heat away, which is why a breeze feels so refreshing on a hot day in Kismaayo. For thousands of years people along coasts have made salt by letting the sun evaporate seawater in shallow pools — one of the oldest uses of science in human history.

concept-6-dissolving-when-a-solid-seems-.explanation:
There is one more everyday change to understand: dissolving. When you stir a spoonful of sugar into a cup of hot shaah, the sugar seems to vanish. Where does it go? The sugar has dissolved. It has not disappeared and it has not melted — the tiny sugar particles have spread out and slipped into the spaces between the water particles, mixing so completely that you can no longer see them. You know the sugar is still there because the tea tastes sweet. A mixture like this, where a solid is completely dissolved in a liquid, is called a solution.

The same thing happens when salt dissolves in water. And here is a lovely connection: if you leave that salty water in the sun, the water will evaporate away and leave the salt behind, visible once more. This is precisely how salt is collected from seawater along the coast. Dissolving hides the solid; evaporation brings it back. Two ideas from this unit working together.

Some things dissolve and some do not. Sugar and salt dissolve well in water. Sand and small stones do not dissolve — stir them as much as you like and they still settle at the bottom. Warm water usually dissolves things faster than cold water, because the faster-moving particles mix more quickly. That is why sugar dissolves more easily in hot tea than in cold.

Problem: Halima is sitting in the evening. There is a lamp on the shelf. On the table there is a yellow banana. Halima can see the banana clearly. Draw and describe the complete path of the light, step by step.

Step 1 — Find the light source. Nothing can be seen without a source. The banana does not glow, and Halima's eyes do not shine. The only source here is the lamp. So the light story must begin at the lamp.

Step 2 — Light travels in straight lines to the object. Light leaves the lamp and shoots out in straight rays in all directions. Some of those rays travel straight to the banana. Draw a straight arrow from the lamp to the banana.

Step 3 — The object reflects the light. The banana skin absorbs most colours but reflects yellow light. That yellow light bounces off in many directions. Draw arrows spreading out from the banana.
