rule-1.title: Key idea 1 — Protect Your Eyes Never look straight at the sun, not even for a moment and not even when squinting. The equatorial sun over East Africa is extremely strong, and its light can permanently burn the retina at the back of your eye, harming your sight forever. Wear a hat or use shade at midday, and if you have sunglasses, wear them outdoors. Never stare into a laser pointer or a very bright torch, and never shine one in anyone's eyes. Rest your eyes from screens often, and keep your hands and face clean to protect your eyes from infection and dust.

concept-1-how-a-shadow-is-born.explanation:
Imagine you are standing in a dark room at night. There are no shadows anywhere, because there is no light. Now switch on a torch and point it at the wall. Place your hand between the torch and the wall. Suddenly a dark shape of your hand appears on the wall. You have made a shadow. But why?

Light from the torch travels outward in straight lines called rays. These rays keep going straight until something stops them. When your hand gets in the way, it blocks the rays that hit it. Those rays cannot bend around your fingers, so they cannot reach the wall behind. The place on the wall where the light is missing stays dark. That dark shape is the shadow.

This tells us something very important: a shadow is not a thing you can hold. A shadow is simply a place where light is missing because an object blocked it. This is why you can never pick up a shadow or put it in a box. It is an absence of light, not a piece of matter.

Let us slow down and picture this even more clearly. Imagine hundreds of tiny straight arrows of light leaving the torch, all flying forward together like a swarm of straight-flying bees. Most of them race past the sides of your hand and splash onto the wall, making it bright. But the arrows aimed at the middle of your hand crash into it and stop. They never reach the wall. So the wall behind your hand is left with no light landing on it, and that empty, unlit patch is the shadow. Every shadow you have ever seen, from the shadow of a camel at dawn to the shadow of a mosque minaret at dusk, is made in exactly this same simple way.

Every single shadow in the world needs exactly three things. If even one is missing, no shadow can form. Think of it like making anjero (canjeero): you need flour, water, and heat. Miss one, and there is no anjero. For a shadow you need:

A light source. Something must be giving out light, such as the sun or a torch. In a completely dark room, nothing makes a shadow because there is no light to block.

An opaque object. Something must block the light. If the object lets light through, like clean glass, the shadow is very faint or does not appear at all.

A surface. The shadow needs somewhere to land, such as the ground, a wall, or a sheet of paper. Without a surface you would not be able to see the shadow.

Try this test in your mind. A book lies on a table in a completely dark room. Is there a shadow? No, because the light source is missing. Now the sun rises and light pours through the window. The book blocks some of that light, and a shadow appears on the table beside it. The moment the third ingredient, light, arrived, the shadow could form.

Did You Know? The Earth itself makes a giant shadow in space. At night, the side of the Earth facing away from the sun sits inside the Earth's own shadow. That is what night really is — you are standing inside the shadow of the whole planet! When the moon passes into the Earth's shadow, we see a lunar eclipse, which Muslims mark with a special prayer called Salat al-Khusuf.

Here is a clever idea. We cannot see light rays flying through the air, so how do we know that light travels in straight lines? Shadows give us the proof. Look at the shadow of a straight pole. Its edge is straight and sharp. If light could curve and bend around the pole like water flowing around a rock in the Jubba River, the light would sneak behind the pole and there would be no clear shadow. But light cannot bend on its own. It goes straight, gets blocked, and leaves a sharp-edged shadow behind. The shadow is the footprint that proves light walked in a straight line.

sci-g05-u06.unitOverview: Look up. Every single day of your life, the Sun climbs into the sky over the Indian Ocean, warms the savanna, and later slips down behind the western hills. Every month the Moon grows from a thin silver curve into a bright full circle, then shrinks away again. When your family watches for the new crescent moon to know that Ramadan or Eid has begun, you are doing exactly what scientists and travellers have done for thousands of years — reading the sky. In this unit you are going to discover the real story behind these everyday wonders.

concept-1-our-home-in-space.explanation:
Let us begin with a big question: what is your address in the universe? You might start with your house, then your town — perhaps Mogadishu, Kismaayo or Dar es Salaam — then your country, then the continent of Africa. But you can keep going. Africa sits on the planet Earth. Earth is one of eight planets that travel around a star we call the Sun. The Sun and everything travelling around it make up our Solar System. And our Solar System is just one tiny corner of a giant collection of billions of stars called a galaxy. That is a very big address!

At the centre of our Solar System sits the Sun. The Sun is a star — an enormous ball of hot, glowing gas so large that more than a million Earths could fit inside it. The Sun makes its own light and heat through powerful reactions deep inside. This is why the equatorial Sun feels so strong on your skin at midday: you are standing almost directly beneath it. Everything else in the Solar System, including Earth, is much smaller and does not make its own light. Planets only reflect the Sun's light, like a wall lit by a lamp.

There are eight planets. In order from the Sun they are: Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune. A helpful way to remember the order is to make up a sentence where each word begins with the same letter as a planet — try inventing your own with your AI tutor. The four planets closest to the Sun (Mercury, Venus, Earth and Mars) are small and made mostly of rock. The four farthest away (Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune) are enormous and made mostly of gas, which is why they are called the gas giants.

Earth is the third planet from the Sun. This position is special. We are not so close that the oceans boil away, and not so far that they freeze solid. We are just the right distance for liquid water, breathable air, and life. When you drink camel milk, watch flamingos wade in a lake, or feel the coastal wind at Berbera, you are enjoying gifts that come from Earth sitting in exactly the right place in space.

Did You Know? The Sun is about 150 million kilometres away from Earth. Its light takes just over 8 minutes to reach us. So the sunrise you see over the Indian Ocean actually left the Sun 8 minutes earlier! If you could drive a car to the Sun at highway speed without stopping, the journey would take over 170 years.

How do we know Earth travels around the Sun, when it feels as if we are standing perfectly still? For a long time, most people believed the Sun moved around the Earth, because that is how it looks. But careful observers like Copernicus and Galileo studied the sky for years and used reasoning and evidence to show that Earth and the other planets travel around the Sun. This is an important lesson in science: what seems obvious to our eyes is not always the truth. We must observe carefully, gather evidence, and be willing to change our minds. Observing creation closely and thinking carefully about it is a way of growing in both knowledge and wonder.
concept-1-our-home-in-space.example: Earth's path around the Sun is called its orbit. The orbit is not a perfect circle — it is a very slightly squashed circle, like an egg shape called an ellipse. But the squashing is so small that Earth stays almost the same distance from the Sun all year round. This is important: it means the seasons are not caused by Earth moving closer to or farther from the Sun. Remember that — it is one of the most common mistakes people make.

concept-2-day-and-night-earth-s-spin.explanation:
Now think about a single day. In the morning the Sun rises in the east, over the Indian Ocean if you live on the coast. By midday it is high overhead — this is noon. In the evening it sinks in the west and sets, and then comes night. It really looks as if the Sun is travelling across the sky above us. But it is not. Here is the true explanation.

Earth spins like a top. This spinning is called rotation. Earth turns all the way around once every 24 hours, which is exactly why a day is 24 hours long. Earth spins around an imaginary line called its axis, which runs straight through the planet from the North Pole to the South Pole. Picture pushing a knitting needle through an orange from top to bottom, then spinning the orange — the needle is the axis.

The Sun shines on Earth from one side only, just as a torch shines on one side of a ball. So at any moment, half of Earth is lit (that half has daytime) and half is dark (that half has night-time). As Earth rotates, your town is carried around into the light and then around into the dark, over and over. When your part of Earth turns to face the Sun, you see the Sun "rise" and you have day. When your part turns away, the Sun "sets" and you have night. The Sun never moved — you did, carried by the spinning Earth.

Because Earth spins from west to east, the Sun appears to move the opposite way, from east to west. This is just like riding in a car: when you look out of the window, the trees and houses seem to rush backwards, even though they are standing still and you are the one moving. In the same way, the whole sky seems to slide from east to west because you are riding on a turning planet.

Because Earth is round and always turning, different parts of the world have day and night at different times. When it is daytime for you, it is night-time on the far side of the planet. To help people keep track of this, the world is divided into time zones — 24 of them, one for roughly each hour of Earth's spin. This is why, when it is midday in Kampala, it is the middle of the night in countries far to the east or west. Understanding rotation helps explain a real everyday thing: why a phone call to a relative in another country might reach them while they are still sleeping.

You can even see the proof of Earth's rotation in a shadow. If you push a straight stick upright into the ground in a sunny spot and mark the tip of its shadow every hour, you will find the shadow slowly swings around and changes length through the day. Around noon, when the Sun is highest, the shadow is at its shortest. In the early morning and late afternoon, when the Sun is low, shadows stretch out long. This moving shadow is the very same idea as a sundial, the oldest kind of clock, and it is caused entirely by Earth turning.
concept-2-day-and-night-earth-s-spin.example: Did You Know? Near the equator — across much of East Africa — day and night stay close to 12 hours each all year round. Far to the north or south, summer days can last many more hours than winter days. This is why the strong midday Sun is such a steady part of daily life close to the equator.

concept-3-the-year-earth-s-journey-aroun.explanation:
While Earth is spinning to give us day and night, it is also slowly travelling all the way around the Sun. One full trip around the Sun takes about 365 days — and that is exactly what we call a year. So Earth is doing two movements at the same time: it is rotating (spinning once a day) and orbiting (circling the Sun once a year). Think of a spinning top that someone is also carrying slowly around a table.

A year is actually a little longer than 365 days — it is closer to 365 and a quarter days. Those extra quarter-days add up. Every four years we save them up into one extra whole day, the 29th of February, and that year is called a leap year. This is one clever way people keep their calendars matching Earth's real journey around the Sun.
concept-3-the-year-earth-s-journey-aroun.example: Earth's axis is tilted — it leans over at an angle rather than standing straight up. As Earth journeys around the Sun, this tilt means that different parts of the planet lean towards the Sun at different times of the year. The part leaning towards the Sun gets more direct sunlight and longer days — that is summer. Six months later the same part leans away, getting less direct sunlight and shorter days — that is winter. This tilt, not the small change in distance, is the real cause of the seasons. Close to the equator the effect is gentle, which is why East Africa has fairly steady daylight but strong dry and wet seasons instead of the icy winters found far to the north.

concept-4-the-moon-and-its-phases.explanation:
Now let us turn to Earth's closest companion in space: the Moon. The Moon is a natural satellite, which means it travels around Earth, just as Earth travels around the Sun. The Moon is much smaller than Earth — about one quarter of Earth's width — and it is our nearest neighbour in space, though still very far away. It takes the Moon about 29.5 days to travel once around Earth.

Here is something surprising: the Moon does not make its own light. It is not glowing like the Sun. The reason the Moon looks bright is that it reflects sunlight, like a mirror or a pale stone catching the light of a lamp. At any moment, the Sun lights up one half of the Moon, and the other half is in darkness. As the Moon travels around Earth, we see different amounts of its bright, sunlit half. That is what makes the Moon appear to change shape. These changing shapes are called the phases of the Moon.

Let us walk through the main phases in order. At new moon, the Moon sits between Earth and the Sun, so its dark side faces us and we can barely see it at all. A day or two later, a thin bright curve appears — the waxing crescent. This slim crescent is the very sign your family looks for to announce the start of a new month in the Islamic (Hijri) calendar. The lit part then grows, or waxes, through the first quarter (when we see half of the lit side) and the waxing gibbous, until we reach the full moon, when the whole sunlit face shines back at us and the savanna is bright enough to walk by at night.

After full moon, the bright part shrinks, or wanes. We pass through the waning gibbous, the third quarter (half lit again, but the other half this time), and the waning crescent, until we return to new moon and the whole cycle begins again. The words waxing means growing and waning means shrinking. Remember: the Moon itself never changes shape or size. It is a round ball the whole time. Only the amount of its bright side that we can see from Earth changes as it orbits us.

Did You Know? The Islamic (Hijri) calendar is a lunar calendar — each month begins with the sighting of the new crescent moon. Because 12 lunar months are about 11 days shorter than a solar year, Ramadan and Eid move earlier each year on the ordinary calendar. This is why Ramadan slowly shifts through all the seasons over a person's lifetime — a beautiful pattern written into the sky.
concept-4-the-moon-and-its-phases.example: Because the phases follow the same pattern every 29.5 days, they can be predicted. People have used this for thousands of years to make calendars, to plan journeys, and to know when the bright full moon would light the way for night travel across the land. The Moon also pulls gently on Earth's oceans, and this pull is one of the causes of the tides — the daily rising and falling of the sea that fishermen along the Indian Ocean coast know so well.

concept-5-stars-constellations-and-findi.explanation:
On a clear night far from city lights — out in the open savanna — the sky fills with countless tiny points of light. These are stars, and every one of them is a Sun of its own: a huge ball of hot, glowing gas making its own light. They look tiny only because they are unimaginably far away. Light from even the nearest star (after our Sun) takes more than four years to reach your eyes. Our Sun looks big and bright only because it is so much closer to us than all the others.

Long ago, people noticed that certain stars form patterns in the sky. We call these patterns constellations. The stars in a constellation are not really close together — some are far behind others — but from where we stand on Earth they make a shape we can recognise. Different cultures have seen different pictures and told different stories about the same stars. This is part of the rich human habit of looking up and finding meaning and beauty in creation.

Stars, like the Sun, seem to move slowly across the sky through the night, rising in the east and setting in the west. Once again, this is because Earth is rotating, not because the stars are moving around us. And because Earth also travels around the Sun through the year, we face different parts of space in different seasons, so different constellations are visible at different times of the year.

For as long as people have travelled, they have used the sky to find direction. The Sun rises in the east and sets in the west, giving you a rough compass every single day. At night, certain stars point the way. Sailors crossing the Indian Ocean, caravans crossing the semi-arid land, and travellers everywhere have read the stars to stay on course. This skill also helped people work out the direction of the qibla for prayer when they were far from home. Even today, the satellites of the GPS system that guide cars and ships still depend on a careful understanding of Earth's rotation and the positions of objects in the sky.
concept-5-stars-constellations-and-findi.example: Did You Know? People built simple star-knowledge into daily life long before modern instruments. By knowing where the Sun sets, you always know west — and from west you can find north, south and east. The clear, dark skies of the savanna are among the best places on Earth to see the stars, because there is little city light to hide them.

concept-6-exploring-space.explanation:
How do we know so much about places we can never visit? People have built clever tools to explore space. Telescopes gather and focus light so we can see distant objects far more clearly than with our eyes alone. Some telescopes sit on the ground; others have been launched above the air, where the view is even sharper. Satellites are machines that we send to orbit Earth. Weather satellites help forecasters warn coastal towns like Mombasa and Kismaayo about storms; communication satellites carry phone calls and the internet across the world; and other satellites watch over forests, farmland and the changing climate.

We also send spacecraft far out into the Solar System. Robots called rovers have driven across the surface of Mars, taking photographs and studying the rocks. Astronauts live and work aboard the International Space Station, floating in orbit high above us. Space is a harsh place — there is no air to breathe, temperatures are extreme, and radiation is dangerous — so every spacecraft must be carefully designed to protect the people and machines inside. Exploring space is difficult and expensive, but it has given us many useful things, from accurate weather forecasts to the navigation that guides ships safely home.

Sending messages across space is slow because of the enormous distances. A radio signal from a rover on Mars can take several minutes to reach Earth, so we cannot steer it moment by moment as we would a toy car — the machine has to be clever enough to make many decisions on its own. This is one reason space robots are built to be so careful and independent. When you think about how far away these machines are, and how well they still work, it is a remarkable achievement of human curiosity and patience.
concept-6-exploring-space.example: Space technology also quietly helps everyday life in East Africa. Satellites watch the movement of clouds and rain, helping to warn people about drought and floods so families and herders can prepare. They track the health of farmland and grazing land from far above, and they carry the phone and internet signals that connect distant towns. Studying the sky is not only about far-off wonders — it also protects and connects people right here at home.

we01.solution:
Worked Example 1 — How many degrees does Earth turn each hour?

Earth makes one full turn — that is 360 degrees — in 24 hours. To find how much it turns in one hour, we divide:

360 degrees divided by 24 hours = 15 degrees per hour.

So every hour, Earth spins 15 degrees, and the Sun appears to move 15 degrees across the sky. This is the reason each time zone is about 15 degrees of longitude wide.

Worked Example 3 — How many times does Earth spin in one year?

Earth spins once each day, and there are about 365 days in a year. So in one full journey around the Sun, Earth spins about 365 times. Reading Comprehension — Waris Watches for the Crescent

Read this short passage carefully, then answer the questions below.

The evening after sunset, Waris climbed with her grandfather onto the flat roof of their house near Berbera. The sky over the Indian Ocean was turning from orange to deep blue. "Tonight," her grandfather said softly, "we look for the new crescent. If we see that thin curve of light, tomorrow begins a new month." Waris searched the western sky where the Sun had just set. For a while she saw nothing. Then, low and delicate, a silver sliver appeared, curved like the edge of a fingernail. "There!" she cried. Her grandfather smiled. "That is the Moon reflecting the light of the Sun that has already gone below the horizon. In a few nights it will grow fatter, and in about two weeks it will be full and bright enough to light the whole savanna." Waris thought about how the same Moon she was watching had guided travellers and marked the months for countless people before her. She decided to keep a moon diary and draw its shape every clear night.

concept-1-ecosystems-and-habitats.explanation:
An ecosystem is made up of two kinds of things working together: the living things, called biotic factors, and the non-living things, called abiotic factors. Imagine the savanna near Garissa early in the morning. The grass, the acacia trees, the gazelles, the lions, the birds, and the tiny insects are all biotic — they are alive. The sunshine warming the ground, the temperature of the air, the water in a nearby waterhole, the soil beneath your feet, and the wind moving the grass are all abiotic — they are not alive, but living things could not survive without them.

A habitat is the specific home where an organism lives and finds everything it needs: food, water, shelter, and a safe place to raise its young. The savanna is the habitat of the gazelle. The Indian Ocean coral reef is the habitat of the parrotfish. A patch of moist soil is the habitat of an earthworm. Different organisms need different habitats because they need different things. A camel is well suited to hot, dry, semi-arid land, but a tilapia would die there in minutes because it needs water. A mangrove crab thrives where salty seawater meets the land, but it could not survive on a dry mountain.

Every habitat must supply four basic needs: food, water, shelter, and space. When one of these is missing or runs short — for example, when a long drought dries up the waterholes — animals must move, adapt, or they may not survive. This is why the same ecosystem can look full of life in the wet season and much quieter in the dry season.

Did You Know? A single teaspoon of healthy soil can contain more living microorganisms than there are people on the whole Earth. The mangrove forests along the East African coast are nurseries where baby fish hide and grow before swimming out to the open ocean.

Living things are shaped by their habitat through adaptation. An adaptation is a special feature or behaviour that helps an organism survive where it lives. The camel is a champion of adaptation to dry, semi-arid land: it stores fat in its hump for energy, can go many days without drinking, has long eyelashes to keep out blowing sand, and wide feet that do not sink into loose ground. The acacia tree has long roots that reach deep for water and sharp thorns that protect its leaves from hungry animals. A gazelle has long legs for fast running to escape lions, and eyes on the sides of its head to watch for danger in every direction. Each adaptation is a clue to the habitat the animal or plant calls home.

Ecosystems come in many types, and East Africa is rich with them. The dry, grassy savanna is home to lions, gazelles, zebras, and giraffes. The semi-arid scrubland, where herders graze their camels and goats, has tough thorny plants that survive with little rain. Along the shore, warm coral reefs shelter thousands of colourful fish, while mangrove forests, where salty seawater meets the land, protect the coast and shelter young fish. Inland, the Rift Valley lakes draw great flocks of flamingos. Each of these ecosystems has its own balance of biotic and abiotic factors, and its own community of living things that fit it perfectly. When you learn to read an ecosystem, you begin to see why each animal lives exactly where it does.

It helps to think of an ecosystem as a large, busy household in which every member has a role, and the non-living surroundings — the walls, the water supply, the warmth — make daily life possible. Change one part of the household and everyone feels it. If the water supply fails, or the temperature soars, the whole community must respond. This is why scientists never study a single animal alone; they study the animal together with everything around it. Throughout this unit, keep asking two questions about any living thing you meet: 'What does it need from its habitat?' and 'What would happen to the others if it disappeared?'

Think about these questions and discuss them with your AI tutor. There is no need to rush — reasoning them out slowly is the point.

Why can a camel survive in dry semi-arid land while a fish cannot? List the abiotic factors that make the difference.

Name three biotic and three abiotic factors in a mangrove ecosystem along the coast near Kismaayo.

concept-2-producers-the-foundation-of-al.explanation:
Every food chain begins with a producer. A producer is a living thing that can make its own food. Green plants are the most common producers on land. They do something amazing that no animal can do: they capture the energy of sunlight and use it to make sugar, a kind of food, inside their leaves. This process is called photosynthesis. The word means 'putting together with light'. During photosynthesis a plant takes in sunlight, water from the soil through its roots, and carbon dioxide gas from the air, and it makes sugar for energy while giving out the oxygen that we breathe.

Because producers make their own food, they do not need to eat other living things. Instead, they trap the sun's energy and store it. This stored energy is the starting point for almost every other living thing on Earth. When a gazelle eats grass, it is really taking in energy that first came from the sun and was captured by the grass. When a lion eats the gazelle, that same sun-energy passes on again. This is why we say producers are the foundation of all life — without them, there would be no energy entering the ecosystem at all.

Producers are everywhere. On the savanna, the grasses and acacia trees are the main producers. In a farm near the Jubba River, the maize, banana, and mango plants are producers. In the Indian Ocean, tiny floating plants and plant-like living things called plankton and algae are the producers — they are so small you often need a microscope to see them, yet they feed the entire ocean and produce a large share of the world's oxygen.

It is worth pausing to picture photosynthesis clearly, because it is one of the most important processes on Earth. Inside every green leaf are countless tiny parts that hold a green colouring called chlorophyll. Chlorophyll is what makes leaves green, and it acts like a trap for sunlight. When sunlight lands on the leaf, the chlorophyll catches its energy. The plant then uses that energy to join together the water it drew up from the soil and the carbon dioxide it took from the air, building them into sugar — the plant's food. As a by-product, the plant releases oxygen into the air. So every breath of clean air you take is a gift from producers busy at work. When you sit under the shade of a mango or baobab tree, remember that its leaves are quietly turning sunlight into food and filling the air with oxygen at the same time.

Because producers turn sunlight into stored food energy, scientists call the amount of food they make the primary production of an ecosystem. Where there is plenty of sunlight, water, and rich soil — such as a well-watered farm or a healthy mangrove — primary production is high and the ecosystem can feed many consumers. Where conditions are harsh — such as bare, dry, semi-arid land during a drought — primary production is low, and far fewer animals can be supported. This simple idea explains why the green savanna after the rains bursts with life, while the same land in a long dry season falls quiet.
concept-2-producers-the-foundation-of-al.example: [*] Remember! Producers make their own food using sunlight. Consumers cannot — they must eat. The energy in every food chain starts as sunlight captured by a producer. No producers means no food and no energy for anything else in the ecosystem.

concept-3-consumers-and-feeding-relation.explanation:
A consumer is a living thing that cannot make its own food, so it must eat other living things to get energy. You are a consumer. So is a gazelle, a lion, a tilapia, a chicken, and a mosquito. Scientists sort consumers into groups in two useful ways: by what they eat, and by where they sit in the food chain.

Sorting by what they eat gives us three groups. A herbivore eats only plants — the gazelle, the goat, the cow, and the camel are herbivores. A carnivore eats only other animals — the lion, the hyena, and the fish-eating heron are carnivores. An omnivore eats both plants and animals — human beings are omnivores, and so are chickens and baboons. Each type has adaptations for its diet: herbivores often have wide flat teeth for grinding grass, while carnivores have sharp pointed teeth for tearing meat.

Sorting by position in the food chain gives us levels called trophic levels. A primary consumer eats producers directly — it is a plant-eater, like the gazelle eating grass. A secondary consumer eats primary consumers — like a snake eating a mouse, or a small fish eating tiny water animals. A tertiary consumer eats secondary consumers — like a lion or a large Nile perch at the top of its chain. The animals at the very top, which nothing else hunts, are called top predators.

Here is a savanna example to hold in your mind. The grass is the producer. A gazelle eats the grass, so the gazelle is a primary consumer. A lion eats the gazelle, so the lion is a secondary consumer. In the ocean, tiny plankton are producers, a small tilapia eats the plankton as a primary consumer, and a larger fish such as a Nile perch eats the tilapia as a secondary consumer. Notice how the same idea works on land and in water.

Consumers depend completely on producers, even the fierce meat-eaters that never touch a plant. Think about it: a lion eats a gazelle, but the gazelle only had energy in its body because it had eaten grass. So the lion's meal is really sun-energy that passed first into the grass and then into the gazelle. This is why we say all consumers depend on producers — the energy in their food always traces back to sunlight captured by a plant. If the grass failed, the gazelles would starve, and then the lions would have nothing to hunt. Every consumer, however powerful, sits on top of the quiet work of producers.

Consumers also help control one another's numbers, keeping the ecosystem in balance. Predators such as lions and hyenas keep the numbers of grass-eaters in check, so the grass is not completely eaten away. In turn, the amount of grass available limits how many gazelles can live in an area. This gentle push and pull between predators and their prey keeps populations from growing too large or crashing too low. When you watch animals near your home, you are watching this balance in action, even if it is not obvious at first glance.

Did You Know? A lion may need to eat many gazelles across a year, which is why a large area of savanna can support only a few lions. Flamingos on East Africa's Rift Valley lakes are pink because of the tiny algae and shrimp they eat.

Classify each of these as herbivore, carnivore, or omnivore: goat, lion, human, heron, camel.

In the chain grass to gazelle to lion, name the producer, the primary consumer, and the secondary consumer.

concept-4-decomposers-nature-s-recyclers.explanation:
When a plant dies, or an animal dies, or an animal leaves droppings, what happens to all that material? It does not simply pile up forever. A special group of living things gets to work: the decomposers. Decomposers are living things that break down dead plants, dead animals, and waste, returning the nutrients locked inside them back into the soil. The main decomposers are bacteria and fungi, but small animals such as earthworms and dung beetles also help.

Think of decomposers as nature's recyclers. When a fallen acacia leaf lies on the savanna floor, fungi and bacteria slowly break it apart. The valuable nutrients inside — the very minerals a plant needs to grow — are released into the soil. Then the roots of new grass and trees take up those nutrients, and grow strong, and become food for gazelles again. This never-ending loop is called the nutrient cycle. Nutrients are used again and again, passed from soil to plant to animal and back to soil.

Decomposers are easy to forget because much of their work happens hidden in the soil, out of sight. But they are absolutely essential. Imagine if there were no decomposers at all. Dead leaves, dead animals, and waste would build up and never break down. Worse, the nutrients trapped inside them would be lost forever, the soil would become poor, and eventually the producers could not grow. Without decomposers, the whole ecosystem would slowly starve. This is why a farmer who makes compost — a rich material made by letting fruit peels, leaves, and food scraps decompose — is really putting decomposers to work to feed the next crop.

Decomposers work best in warm, moist conditions, which is why food left out in warm weather spoils quickly, while food kept cool and dry lasts far longer. This same knowledge helps families in practical ways. Drying meat and fish in the sun, or keeping grain dry, are old and clever ways of slowing decomposers down so that food is not spoiled before it can be eaten. On the other hand, a farmer who wants to make good compost does the opposite: keeping the heap moist and warm so decomposers work faster and turn scraps into rich soil sooner. Understanding decomposers, then, is not only about science lessons — it helps you store food safely and grow healthier crops at home.

concept-5-food-chains-food-webs-and-the-.explanation:
A food chain is a simple way to show how energy passes from one living thing to the next. We draw it with arrows, and here is the most important rule to remember: the arrow always points in the direction the energy flows — that is, from the thing being eaten to the thing that eats it. So we write grass -> gazelle -> lion. The arrow from grass to gazelle means 'energy flows from the grass into the gazelle because the gazelle eats the grass'. A common mistake is to point the arrow the wrong way, toward the food. Always follow the energy, not the mouth.

In the real world, living things rarely eat just one thing, and they are rarely eaten by just one thing. A gazelle is hunted by lions, hyenas, and leopards. A lion eats gazelles, zebras, and buffalo. When we join many food chains together, we get a food web — a network that shows all the feeding relationships in an ecosystem at once. A food web is a truer picture of nature than a single chain, because it shows how many living things are connected.

Food webs teach us a powerful lesson: everything is connected. If one part changes, the whole web feels it. Suppose hunters removed all the lions from a savanna. With no lions to hunt them, the gazelle population might grow very large. Too many gazelles would eat too much grass, and the grass could be stripped bare. Then, with little grass left, many gazelles would starve, and other grass-eating animals would suffer too. Removing just one species can shake the entire system. This is why protecting each species matters.

Now, an important idea about energy. Energy enters the ecosystem as sunlight and is captured by producers. As it flows up the chain, something happens at every step: most of the energy is lost, mainly as heat and through the daily living, moving, and breathing of each animal. Only about one tenth — roughly ten percent — of the energy at one level passes on to the next level. The rest is used up staying alive.

This 'energy tax' at every step explains two things you can see in nature. First, it explains why food chains are usually short, with only four or five levels — after a few steps, there is simply not enough energy left to support another level of hunters. Second, it explains why there are always fewer animals at the top. A savanna has vast amounts of grass, many gazelles, but only a few lions. There is plenty of energy at the bottom of the chain and very little at the top. This pattern is sometimes drawn as a pyramid, wide at the producer base and narrow at the top predator tip.

Did You Know? Only about ten percent of the energy at one level of a food chain passes to the next level — the other ninety percent is used up living and moving. This is exactly why an ecosystem can feed thousands of grass plants, hundreds of gazelles, but only a handful of lions.

Let us work through the energy idea with numbers, step by step. Suppose the grass in one area captures 10,000 units of energy from the sun. Only about ten percent passes to the next level each time.

The grass (producer) holds 10,000 units of energy.

The gazelle (primary consumer) eats grass and receives about ten percent of 10,000, which is 1,000 units.

The lion (secondary consumer) eats the gazelle and receives about ten percent of 1,000, which is 100 units.

If a bigger predator ate the lion, it would receive only about 10 units — very little energy indeed.
concept-5-food-chains-food-webs-and-the-.example: Notice how quickly the energy shrinks: 10,000, then 1,000, then 100, then 10. After only a few steps there is almost nothing left. This is the clearest way to understand why food chains are short and why top predators must be few in number. When your AI tutor gives you a starting energy amount, you can find each level by taking ten percent — that is, dividing by ten — each time you move up the chain.

concept-6-human-impact-and-caring-for-th.explanation:
Human beings are part of ecosystems too, and our actions can help or harm them. Sadly, many human activities damage the natural world, and East Africa faces several of these challenges directly. Understanding the problems is the first step to solving them.

Deforestation means cutting down forests and trees, often for firewood, charcoal, or to clear land for farming. Trees are producers and homes; when they are removed, the animals that lived among them lose their habitat, the soil is no longer held by roots and washes away, and less rain may fall. Overfishing happens when people catch fish faster than the fish can breed and replace themselves. Along the Indian Ocean coast, taking too many fish can cause fish populations to collapse, hurting both the ocean food web and the families who depend on fishing for food and income.

Plastic pollution is a growing danger, especially on beaches and in the ocean. Plastic bags and bottles dropped on the sand are washed into the sea, where turtles may swallow them thinking they are jellyfish, and fish become tangled. Plastic does not decompose for hundreds of years. Drought, made worse by a changing climate, dries up waterholes and rivers, kills crops and grass, and forces both wild animals and herders with their camels and goats to travel far in search of water. Each of these problems ripples through the food web, harming many species at once.

But there is very good news: people can also protect and repair ecosystems. This work is called conservation. Conservation includes replanting trees to bring back forests, setting up protected areas where wildlife is safe, fishing in careful limits so fish stocks recover, cleaning plastic from beaches, and saving water during dry seasons. Every one of us can take part — planting a tree, avoiding littering, saving water, and telling others why nature matters.

For a Muslim, caring for the Earth is part of faith. The Qur'an describes people as khalifah, meaning stewards or caretakers entrusted with looking after the world. The Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, taught kindness to animals and even encouraged the planting of trees. So when you protect a habitat, save water, or care for an animal, you are doing something both scientific and good. Observing creation closely, with wonder and care, is one of the beautiful ways to reflect on the One who made it all.

Did You Know? A single mature tree can give a home to hundreds of insects, birds, and small animals, which is why replanting forests helps so many species at once. Sea turtles along the East African coast can mistake floating plastic bags for jellyfish, which is one reason keeping beaches clean saves lives.
concept-6-human-impact-and-caring-for-th.example: [*] Remember — You Are a Khalifah! Human actions like deforestation, overfishing, and pollution can damage whole food webs. Conservation means protecting and repairing nature: plant trees, save water, keep beaches clean. Caring for the Earth is a responsibility we all share.

outcomes: By the end of this unit, you will be able to:
Tell the difference between a reversible change and an irreversible change, and give clear examples of each from your own life.
Explain the difference between a physical change and a chemical change, and describe the evidence that a new material has been made.
Describe what mixtures and solutions are, and how they are different from pure substances.
Investigate and choose the right method to separate a mixture, such as filtering, evaporating, sieving, or using a magnet.
Use particle theory — the idea that everything is made of tiny particles — to explain melting, dissolving, and other changes.
Identify the factors that make a solid dissolve faster, such as heat, stirring, and grinding into smaller pieces.
Connect what you learn to real life in your community, from rusting roofs to making yoghurt and collecting salt.

Before we begin, here are the important words for this unit. Do not try to memorise them all at once. You will meet each one many times, and they will start to feel familiar. Keep coming back to this table whenever you forget a word.
A change that can be undone, so you can get the original material back.

concept-1-two-big-families-of-change.explanation:
Every change you can think of belongs to one of two big families. The first family is reversible changes. These are changes you can undo, so the material goes back to how it started. The second family is irreversible changes. These are changes you cannot undo — once they happen, the material is different forever, and often a completely new material has been made.

Let us think about water. When Amina puts water in the freezer, it turns into hard ice. This is a change — the water went from liquid to solid. But is it reversible? Yes! If she takes the ice out and leaves it in the warm Mogadishu air, it melts straight back into water. Nothing was lost, and nothing new was made. Melting and freezing are reversible changes.

Now think about canjeero. When Khadija pours the runny, sour batter onto the hot pan, it bubbles, sets, and becomes soft, spongy bread. Can she ever turn that cooked canjeero back into runny batter? No, never. Cooking has made a new material with new properties — it looks different, feels different, and tastes different. Cooking is an irreversible change.

The easiest test to remember is this: ask yourself, "Can I get the exact original material back?" If the answer is yes, the change is reversible. If the answer is no, and especially if a new material seems to have appeared, the change is irreversible.

It also helps to know that reversible changes are usually about energy going in and out. When you add heat, ice melts; when you take heat away, water freezes again. The change follows the energy back and forth. Irreversible changes are different: once the new material is made, taking the energy away does not bring the old material back. A burnt log stays as ash no matter how much it cools. Holding on to this idea — reversible changes can go both ways, irreversible changes only go one way — will help you sort almost any change you meet.

Did You Know? A fried egg cannot be turned back into a raw egg no matter how much you cool it down. But melted candle wax or melted ghee will happily turn solid again when it cools. The difference is that cooking the egg made a brand new material, while melting the wax only changed its state.

Here are some reversible changes you already know: melting ghee in a hot pan, freezing water into ice, dissolving sugar or salt in water, boiling water into steam and letting the steam cool back into water, and squashing soft dough into a new shape. In every one of these, you could get the starting material back if you tried.

concept-2-physical-changes-and-chemical-.explanation:
Scientists have a more exact way of talking about the two families of change. They use the words physical change and chemical change. These are closely linked to reversible and irreversible, so once you understand one, the other becomes easy.

A physical change only changes how a material looks or what state it is in — solid, liquid, or gas. No new material is made. If you crush a lump of rock salt into powder, it is still salt. If you melt a block of ghee, it is still ghee, just in liquid form. If you tear a sheet of paper into small pieces, every piece is still paper. Physical changes are usually reversible, because the material itself has not truly changed — only its shape or state.

A chemical change is deeper. During a chemical change, the tiny particles rearrange themselves and join up in new ways, making one or more new materials with different properties. When Yusuf lights the charcoal, the black carbon joins with invisible oxygen from the air and turns into new gases and grey ash. The ash is nothing like the charcoal we started with. That is a chemical change, and it cannot be undone.

Because you cannot see the tiny particles moving, scientists look for clues or evidence that a chemical change has happened. Watch out for these signs:

A colour change — shiny grey iron slowly turns orange-brown when it rusts.

A gas is made — bubbles fizz up when vinegar meets baking soda, even though you added no air.

Heat or light is given out — burning charcoal glows and feels hot; this heat cooks your food.

A new smell — the smell of frying meat or baking bread comes from brand new materials.

A change that will not reverse — once the new material is made, you cannot get the old one back.

If you see one or more of these clues, you are almost certainly watching a chemical change. If you see none of them and the material only changed shape or state, it is probably a physical change.
concept-2-physical-changes-and-chemical-.example: Did You Know? When milk becomes yoghurt, tiny helpful living things called bacteria change the milk sugar into acid. That acid makes the milk thick and gives yoghurt its sour taste — a real chemical change happening in your kitchen. This is why yoghurt (caano fadhi) can never be turned back into fresh milk.

concept-3-rusting-burning-and-cooking.explanation:
Three of the most important irreversible changes in your life are rusting, burning, and cooking. Let us look at each one closely, because they show up everywhere in your community.

Along the humid coast near Mombasa, Berbera, and Lamu, you will see metal roofs, nails, gates, and fishing hooks slowly turning orange and crumbly. This is rusting. Rust forms when iron meets both water and oxygen from the air over time. The iron joins with the oxygen to make a new orange material called iron oxide, which is soft and flaky, not strong like iron. This is why old tools break and roofs get holes. Rusting is a chemical change, and it happens faster where the air is damp and salty, which is exactly why coastal metal rusts quicker than metal in dry Garissa.

People slow down rusting by keeping iron dry, by painting it, or by covering it with oil or grease. A painted gate or an oiled knife lasts much longer, because the paint and oil keep the water and oxygen away from the iron.

When Omar burns charcoal or firewood to cook, the fuel joins with oxygen from the air and gives out heat and light. New materials are made — gases that float away and grey ash that is left behind. You can never turn the ash and smoke back into charcoal, so burning is an irreversible chemical change. Burning is very useful, but it must always be done carefully and with an adult, because fire can spread and the smoke can be harmful to breathe in a closed room.

Cooking is a chemical change that we do on purpose because it makes food safe and tasty. When Sahra fries an egg, the runny clear part turns solid and white forever. When Ibrahim bakes bread or canjeero, the soft dough becomes firm bread. When goat meat roasts over the coals, it changes colour, smell, and texture. None of these can be undone. New materials have been made, and that is what makes cooked food different from raw food.

It is worth noticing that heat causes both reversible and irreversible changes, so heat alone is not the difference. When you heat ghee it melts, and that is reversible — the ghee is still ghee. But when you heat an egg it sets solid forever, and that is irreversible — a new material has formed. The real question is always the same: did a new material appear, or did the material only change its state? Melting the ghee only changed its state, but cooking the egg made something new. Keep this in mind, because it is one of the easiest points to get confused about.

concept-4-mixtures-and-pure-substances.explanation:
Not every change makes a new material. Sometimes we simply mix materials together. A mixture is two or more materials that are stirred or jumbled together but are not joined chemically. The important thing about a mixture is that each material keeps its own properties, and — here is the key idea — you can usually separate them again.

Think of a bag of rice (bariis) that has small stones mixed in. The rice is still rice and the stones are still stones. They are just sitting together. With patience you can pick out every stone, because nothing new was made. That is a mixture. In the same way, sand mixed with iron filings, or beans mixed with lentils, or tea leaves floating in water, are all mixtures.

A pure substance, on the other hand, is made of only one kind of material, like clean water or pure salt. There is nothing else mixed in. Most things around you are actually mixtures, not pure substances — even the air you breathe is a mixture of several gases, and seawater is a mixture of water and many dissolved salts.

concept-5-solutions-and-dissolving.explanation:
A solution is a very special kind of mixture. It forms when a solid dissolves completely into a liquid, spreading out so evenly that you cannot see it any more. When you stir sugar into hot shaah and it vanishes, you have made a solution. The tea now tastes sweet, so you know the sugar is still there — it has not disappeared, it has just spread out into tiny particles that are too small to see.

Scientists give the parts of a solution special names. The solid that dissolves is called the solute. The liquid that does the dissolving is called the solvent. And the sweet or salty mixture they make together is the solution. So in a cup of sweet shaah, sugar is the solute, tea is the solvent, and sweet tea is the solution. In seawater, salt is the solute, water is the solvent, and salty water is the solution.

It is very important to understand that dissolving is a reversible change and a physical change. The sugar has not turned into a new material — it is still sugar, just hidden. If you gently heat the solution and let all the water evaporate away, the sugar or salt will be left behind, exactly as it was. This is a wonderful proof that the solute never truly disappeared.

You may have noticed that sugar dissolves much faster in hot shaah than in cold water. Scientists have found three main things that make a solid dissolve faster:

Heat — warming the liquid makes its particles move faster, so they bump into the solute and break it apart more quickly. Sugar melts into hot tea almost at once.

Stirring — stirring with a spoon keeps fresh liquid moving past the solute, carrying the dissolved particles away and speeding things up.

Smaller pieces — crushing or grinding the solid into a fine powder gives the liquid more surface to work on, so it dissolves faster than one big lump.

There is also a limit to how much can dissolve. If Maryam keeps adding salt to a cup of water and stirring, at some point no more salt will dissolve, and extra salt just sits at the bottom. We then say the solution is saturated — it is full and cannot hold any more. Warming the water usually lets a little more dissolve.

concept-6-separating-mixtures.explanation:
Because the materials in a mixture are not chemically joined, we can pull them apart again. This is called separation, and choosing the right method depends on the mixture. Here are the main methods you should know.

Picking or sorting by hand — useful when the pieces are big enough to see, like taking stones out of rice.

Sieving — shaking a mixture through a sieve or mesh lets small pieces fall through while large pieces stay on top, like sifting flour to remove lumps.

Using a magnet — a magnet pulls out iron pieces from a mixture, because only iron and a few metals are magnetic. This separates iron filings from sand.

Filtering — pouring a mixture of liquid and an undissolved solid through cloth or a filter catches the solid and lets the clean liquid through, like straining tea leaves or cleaning muddy water through a cloth.

Evaporating — gently heating a solution until the liquid turns to gas and floats away, leaving the dissolved solid behind. This is exactly how people collect salt from seawater.

The clever part is that you often need more than one method for a tricky mixture. Imagine a mixture of iron filings, sand, and salt. First you use a magnet to pull out the iron. Then you add water so the salt dissolves but the sand does not, and you filter to catch the sand and keep the salty water. Finally you evaporate the salty water to leave pure salt behind. Three methods, one clever plan.

Along the East African coast, people have collected salt this way for hundreds of years. They let seawater flow into shallow pans dug into the ground. The strong sun evaporates the water, and gleaming white salt is left behind to be gathered, dried, and sold. It is a beautiful example of separating a solution using nothing but sunshine.

we01.solution:
Problem: Zahra has accidentally mixed together a spoon of sand, a spoon of salt, and some small iron filings in one bowl. She wants to separate all three back into clean, separate piles. How can she do it?

Step 1 — Look at the properties. Iron is magnetic; sand and salt are not. Salt dissolves in water; sand and iron do not. These two facts are the keys to the whole plan.

Step 2 — Remove the iron first. Move a magnet over the dry mixture. The iron filings jump to the magnet, and Zahra lifts them clean away. Now only sand and salt are left.

Step 3 — Dissolve the salt. Add water and stir. The salt dissolves and disappears into the water, but the sand sinks and stays solid. Now she has a mixture of salty water and sand.

concept-1-a-force-is-a-push-or-a-pull.explanation:
Everything begins with one simple idea. A force is a push or a pull. That is it. When you push open a wooden door, you use a force. When you pull a bucket of water up from a well, you use a force. A force can never be seen with your eyes, but you can always see or feel what it does. Forces are like the wind: you do not see the wind itself, only the way it bends the acacia trees and fills the sail of a dhow.

Every force has two important features. The first is its size — how strong the push or pull is. Pushing a small child on a swing needs a gentle force; pushing a fully loaded donkey cart out of soft sand needs a much larger force. The second feature is its direction — which way the push or pull points. If you push a football to the left, it rolls left. If you push it forward, it rolls forward. Because forces have both size and direction, scientists draw them as arrows. A longer arrow means a bigger force, and the way the arrow points shows the direction of the force.

Some forces work only when two objects touch each other. These are contact forces. When you kick a ball, cut vegetables with a knife, or push a wheelbarrow, your object must touch the thing it moves. Other forces can act across a gap without touching. These are non-contact forces. Gravity is the most important non-contact force: the Earth pulls a mango down even though the Earth is not touching the mango. A magnet pulling a nail from a small distance is another non-contact force you may have seen.

Did You Know? A force is measured in a unit called the newton, written with a capital N. It is named after Sir Isaac Newton, an English scientist who lived over 300 years ago. The story says he began thinking about gravity after watching an apple fall from a tree — much like a mango falling in your own garden.

concept-2-gravity-mass-and-weight.explanation:
Hold a stone in your hand and let go. It drops straight down. Every single time, no matter where you stand, objects fall toward the ground. The force that pulls them down is gravity. Gravity is the pull between any two objects that have mass, but the Earth is so enormous that its gravity is the pull we notice most. Earth's gravity reaches out and pulls everything toward the centre of the planet. That is why a dropped mango falls down and never sideways or up.

To understand gravity properly, you must learn the difference between two words that people often mix up: mass and weight. They are not the same thing, and keeping them separate is one of the most important ideas in this whole unit.

Mass is the amount of matter — the amount of 'stuff' — inside an object. Mass is measured in grams (g) and kilograms (kg). A bag of rice with a mass of 5 kg contains a certain amount of rice, and that amount never changes. Whether you carry that bag in Nairobi, on top of a mountain, or all the way to the Moon, it still contains exactly 5 kg of rice. Mass stays the same everywhere in the universe because the amount of stuff has not changed.

Weight is different. Weight is the force of gravity pulling on that mass, and because it is a force, it is measured in newtons (N). Weight can change. On the Moon, gravity is much weaker than on Earth — only about one sixth as strong. So your 5 kg bag of rice would still have a mass of 5 kg on the Moon, but it would weigh far less because the Moon pulls on it more gently. Mass is about how much stuff there is; weight is about how hard gravity pulls on that stuff.

On Earth, there is a simple rule that connects mass and weight. For every 1 kilogram of mass, gravity pulls with a force of about 10 newtons. Scientists call this number the gravitational field strength, and on Earth it is about 10 newtons for every kilogram (written 10 N/kg). This gives us a very useful rule that you will use again and again:

Weight = mass x gravity, or in short, W = m x g, where g = 10 N/kg on Earth.

This rule lets you work out the weight of anything if you know its mass. It also explains why a bigger mass always weighs more: the more matter there is, the harder gravity pulls. A camel has a much greater mass than a chicken, so gravity pulls on the camel with a far greater force, and the camel weighs much more.

Let us practise the weight rule together, one careful step at a time. Read each example slowly and make sure you understand every line before moving on. Keep the rule in front of you: Weight = mass x gravity, and on Earth gravity g = 10 N/kg.

Amina buys a bag of rice with a mass of 5 kg in the market at Garissa. What is its weight on Earth?

Write down what you know. Mass m = 5 kg. Gravity g = 10 N/kg.

Write the answer with the correct unit. The weight of the rice is 50 newtons (50 N).

Notice that the mass is written in kilograms and the answer is written in newtons. Weight is always a force, so it is always measured in newtons, never in kilograms.

concept-3-friction-the-force-that-grips-.explanation:
Push a wooden box across the floor and let go. It slides a little way and then stops. What made it stop? A force called friction. Friction is a force that appears whenever two surfaces rub against each other, and it always pushes against the direction of movement. When the box slides forward, friction pushes backward and slows it down until it stops.

Friction depends on how rough or smooth the surfaces are. Two rough surfaces rubbing together produce a large friction force. Two smooth surfaces produce much less. You can feel this difference under your own feet. Think about walking on a sandy road near the coast: the loose, gritty sand grips your sandals, and it takes real effort to drag your feet or push a cart through it. Now think about walking on a smooth paved road in the city: your feet slide along easily and a cart rolls with far less effort. The paved road has less friction than the sandy road.

Did You Know? Friction always turns movement energy into heat. Rub your two hands together quickly and you will feel them grow warm — that heat comes from friction. This is the same reason bicycle brakes and car tyres become hot after being used for a long time.

It is easy to think of friction as a nuisance because it slows things down and wears them out. But friction is often our friend. Without friction between your sandals and the ground, you could not walk at all — your feet would slip out from under you like they do on wet, slippery mud. Friction lets a footballer stop and turn quickly. Friction lets the wheels of a car grip the road instead of spinning uselessly. Friction lets you hold a pencil without it sliding out of your fingers. Whenever you need grip, friction is helping you.

At other times we want less friction. A fisherman greases the moving parts of his boat so they slide smoothly. Machine parts are oiled so they do not wear each other away. Race cars and even dhows are shaped to slip through air and water with as little resistance as possible. Learning when to increase friction and when to reduce it is a big part of engineering.

concept-4-air-resistance-and-water-resis.explanation:
Air and water are all around us, and although they feel light and thin, they push back against anything that moves through them. Air resistance is a special kind of friction between a moving object and the air it pushes through. It is also called drag. The faster you move and the bigger your surface, the more air resistance you feel. Run fast on a windy day and you can feel the air pushing against your chest and face.

The clearest example of air resistance is a parachute. When a person jumps and opens a parachute, the wide sheet of cloth traps a huge amount of air beneath it. The air cannot rush out of the way quickly, so it pushes up hard against the parachute. This large upward air resistance balances much of the downward pull of gravity, so the person floats down gently and safely instead of falling fast. You can see the same idea when a light seed or a piece of paper drifts slowly to the ground while a stone drops straight down — the flat, light object catches far more air.

Water resistance works in the same way but in water. Anything that moves through water must push the water aside, and the water pushes back. A fisherman on the Indian Ocean feels water resistance every time he pulls a net through the sea. A swimmer feels it with every stroke. This is why fish have smooth, pointed, streamlined bodies: a streamlined shape lets water slide past easily, so the fish can move quickly using less effort. Boats and dhows are built with narrow, smooth hulls for exactly the same reason — to reduce water resistance and glide more easily across the waves.
concept-4-air-resistance-and-water-resis.example: Interestingly, the wind can also be a helpful pushing force rather than a resistance. When a dhow raises its sail on the Indian Ocean, the sailors are using the force of the wind to push the whole boat forward. Here the moving air is not slowing the boat down — it is providing the push that carries cargo and fishermen up and down the coast. The very same air that resists a running child can drive a heavy boat across the sea when it is caught in a sail. Forces depend on how we use them.

concept-5-balanced-and-unbalanced-forces.explanation:
Usually more than one force acts on an object at the same time. To predict what will happen, you must add up all the forces and see which way they win. This is where the ideas of balanced and unbalanced forces come in, and they are the key to predicting motion.

Balanced forces are forces that are equal in size but pull or push in opposite directions, so they cancel each other out. When forces are balanced, there is no overall force, and so the motion of the object does not change. Think of a book resting on a table. Gravity pulls the book down, and the table pushes the book up with exactly the same force. The two forces are balanced, so the book stays perfectly still. In a game of tug-of-war, when two evenly matched teams pull the rope in opposite directions with equal force, the rope does not move — the forces are balanced.

Unbalanced forces are forces that are not equal. When forces are unbalanced, there is an overall force — scientists call it a net force — pushing one way, and this net force changes the object's motion. The object may start moving, speed up, slow down, stop, or change direction. In that same tug-of-war, the moment one team pulls harder than the other, the forces become unbalanced and the rope suddenly moves toward the stronger team.

You can find the net force by simple adding and subtracting. If two forces push the same way, you add them together. If two forces push in opposite directions, you subtract the smaller from the larger, and the net force points in the direction of the larger force. For example, imagine two friends pushing a stuck donkey cart. Yusuf pushes forward with 100 N and Omar pushes forward with 80 N. Both push the same way, so the total forward force is 100 + 80 = 180 N. Now suppose friction pushes back against them with 150 N. The net force is 180 — 150 = 30 N forward. Because there is a leftover forward force of 30 N, the cart finally begins to roll forward.

A football is being blown by the wind. The wind pushes it to the right with a force of 12 N. A child kicks it to the left with a force of 20 N. What is the net force, and which way does the ball go?

List the forces. Wind: 12 N to the right. Kick: 20 N to the left.

The forces are in opposite directions, so subtract. 20 — 12 = 8.

concept-6-measuring-forces-in-newtons.example: Did You Know? A medium-sized apple or mango weighs roughly 1 to 3 newtons. A 1-litre bottle of water weighs about 10 newtons. A Year 6 pupil with a mass of about 35 kg weighs around 350 newtons — that is how hard gravity pulls you toward the Earth right now.
