sci-g07-u02.unitOverview: Look around you right now. The device you are reading this on, the air you are breathing, the water in the well or tap near your home, the goat milk cooling in a clay pot, the salt sprinkled on your bariis — every single one of these is made of matter. And here is one of the most powerful ideas in all of science: even though these things look completely different, they are all built from unbelievably tiny pieces called particles. In this unit you will learn to see the world the way a scientist does, imagining the invisible particles that make up everything, and using that idea to explain things you have seen your whole life but perhaps never questioned.
outcomes: By the end of this unit, you should be able to do each of the following. Keep this list close, and tick each item off when you are confident.
Describe the three states of matter — solid, liquid and gas — in terms of the arrangement, movement and energy of their particles.
Use the particle model to explain everyday properties, such as why solids keep their shape, why liquids flow and take the shape of their container, and why gases spread out to fill any space.
Explain changes of state (melting, freezing, evaporation, boiling, condensation and sublimation) in terms of particles gaining or losing energy.
Describe the water cycle and connect it to the seasonal rains of East Africa, using the particle model to explain evaporation and condensation.
Define atoms and elements, and explain that an element is made of only one type of atom.
Distinguish between an element, a compound and a mixture, and give local examples of each.
Explain how mixtures can be separated using methods such as filtration, evaporation and distillation.
Apply these ideas to real situations, such as separating salt from seawater or cleaning muddy water for safe drinking.

Before we build our understanding, study this table of the most important words in the unit. You will meet each of them again and again. Read the example in the third column carefully — it links the science to things you already know.

concept-1-everything-is-made-of-particle.example: Notice that the model is invisible — you cannot see particles directly. So how do scientists know they exist? They know because the model explains and predicts so many things we can see. This is how science works: a good model must account for the evidence. When you see a drop of dye spreading through a glass of water without anyone stirring it, you are watching the particles move all by themselves. That silent spreading is called diffusion, and it is powerful evidence that particles are real and always moving.

concept-2-the-three-states-of-matter.explanation:
All the matter you have ever touched exists in one of three main states: solid, liquid or gas. What makes them different is not what the particles are, but how the particles are arranged, how they move, and how strongly they are held together. Let us build a clear picture of each one.

Think of a stone from the Jubba River, a block of ice, or a lump of frankincense resin. In a solid, the particles are packed very closely together, usually in a neat, regular pattern like oranges stacked carefully in a market stall. The forces of attraction between the particles are strong, holding each particle firmly in its place. The particles are not completely still — they vibrate back and forth — but they cannot move away from their fixed positions. This is why a solid keeps its own shape and has a fixed volume. You cannot squash a stone into a smaller space because there is almost no gap between its particles.

Now think of water in a jerrycan, camel milk in a bowl, or cooking oil in a pan. In a liquid, the particles are still close together — almost touching — but they are no longer locked in a fixed pattern. The forces between them are weaker than in a solid, so the particles can slide and roll past one another. This is why a liquid can flow and why it takes the shape of its container while still keeping a fixed volume. Pour water from a round pot into a tall glass and its shape changes, but the amount of water stays the same.

Finally, think of the air around you, the steam above a boiling pot, or the gas that fills a football. In a gas, the particles are spread far apart with large empty spaces between them. The forces of attraction are so weak that they hardly matter, so the particles zoom around freely and quickly in all directions. This is why a gas has no fixed shape and no fixed volume — it spreads out to fill whatever container it is in. It is also why a gas can be squashed (compressed): there is plenty of empty space to push the particles into. When you pump air into a bicycle tyre, you are forcing more and more gas particles into a small space.

The table below summarises everything. Study it until you can reproduce it from memory, because it explains almost every property of materials you will ever meet.

Did You Know? There is a fourth state of matter called plasma, and it is actually the most common state in the whole universe. The Sun that ripens the mangoes and dries the coastal salt pans is a giant ball of glowing plasma — a superheated gas whose particles carry electric charge. So the three states you handle every day are only part of the full story of matter.
concept-2-the-three-states-of-matter.example: A helpful way to picture the three states is to imagine a group of children. In the solid state, the children stand in a tight, neat grid, holding hands firmly and only able to sway on the spot. In the liquid state, they let go of a few hands and begin to shuffle and slide around each other, still close but no longer in rows. In the gas state, they release all hands and run around the whole playground as fast as they can, far apart from one another. Same children, three very different behaviours — and the only thing that changed was how much energy they had.

concept-3-changes-of-state.explanation:
Here is one of the most important ideas in this unit: the same substance can exist in all three states, and it can change from one to another. Water is the perfect example. It can be solid ice, liquid water, or a gas called water vapour. It is still water the whole time — the same particles — but the way those particles behave has changed. What causes the change? Energy, usually in the form of heat.

When you heat a substance, you give its particles more energy. They vibrate and move faster, and eventually they have enough energy to break free from the forces holding them in place. When you cool a substance, the particles lose energy, slow down, and the forces pull them back together. Every change of state has a name. Learn these carefully:

Melting — a solid changes to a liquid when heated (ice to water). The temperature at which this happens is the melting point.

Freezing — a liquid changes to a solid when cooled (water to ice). This happens at the freezing point, which is the same temperature as the melting point.

Evaporation — a liquid changes to a gas at the surface, at temperatures below boiling point (a puddle drying in the sun).

Boiling — a liquid changes to a gas rapidly throughout the whole liquid, at the boiling point (bubbles rising in a pot of tea).

Condensation — a gas changes to a liquid when cooled (steam forming droplets on a cold surface).

Sublimation — a few substances change directly from solid to gas without becoming liquid (dry ice, or frankincense smoke rising from burning resin).

Notice something clever about the words. Melting and freezing are opposites. Evaporation/boiling and condensation are opposites. Adding energy pushes a substance towards the gas state; removing energy pushes it towards the solid state. If you can hold that one idea in your mind, you can predict any change of state.

The special truth about boiling and melting temperatures

concept-4-the-water-cycle-and-the-east-a.explanation:
Now let us use everything we have learned to explain something that shapes the lives of millions of people across East Africa: the water cycle, and the seasonal rains known as the Gu (the long rains around April to June) and the Deyr (the shorter rains around October to December). Farmers and herders watch the skies for these rains because their crops, their goats, cattle and camels depend on them. Behind those clouds is pure particle science.

Follow the journey of a single water particle. It begins in the Indian Ocean. The hot sun shines on the surface, giving the water particles energy. The fastest particles at the surface break free and float up into the air as invisible water vapour — this is evaporation. As the warm, moist air rises high into the sky, it cools down. The water vapour loses energy, and the particles slow and join together into tiny droplets of liquid water — this is condensation. Billions of these droplets together form the clouds you see gathering before the Gu rains.

The wind carries these clouds over the land — over Mogadishu, over the Rift Valley, over the highlands. When the droplets grow heavy enough, they fall as rain (this is called precipitation). Some rain soaks into the ground to fill wells and feed the roots of acacia and mango trees. Some flows into the Jubba and other rivers, and eventually makes its way back to the ocean. Then the sun shines again, and the whole cycle repeats — endlessly, silently, driven entirely by the Sun heating water particles and the sky cooling them.

Did You Know? The water you drank this morning may once have flowed in the Jubba River, evaporated from the Indian Ocean, floated over the Arabian Peninsula, or even been part of a cloud a thousand years ago in the time of your ancestors. Water is never created or destroyed on Earth — the same water is recycled again and again through the water cycle. Every raindrop is ancient.
concept-4-the-water-cycle-and-the-east-a.example: Understanding the water cycle is not only beautiful — it is practical. It helps us understand drought, which happens when the rains fail. It helps us see why keeping wells and rivers clean matters, since the same water is used over and over. And it reminds us of our duty, as Muslims, to be careful stewards (khalifah) of water, never wasting it, because it is a trust and a mercy that the whole community shares.

concept-5-atoms-and-elements-the-alphabe.explanation:
So far we have talked about 'particles'. Now we go one level deeper. The smallest particle of a pure substance like iron or oxygen is called an atom. Atoms are the true building blocks of all matter, and they are almost unimaginably small — millions of them would fit across the width of a single one of your hairs.

A substance made of only one type of atom is called an element. Elements are the simplest pure substances there are; you cannot break an element down into anything simpler by ordinary means. Think of elements as the letters of an alphabet. Just as every word in Somali, Arabic or English is built from a small set of letters, everything in the entire universe is built from about 100 different elements. Some elements you already know:

Oxygen — the element in the air that you and every goat, camel and person must breathe to live.

Iron — the strong metal used to make tools, cooking pots, gates and the frames of buildings.

Gold — a precious element used for jewellery, valued for its beautiful shine that never rusts.

Carbon — found in charcoal used for cooking, in the diamond of a ring, and inside every living thing, including you.

Aluminium — a light, strong metal used for cooking pots and drinks cans.

Hydrogen — the lightest element of all, and part of every drop of water.
concept-5-atoms-and-elements-the-alphabe.example: Scientists arrange all the known elements in a giant chart called the Periodic Table. Each element has a short chemical symbol — a kind of shorthand. Oxygen is written as O, hydrogen as H, carbon as C, iron as Fe, and gold as Au. These symbols are used by scientists all over the world, so a chemist in Nairobi, Cairo or Tokyo can all read the same 'chemical language'. You do not need to memorise the whole table this year, but you should be comfortable with the idea that a small number of elements combine to make everything.

concept-6-compounds-and-mixtures-how-ato.explanation:
Elements rarely stay by themselves. They join with other elements to make new substances. There are two very different ways this can happen, and telling them apart is one of the most important skills in chemistry: the difference between a compound and a mixture.

A compound is formed when atoms of two or more elements join together chemically. This is a strong, permanent joining — the atoms are locked together, and the new substance has completely different properties from the elements that made it. The most important example is water. Water is a compound of two elements: hydrogen and oxygen, joined in a fixed ratio (its chemical formula is H2O, meaning two hydrogen atoms joined to one oxygen atom). Think about how amazing this is: hydrogen is an explosive gas, and oxygen is a gas that helps things burn — yet when they join chemically, they make water, the very thing we use to put out fires and to drink. The compound is nothing like its ingredients.

Another everyday compound is table salt, which chemists call sodium chloride. It is made of the elements sodium (a soft, dangerous metal that reacts violently with water) and chlorine (a poisonous green gas). Joined chemically, they make the harmless white crystals that flavour your food and that coastal families harvest from the sea. To separate the elements in a compound, you need a chemical reaction — simply stirring or filtering will never do it.

A mixture is completely different. In a mixture, two or more substances are simply mixed together without joining chemically. The substances keep their own properties, and they are usually easy to separate again. There is no fixed ratio — you can have a little or a lot of each part. Look around and you will find mixtures everywhere in daily life:

Air is a mixture of gases — mostly nitrogen and oxygen, with small amounts of others.

Seawater is a mixture of pure water and dissolved salts.

Sweet tea is a mixture of water, tea and sugar — and you can make it more or less sweet, proving there is no fixed ratio.

Sand and water stirred in a bucket is a mixture you can easily separate again.

Muddy river water is a mixture of clean water with soil and grit.

Soil is a mixture of sand, clay, tiny stones, water and bits of dead plants.

The key difference is the word chemically. In a compound, elements are chemically joined and hard to separate. In a mixture, substances are only physically mixed and are usually easy to separate. Study the comparison table below carefully — this is a favourite topic for exam questions.

New properties, different from the elements
concept-6-compounds-and-mixtures-how-ato.example: Did You Know? Sea salt harvested along the Indian Ocean coast is actually a mixture that contains the compound sodium chloride plus small amounts of other minerals like magnesium and calcium salts. That is why natural sea salt can taste slightly different from factory-made table salt — the extra minerals in the mixture add their own subtle flavours.

Look closely at the underside of the cold spoon. Record what you see forming on it.
Observation Recording Sheet

Observe that the water looks clear — the salt has not disappeared, it has dissolved and spread through the water.

Step 1 — Think about the properties. Sand is an insoluble solid (it does not dissolve). Salt is a soluble solid (it dissolves). Water is the liquid. Each property points to a method.

Step 2 — Filter to remove the sand. Amina pours the mixture through a filter cloth. The sand is trapped as residue on the cloth. What passes through is salty water (the filtrate), because the dissolved salt is too small to be trapped. She now has wet sand and a jar of salty water.

Step 3 — Dry the sand. Amina spreads the wet sand in the sun. The water evaporates, leaving dry sand. That is her first separated substance.

Step 4 — Get the salt and water. Now she must decide: does she want the salt, the water, or both? If she only wants the salt, she evaporates the salty water in a shallow dish in the sun, and dry salt is left behind. If she wants the clean water too, she uses distillation instead: she boils the salty water, leads the steam to a cool surface, and collects the pure water as it condenses, while the salt stays behind.

concept-1-sorting-life-into-big-groups-t.explanation:
Once we agree that something is alive, the next question is: what kind of living thing is it? To answer this, biologists sort all organisms into a few very large groups called kingdoms. Think of a kingdom as the biggest box on the shelf. Inside each big box are smaller boxes, and inside those are smaller boxes still, until finally we reach a single species. Sorting life into groups like this is called classification.

Scientists have used different numbers of kingdoms over the years. A simple and common system uses five kingdoms. Some newer systems split these further into six or seven groups, but the five-kingdom idea is a clear place to start.

Many cells; cannot make their own food, so must eat other organisms; usually move about.

Lions, camels, flamingos, tilapia, beetles, humans.

Many cells; make their own food by photosynthesis using sunlight; usually green; do not move about.

Made of cells with walls but no chlorophyll; feed on dead or living material; reproduce by spores.

Mostly single-celled; a mixed group; some are like tiny animals, some like tiny plants.

Amoeba; the parasite that causes malaria; many pond algae.

Single-celled and very tiny; have cell walls but no nucleus; found almost everywhere.

The bacteria in soil, in yoghurt and camel milk, and some that cause disease.

Notice how the kingdoms are separated by big, clear differences: whether an organism makes its own food or eats others, whether it is made of one cell or many, and whether its cells have a nucleus. These same 'either/or' differences are exactly the kind of questions we will use later to build identification keys.

It helps to think of classification as a set of boxes inside boxes, getting smaller as you go in. The kingdom is the biggest box. Inside a kingdom, organisms are sorted into a phylum, then into a class, and on through smaller and smaller groups until you reach a single species. You do not need to memorise every level in Year 7, but it is worth knowing the idea: a camel and a lion share the same kingdom (animals) and even the same class (mammals), but they part ways lower down, ending in two different species. The closer two organisms sit in this system of boxes, the more features they share. This is why a camel is far more like a goat than either is like an acacia tree.

The animal kingdom is huge, so biologists split it in two using a single important feature: the backbone, also called the spine. Run your fingers down the middle of your back and you will feel a line of small bones — that is your backbone. Animals with a backbone are called vertebrates. Animals without a backbone are called invertebrates.

The vertebrates are divided into five familiar classes. Fish (such as tilapia and Nile perch) live in water and breathe using gills. Amphibians (such as frogs) live partly in water and partly on land. Reptiles (such as lizards, snakes and crocodiles) have dry, scaly skin. Birds (such as flamingos, ostriches and chickens) have feathers and wings. Mammals (such as camels, lions, elephants and humans) have hair or fur and feed their young on milk.

Even though vertebrates are the animals we notice most easily, they are actually the minority. The great majority of animals on Earth — well over nine out of every ten known species — are invertebrates. These include insects (beetles, mosquitoes, bees, grasshoppers), spiders and scorpions, crabs and prawns from the Indian Ocean coast, and worms and snails from the soil. The mosquito that spreads malaria is an invertebrate, which is why classifying and understanding insects can be a matter of life and health.

One quick trick to tell an insect from a spider — two invertebrates people often mix up — is to count the legs. An insect always has six legs and its body is in three parts; a spider has eight legs and its body is in two parts. So the beetle Khadija finds on the windowsill is an insect, but the small creature spinning a web in the corner is a spider. This single 'six legs or eight legs?' question is a perfect example of the clear, either-or thinking you will use when you build a key later in this unit. Careful counting beats guessing every time.

Did You Know? There are more kinds of beetle than any other type of animal on Earth — well over 350,000 described species, with more found every year. If you gathered every animal species and picked one at random, there is a good chance it would be a beetle.

Some things sit right on the border between living and non-living, and the most famous example is the virus. Viruses are the cause of illnesses you will know well: the common cold, influenza (flu), measles, and COVID-19, which is caused by a virus called SARS-CoV-2.

Viruses are astonishingly small — far smaller than one of your own cells. You cannot see a virus with an ordinary school microscope, no matter how good it is. To see one, scientists use a special and very powerful instrument called an electron microscope, which uses beams of electrons instead of light. In photographs from an electron microscope, viruses are shown magnified around 100,000 times, and even then they look tiny.

A virus has a very simple structure. On the outside is a coat made of protein. Sticking out of this coat are little pegs or spikes. Inside the coat is the virus's set of instructions, written in genetic material such as RNA. That is almost all there is to a virus: instructions wrapped in a protein coat. A virus is not made of cells. It has no cell membrane, no cytoplasm and no nucleus.

Here is the crucial point. On its own, a virus can do nothing at all. It does not respire, does not feed, does not grow, does not excrete, is not sensitive and cannot move. It is only when a virus gets inside a living cell that anything happens. The spikes on the coat let the virus stick to one of your cells and slip inside. Once in, the virus forces your cell to read its instructions and build many new copies of the virus. This copying is called replication. The new viruses then burst out, usually killing the cell, and spread to infect more cells. That is what makes you feel ill.

Did You Know? The H3N2 influenza virus that spread around the world in 1968 and 1969 caused a flu pandemic that is thought to have killed around one million people. A particle far too small to see with a school microscope changed the lives of millions — a powerful reminder of why hygiene matters.

So, are viruses alive? Scientists genuinely disagree. On one hand, a virus can reproduce (replicate) and it has genetic instructions, just like living things. On the other hand, it shows none of the other characteristics of life on its own — it cannot respire, feed, grow, excrete, sense or move without hijacking a living cell. For this reason, most biologists place viruses in a category of their own, on the borderline between living and non-living. There is no single 'correct' answer, and that is exactly what makes viruses such a fascinating puzzle.

Understanding viruses is also deeply practical. Because viruses spread from person to person, simple habits protect whole communities: washing your hands with soap and clean water, covering your mouth when you cough or sneeze, staying home when unwell, and taking vaccinations such as the measles vaccine. In Islam, cleanliness is greatly encouraged, and keeping yourself and your surroundings clean is one of the best defences against these invisible particles.

We have sorted life into kingdoms, and animals into vertebrates and invertebrates. But the smallest and most important group of all is the species. When you name a single kind of organism — a lion, a camel, an acacia tree — you are naming a species.

All the members of one species share the same basic characteristics, but they are not identical to one another. Some camels are taller, some are a lighter colour, some have longer eyelashes. These differences between members of the same species are called variation. Variation is completely normal — look around any classroom and you will see that all the students are human, yet no two are exactly alike.

Because of variation, it can be hard to decide whether two similar-looking organisms are the same species or two different species. Imagine two birds in your garden that look nearly the same. How can a scientist be sure? The clearest test is reproduction. Scientists define a species as a group of organisms that can reproduce together to produce fertile offspring.

The word fertile is the key. Fertile offspring are able to grow up and have young of their own. For example, the African elephant and the Indian elephant look similar but belong to two different species: they live in different places and normally do not reproduce together. By contrast, all camels can breed with one another and their calves can grow up and breed too, so all camels are one species.

Did You Know? Very rarely, a male lion and a female tiger kept together in a zoo produce a cub called a 'liger'. Ligers are healthy, but they are infertile — they cannot have young of their own. This is one of the strongest reasons scientists say lions and tigers are two different species, even though they can occasionally breed.

So when a scientist studies two kinds of parakeet and never once finds them making nests together in the wild, that is good evidence they are separate species. To be even more certain, the scientist would check many more pairs in the wild, because a single observation could be a coincidence. Careful, repeated observation is what turns a guess into scientific evidence.
concept-1-sorting-life-into-big-groups-t.example: There is a neat way to remember the species idea. Members of the same species usually look similar to one another, and look different from members of other species. But looks alone are not enough, because variation can make two members of one species look quite different, while two separate species can look almost the same. The reliable test is always reproduction: can they breed together and produce young that can, in turn, breed? For example, a donkey and a horse can produce a mule, but the mule is infertile — so donkeys and horses are two different species, just like lions and tigers. This is why scientists treat the 'fertile offspring' rule as the final word.

concept-2-identifying-organisms-with-key.explanation:
Suppose Amina finds an insect near Hargeisa that she has never seen before, and she wants to know its name. She could look through pictures in a book or on the internet and hope to spot a match — but with millions of species, that could take a very long time. Biologists have a much smarter tool: a key.

A key is a set of questions or statements about an organism. Each answer sends you to the next question, and you keep going until you arrive at the organism's name. The most common type is a dichotomous key. The word dichotomous means 'branching into two', because at every step you choose between exactly two options — yes or no, this or that.

A key can be written in two styles. The first style uses branching questions. You start at the top and follow the branches. For example, a simple key to sort five small animals — a crab, an earthworm, a housefly, a dragonfly and a slug — might work like this:

Does it have legs? If NO, ask: is its body made of rings? If yes it is an earthworm; if no it is a slug.

If it DOES have legs, ask: does it have more than six legs? If yes it is a crab.

If it has exactly six legs, ask: does it have four wings? If yes it is a dragonfly; if no it is a housefly.

The second style uses numbered pairs of statements. Instead of a picture with branches, you read a pair of statements, choose the one that fits, and it tells you which number to go to next. Here is exactly the same key written in the numbered style:

Both styles contain exactly the same information — they are just laid out differently. Many people find the numbered style easier because you never lose your place. Being able to change a key from one style to the other is a useful scientific skill.

Keys are used for far more than small animals. Scientists have keys to identify fish, birds, leaves, flowers, seeds and even bacteria grown in a laboratory. A fisherman on the Indian Ocean coast could use a key to name a fish by asking whether it has stripes, whether the stripes are vertical, and whether its fins have spines. A farmer could use a key to name a weed growing in the maize. Whatever the organism, the method is always the same: start at the top, answer one clear question at a time, and let each answer carry you closer to a single name. The power of a key is that it turns a hard problem — 'what on earth is this?' — into a short series of easy choices.

Worked Example: Using the Key Step by Step

Let us identify the dragonfly using the numbered key above. We will show every step so you can see exactly how a key is used. Imagine you are holding the whole animal and can look at it carefully.

Start at step 1. Look at the dragonfly. Does it have legs? Yes. Statement 1a says 'It has legs — go to 2.' So we go to step 2.

Step 2. Does it have exactly six legs? Yes, like all insects it has six legs. Statement 2a says 'It has exactly six legs — go to 4.' So we go to step 4.

Step 4. Does it have four wings? Yes, a dragonfly has four wings. Statement 4a says 'It has four wings — dragonfly.'

We have arrived at the answer: dragonfly. The path we followed was 1a, 2a, 4a.
concept-2-identifying-organisms-with-key.example: Now try the earthworm yourself before reading on. Start at step 1. An earthworm has no legs, so statement 1b sends you to step 3. At step 3, an earthworm's body is made of rings, so statement 3a gives the answer: earthworm. The path was 1b, 3a. Notice that you never needed steps 2 or 4 — a good key lets you reach an answer in as few steps as possible.

concept-3-building-your-own-key.explanation:
Using a key is one skill; making one is the real test of understanding. Suppose you want a key to tell apart four different leaves you collected from your compound — say an acacia leaf, a mango leaf, a maize leaf and an aloe vera leaf. Here is the method:

Lay out all four specimens and look for one feature that splits them into two groups. For example, 'Is the leaf long and narrow?' might put maize and aloe in one group, and acacia and mango in the other.

Take one group and find a feature that separates it into two. For example, among the long narrow leaves: 'Is the leaf thick and fleshy?' separates aloe vera (yes) from maize (no).

Repeat for the other group until every specimen is identified on its own.

Write your steps as numbered pairs, each ending either in another step or in the name of a leaf.

A good key follows two golden rules. First, every question must have a clear yes-or-no answer that anyone would agree on. 'Does the leaf have a smooth edge?' is a good question. 'Is the leaf pretty?' or 'Is the plant tall?' are bad questions, because different people will answer them differently — one person's 'tall' is another person's 'short'. Second, keep your key short: for four organisms you should need only three pairs of statements.
concept-3-building-your-own-key.example: Did You Know? Conservationists in East Africa use keys and careful classification to decide which animals are separate, endangered species that need protecting. Sometimes scientists disagree about whether two similar animals are one species or two — and that disagreement can decide whether a whole forest or habitat is saved. Classification is not just naming; it can protect creation.

concept-6-passage-halima-s-beetle.explanation: One warm afternoon in Garissa, Halima was helping her grandmother sort dried beans when a shiny black beetle scuttled across the mat. 'What is it?' she asked. Her older brother Yusuf, who was studying science, smiled. 'Let us find out like a scientist,' he said. 'First, is it alive?' Halima watched it move, saw it sense her shadow and dart away, and remembered it must also feed, grow, respire, excrete and one day reproduce. 'Yes,' she said, 'it shows all seven signs of life.' Yusuf nodded. 'Good. Now, does it have a backbone?' Halima thought. 'No — it has a hard shell on the outside instead. So it is an invertebrate, an insect.' Yusuf then drew a small key on paper: does it have wings, how many legs, what colour. Working through it together, they gave the beetle a name. 'You see,' Yusuf said, 'you did not need a book of a million pictures. You only needed careful questions, one at a time.' Halima grinned, already planning a key for every insect in the compound.

sci-g07-u05.unitOverview: Look around you right now. The spoon you eat your bariis with, the pot your mother boils camel milk in, the corrugated iron roof over your head, the plastic jerrycan you carry water in, the glass in the window, the lemon in the kitchen and the bar of soap by the washing basin — every single one of these is made from a material, and every material was chosen because of its properties. A property is simply a feature of a material and how it behaves. In this unit you will become a materials detective. You will learn why cooking pots are made of metal but their handles are often wrapped in plastic or cloth, why the iron sheets on a coastal roof in Berbera or Mombasa go rusty and orange while a gold ring stays shiny for a lifetime, and why a squeeze of…

Explain why a particular material is chosen for a particular job by linking its property to its use.

Study this table carefully. These words are the tools of a materials scientist. Notice how the example column ties each word to something you already know.

concept-1-the-metals.explanation:
Metals are among the most useful materials in the world. Think of everything made from metal in a busy market in Hargeisa or Nairobi: knives, pots, spoons, hoes, machetes, coins, wire, roofing sheets, water taps, padlocks and jewellery. Metals do so many different jobs because they share a set of very handy properties. Let us build up a picture of what makes a metal a metal.

Metals do not crack or shatter easily. When you drop a metal spoon on the floor it bounces and stays whole; drop a clay cup and it smashes. Because metals are strong, they can hold heavy weights without breaking. This is exactly why the great bridges that cross rivers, and the frames of tall buildings, are built from iron and steel.

When a metal is freshly cut or polished it reflects light and looks bright and shiny. This is why gold and silver are prized for jewellery — a polished gold ring catches the light beautifully, and because gold does not rust or tarnish it keeps that shine for generations. Notice, though, that the surface of most metals becomes dull after a while as the air slowly attacks it. Silver goes grey; copper turns a dull brown or even green.

These two words describe how metals can be shaped. Malleable means a metal can be hammered or pressed into a new shape without breaking — think of a blacksmith beating a red-hot bar of iron into the curved blade of a farming hoe. Ductile means a metal can be drawn out into thin wires — think of copper being stretched into the wire that carries electricity to a light bulb. A brittle material like charcoal could never do either; it would simply crumble.

Metals are excellent conductors. Heat energy flows through them easily, which is why cooking pots and pans are made of metal — the heat of the charcoal fire passes quickly through the metal base into the food. This same property is why a metal spoon left in a hot pot of shaah (tea) soon becomes too hot to hold, while a wooden spoon stays cool. Metals also let an electric current flow through them, which is why the wires inside every phone charger and every solar panel cable are made of metal, usually copper.

Strike a metal and it rings like a bell — this musical property is called being sonorous. It is why bells, cymbals and gongs are made of metal. Be careful, though: a glass bottle or a china cup can also make a ringing sound when tapped, yet they are not metals. A good scientist never relies on one test alone.

Metals have high melting points, and some are magnetic

Most metals need a great deal of heat before they melt — they have high melting points and high boiling points. That is why a metal pot can sit over a fire without melting. There is one strange exception: mercury is the only metal that is a liquid at room temperature. Finally, a few metals — iron, steel, nickel and cobalt — are magnetic, meaning they are pulled towards a magnet. This is a useful test, but remember that most metals, such as copper, aluminium and gold, are not magnetic at all.

Did You Know? Mercury is the only metal that is liquid at ordinary temperatures — it flows like shining silver water. Long ago it was even called 'quicksilver'. It is also very poisonous, so scientists today handle it with great care. Gold is so unreactive that gold coins and jewellery buried for thousands of years come out of the ground still gleaming.

concept-2-the-non-metals.explanation:
The non-metals are the other great family. There are fewer of them than metals, but they are just as important. In many ways non-metals are the mirror-image of metals: where a metal is shiny, a non-metal is dull; where a metal bends, a non-metal snaps. Let us look at their properties.

Dull, not shiny — non-metals do not reflect light well and often feel rough. Think of a lump of charcoal or a piece of sulfur.

Brittle — solid non-metals shatter when you drop or hit them. Charcoal crumbles; it is not malleable at all.

Poor conductors of heat — this makes some non-metals perfect for pot handles and oven cloths, because they do not carry the heat to your hand.

Poor conductors of electricity — most non-metals are insulators. This is why the covering around an electric cable, and the case of a plug, are made of plastic — a non-metal — so the electricity cannot escape and shock you.

Many are gases — a large number of non-metals, such as oxygen and helium, are gases at room temperature. Those that are solid usually have low melting points.

Non-metals are especially useful because of the chemical reactions they take part in. Here are some non-metals you may already know about:

Oxygen — the gas we breathe. Pure oxygen is given in hospitals to people who are struggling to breathe, for example during a serious bout of malaria or pneumonia.

Carbon — as charcoal it is used every day for cooking; it is also used to purify water and to treat an upset stomach.

Chlorine — dissolved in water it kills the germs that cause disease, which is why a little is added to swimming pools and to treated drinking water.

Sulfur — added to rubber to make it harder and tougher, for example in tyres.

Helium — a very light gas that floats, so it is used to fill balloons.

Silicon — used to make the tiny computer chips inside phones and laptops.

The clearest way to remember the difference is to compare the two families directly. A good scientist uses words like whereas and compared with to make a proper comparison, rather than just listing two separate sets of facts. For example: metals are shiny whereas non-metals are dull; metals conduct electricity well whereas most non-metals do not.

concept-3-metal-mixtures-called-alloys.explanation:
Here is a clever secret that people discovered thousands of years ago: if you melt two metals together and let them cool, you get a new material that is often much better than either metal on its own. A mixture of metals like this is called an alloy. In an alloy the atoms of the different metals mix together, but they do not chemically bond — it is still a mixture, not a compound.

The very first alloy people learned to make was bronze, a mixture of copper and tin. Bronze is harder than either copper or tin alone, and it was so important that a whole period of human history is called the Bronze Age. Even today bronze is used for bells, cymbals, statues and ship fittings that sit under water.

The most important alloy in the modern world is steel. Steel is an unusual alloy because one of the ingredients is not a metal at all — it is the non-metal carbon. Steel is a mixture of iron and a small amount of carbon. Pure iron is too soft to be really useful, but adding carbon makes it much harder and stronger. When chromium and nickel are also added, you get stainless steel, which does not rust — perfect for the knives, forks and cooking pots in your kitchen.

Why is an alloy harder? A picture with particles

To understand why alloys are harder, imagine the atoms inside a metal. In a pure metal all the atoms are the same size and they line up in neat, regular rows, like sacks of grain stacked tidily in a store. When you hit the metal with a hammer, whole layers of atoms can slide smoothly over one another — this sliding is what lets the metal change shape, and it is why pure metals are soft and easy to bend.

Now imagine mixing in some atoms of a different metal that are a different size. These odd-sized atoms disrupt the neat rows, like a few larger sacks jammed into the tidy stack. Now the layers cannot slide past one another easily — they get stuck. Because the layers can no longer slip, the alloy is much harder and stronger than the original pure metal. That single idea — different-sized atoms blocking the sliding layers — explains why steel is tougher than iron and bronze is tougher than copper.

Did You Know? The 'silver' coins in your pocket usually contain no silver at all — real silver is too soft and far too expensive. They are made from a hard-wearing alloy of copper and nickel. Aeroplanes are built mainly from an aluminium alloy called duralumin, which is about five times stronger than pure aluminium — strong enough that the wings do not fall off in flight.
concept-3-metal-mixtures-called-alloys.example: Alloys are everywhere in daily life. Coins must be hard-wearing yet soft enough to be stamped with a pattern, so they are made of alloys. Most gold jewellery is actually an alloy of gold with a little copper, because pure gold is too soft for a ring that is worn every day — a wedding ring of pure gold would slowly wear away. Even the replacement hip and knee joints that doctors fit inside the body are made of strong, non-rusting alloys of titanium, because they must survive years of wear without harming the body.

concept-4-separating-mixtures.explanation:
A mixture is made of different substances that are simply mixed together and not chemically joined. Because the substances keep their own properties, we can pull a mixture apart by cleverly using the differences between those properties. Choosing the right method is a real scientific skill.

Using a magnet — if one substance is magnetic and the other is not, a magnet separates them. A mixture of iron filings and sulfur can be separated because iron is magnetic and sulfur is not.

Filtering — if you have a solid that will not dissolve mixed into a liquid, pour it through filter paper. The liquid passes through but the solid stays behind. This is how you would clear the sand out of sandy water — the same idea as a cloth filter used to make water cleaner before boiling it.

Evaporating — if a solid is dissolved in a liquid, gently warm the liquid until it turns to a gas and escapes, leaving the solid behind. Leave salty water in a warm dish and, as the water evaporates, the salt is left in the dish. This is exactly how sea salt is made along the Indian Ocean coast.

Distillation — if you want to keep the liquid itself, you boil the mixture, catch the steam, and cool it back into a pure liquid in a cooled tube called a condenser. This separates two liquids that boil at different temperatures.
concept-4-separating-mixtures.example: Notice the pattern: in every case we look for a property that is different between the substances — magnetism, whether something dissolves, or its boiling point — and we use that difference to do the separating.

concept-5-acids-and-alkalis.explanation:
Some of the most interesting materials of all are the liquids we call acids and alkalis. You already know many of them, even if you did not know their scientific names.

Foods that taste sour and sharp usually contain an acid. When you suck a slice of lemon or lime, that mouth-puckering sourness comes from citric acid — a weak acid. Vinegar, used in cooking and for cleaning, contains a weak acid too. Even the drink of cola contains acid. Your own stomach makes a much stronger acid to help break down food. Weak acids like these are safe to eat in food, but strong acids, such as the sulfuric acid inside a car battery, are very dangerous and corrosive — they can eat away your skin and cause a chemical burn.

Alkalis are the chemical opposites of acids. Many cleaning products contain them. Soap and soapy water are mildly alkaline, which is why they feel slippery between your fingers. Baking soda (bicarbonate of soda) dissolved in water is a mild alkali. Lime water and the ash left from a wood fire are alkaline too. Just like acids, strong alkalis — such as the sodium hydroxide in some drain and oven cleaners — are corrosive and can burn your skin, which feels soapy as it is attacked. Whether they are strong or weak, acids and alkalis should always be treated with respect.

Did You Know? Acids and alkalis are chemical opposites — if you mix the right amounts together they cancel each other out. This is why a mild alkali can calm the sting of an acid. The soapy, slippery feeling of a strong alkali on your skin is actually the alkali starting to break down the natural oils in your skin — which is exactly why you must wash it off at once with plenty of water.

Because some acids and alkalis are harmful, scientists follow careful safety rules, and so should you. Never taste a chemical to find out what it is. Keep chemicals away from your eyes. If you ever spill an acid or an alkali on your skin, wash the area with lots of clean water straight away — the water dilutes the chemical and makes it far less dangerous. Diluting a strong chemical with water always makes it safer.

Dangerous chemicals carry printed hazard warning symbols so that anyone can see the danger at a glance, even if they cannot read the label. Learning these symbols is a life skill — you will see them on cleaning bottles, fuel cans and pesticides at home.

The substance can destroy living tissue and cause burns.

The substance can irritate your skin and eyes.

The substance gives off a lot of heat when it touches other substances.

concept-6-indicators-and-the-ph-scale.example: A very common laboratory indicator is litmus, usually soaked into small strips of paper. Litmus follows a simple rule: it turns red in acids, blue in alkalis, and stays purple in a neutral substance such as pure water. Because water turns litmus purple, we know water is neutral — neither acid nor alkali.

we01.solution:
Worked Example 1

Question: Amina tests some vinegar with universal indicator and it turns orange. Roughly what is the pH, and is the vinegar acidic, neutral or alkaline?

Step 1 — Recall the colour code. Universal indicator turns red at the strongest acids (around pH 1) and moves through orange and yellow for weaker acids (about pH 3 to 6).

Step 2 — Match the colour. Orange sits between red and yellow, so it points to a weakly acidic liquid, about pH 3 to 4.

we02.solution:
Step 1 — Recall the colour code. Universal indicator turns red at the strongest acids (around pH 1) and moves through orange and yellow for weaker acids (about pH 3 to 6).

Step 2 — Match the colour. Orange sits between red and yellow, so it points to a weakly acidic liquid, about pH 3 to 4.

Answer: The vinegar has a pH of roughly 3 to 4, so it is acidic — which fits, because vinegar tastes sour.

Worked Example 2

we03.solution:
Step 1 — Recall the code. Green is neutral (pH 7); blue means weakly alkaline (around pH 8 to 10); purple means strongly alkaline (pH 13 to 14).

Step 2 — Match. Blue is above green but not as far as purple, so the liquid is weakly alkaline, about pH 9.

Answer: The soapy water is about pH 9 and is a weak alkali — which fits its slippery, soapy feel.

Worked Example 3

we04.solution:
Step 1 — Notice the direction. The pH is rising from a low, acidic number towards 7. Adding an alkali is cancelling out the acid.

Step 2 — Name it. Moving an acid up towards pH 7 by adding an alkali is neutralisation. At pH 7 the mixture is neutral.

Answer: The alkali is neutralising the acid; when it reaches pH 7 the liquid is neutral.

concept-1-how-sound-is-made.explanation:
Let us begin with something you have heard every day of your life: sound. Close your eyes for a moment and imagine the sounds around you right now. Perhaps you can hear voices, a goat bleating outside, the wind moving through an acacia tree, or a cooking pot being placed on the fire. Every one of these sounds started in exactly the same way: something vibrated.

To vibrate means to move backwards and forwards very quickly. When something vibrates, it pushes against the air around it and makes a sound. Think of the men playing the drum at a celebration. When a drummer strikes the skin of the drum, the tight surface moves up and down very fast, too fast for your eyes to follow. That fast movement is the vibration, and the vibration is what makes the sound you hear. If the drummer hits the drum with more force, the skin vibrates further and the sound becomes louder. If they tap it gently, the skin barely moves and the sound is soft.

You can feel a vibration in your own body. Place two fingers gently on the front of your throat and say your name out loud, or softly recite 'Bismillah'. Can you feel the gentle buzzing? That buzzing comes from your vocal cords, two small flaps inside your throat that vibrate when you speak. When you stop speaking, the vibration stops and so does the sound. This simple test proves an important rule: no vibration means no sound.

The same idea explains many musical instruments. A guitar or an oud makes a sound because its strings vibrate when you pluck them. It is not the wood, or the metal parts, or the air trapped inside that makes the note, it is the vibrating string. A loudspeaker in a radio or phone has a paper cone inside that vibrates in and out. If you place tiny grains of rice on a loudspeaker while music plays, the grains jump and bounce, showing you the cone is vibrating even when the movement is too small to see clearly.

Loudness and Pitch — Two Different Things

Not all sounds are the same, and scientists describe sound using two separate ideas that you must not mix up: loudness and pitch. Loudness (also called volume) is how loud or quiet a sound is. It depends on how much the object vibrates, or how big the vibration is. A big vibration carries more energy, so it makes a louder sound. This is why hitting a drum harder, or plucking a string with more force, makes the sound louder.

Pitch is different. Pitch is how high or low a sound is. Thunder rolling over the Rift Valley is a low-pitched sound. A baby crying, a whistle, or a small bird is a high-pitched sound. Pitch depends on how fast something vibrates: fast vibrations make high sounds, and slow vibrations make low sounds. A thin, tight guitar string vibrates quickly and gives a high note, while a thick, loose string vibrates slowly and gives a low note. Remember: loudness is about the size of the vibration, and pitch is about the speed of the vibration. These are two separate properties, and a sound can be loud and low, quiet and high, or any other combination.

concept-2-how-a-sound-wave-travels.explanation:
Now we come to a deeper question. When the muadhin calls the adhan at the mosque, how does that sound reach your house far away? The vibration happens at the mosque, but you hear it in your home. Something must carry the sound across the distance. That something is a sound wave.

Here is how it works, step by step. When an object vibrates, it moves forwards and pushes the air particles in front of it. Those particles get squeezed together for a moment. Then the object moves back, and the particles spread out again. But here is the clever part: the squeezed particles bump into the particles next to them and pass the push along. Those particles bump the next ones, and so on, and so on, like a message passed from hand to hand down a long line of people. In this way the vibration travels outward through the air as a sound wave, even though each particle only moves a tiny bit backwards and forwards and then stays roughly where it was.

This is a very important idea, so let us be clear about it. The particles themselves do not travel all the way from the mosque to your house. The air does not fly across the town. Instead, each particle nudges the next one, and it is the vibration, the energy, that travels. Think of a long line of children standing shoulder to shoulder. If the first child gently sways and bumps the next, the bump can pass all the way down the line, but no single child leaves their place. That is exactly how a sound wave moves through the air.

Sound travels quickly, but not instantly. In air, sound travels at about 343 metres every second. That is fast, but light is far faster. This is why, during a thunderstorm over the coast near Berbera or Mombasa, you see the flash of lightning first and hear the thunder a few seconds later, even though they happen at the same moment. The light reaches you almost instantly, but the sound takes time to travel to your ears.

Sound Needs a Medium — Solids, Liquids and Gases

Because a sound wave works by making particles vibrate, sound can only travel through a substance that has particles. The substance that a sound wave travels through is called the medium. Solids, liquids and gases can all be a medium for sound, because all of them are made of particles.

You can prove sound travels through a solid with a simple test. Tap gently on one end of a wooden table or bench and ask a friend to listen normally, then ask them to press their ear flat against the table and listen to the same tap again. The tap sounds clearer and stronger through the solid wood, because the particles in a solid are packed tightly together and pass the vibration along very efficiently. Sound also travels well through liquids. This is how whales and dolphins in the Indian Ocean communicate over long distances, singing to one another through the water. And of course sound travels through the gas we call air, which is how you hear almost everything in daily life.

Now for one of the most surprising facts in all of science. A vacuum is a space with no particles at all. Outer space is very close to a perfect vacuum. Because there are no particles in a vacuum, there is nothing to vibrate, and so a sound wave cannot form or travel. This means space is completely silent.

Think about what that means. If two astronauts on the Moon stood right next to each other and one hammered on a rock, the other would not hear a single sound through the space around them, because the Moon has almost no air. This is why astronauts talk to each other using radios, which send the message as radio waves that can cross a vacuum, not as sound. In science-fiction films you often see huge explosions in space with a loud 'BOOM'. Now you know the truth: a real explosion in space would make no sound at all, because there is no medium to carry the wave. The film-makers add the sound only because it is dramatic.

we01.solution:
Problem: Halima stands in a valley and shouts towards a tall cliff. She hears the echo return exactly 2 seconds later. Sound travels at about 343 metres per second in air. How far away is the cliff?

Step 1 — Find the total distance the sound travelled. We use the rule distance = speed x time. The sound travelled for 2 seconds at 343 metres per second, so distance = 343 x 2 = 686 metres.

Step 2 — Remember the sound made a round trip. The 686 metres is the distance to the cliff and back again. To find the distance to the cliff alone, we must halve it: 686 / 2 = 343 metres.

Answer: The cliff is about 343 metres away. The key idea to remember is that an echo always travels double the distance to the surface, so you divide the total by two to find the one-way distance.

concept-1-what-is-a-microorganism.explanation:
A microorganism is a living organism that is so small you cannot see it clearly without a microscope. The word is built from two parts: 'micro', meaning very small, and 'organism', meaning a living thing. Like every other living thing — like you, like a camel, like an acacia tree — microorganisms are made of cells. The difference is size. Many microorganisms are made of just a single cell, and that one cell is so tiny that thousands of them together would still be smaller than a grain of sand.

It helps to picture the scale. A cell in your own body is already too small to see on its own. A single bacterium is far smaller still — many times smaller than one of your cells. That is why, for thousands of years, human beings had no idea these creatures existed. People saw milk turn sour, bread rise, and wounds go bad, but they could not see the living things causing it. Only when the microscope was invented could scientists finally look closely enough to discover a hidden living world.

There are several different kinds of microorganism. The main groups you will study are bacteria, microscopic fungi, protozoa and algae. Viruses are also extremely small, but scientists usually treat them separately, and you will soon learn why. Let us take each group in turn.

Bacteria are everywhere — in the air, in the soil, in water, on every surface, on your skin and inside your gut. The word 'bacteria' is plural; a single one is called a bacterium. Each bacterium is made of just one cell, and that cell is much smaller than an animal cell or a plant cell. As you read earlier, you could line up about 1000 bacteria end to end in the space between two millimetre marks on your ruler. Bacteria have a cell wall, but unlike plant and animal cells they have no nucleus.

It is easy to think that all bacteria are 'germs' that make us ill, but this is a mistake. Most bacteria are completely harmless, and many are extremely useful. Right now, helpful bacteria are living in your digestive system, helping you to break down your food. Other helpful bacteria turn milk into yoghurt and into the fermented camel milk that many families across the Horn of Africa enjoy. Only a small number of bacteria cause disease.

Fungi (a single one is a fungus) are not always microorganisms. Many fungi, such as the mushrooms and toadstools you might see pushing up from damp ground after rain, are large and easy to see without any microscope. But a mushroom is only a small part of the fungus — the part that makes new spores. Most of the fungus is a tangle of very fine threads spreading through the soil or through a dead log, so thin that you would need a microscope to see them.

Some fungi never make mushrooms at all. They are made of single cells, so these ones truly are microorganisms. The most famous example is yeast. The dusty, powdery bloom you sometimes see on the skin of grapes or dates is made of millions of yeast cells feeding on the sugar in the fruit. Yeast is a single-celled fungus, and under a microscope you can watch tiny buds growing out of the cells — that is how yeast makes more of itself. Mould, the fuzzy growth on old bread or a forgotten mango, is another fungus; it grows as fine threads and is a very common decomposer.

Did You Know? The bubbles that make bread and canjeero rise are made by yeast. As the yeast feeds on sugar in the dough, it produces a gas that puffs the dough up. Fungi are neither plants nor animals. They belong to a kingdom of living things all of their own.

Viruses are even smaller than bacteria — so small that ordinary microscopes cannot show them at all. A virus is not made of a cell. It is a tiny particle, just a small package of instructions wrapped in a protein coat. Because it is not a cell and cannot feed, grow or reproduce on its own, most scientists do not call a virus a true microorganism, and many do not even call it fully 'alive'. A virus can only make copies of itself by getting inside the living cell of another organism and taking over that cell's machinery. The illnesses called colds, flu (influenza), measles and COVID are all caused by viruses.

If you put a single drop of pond water or river water under a microscope, you would see it teeming with life. Some of the tiny creatures are protozoa — single-celled microorganisms whose cells are like animal cells, often moving about actively as they hunt for even smaller food. One kind of protozoan is very important to your community: it causes malaria, and it is carried from person to person by mosquitoes. Other tiny organisms in the water are algae — single-celled microorganisms whose cells are like plant cells. Like plants, algae are green and can use sunlight to make their own food. The green tinge you sometimes see in still water is made of countless algae.

concept-2-growing-microorganisms-into-co.explanation:
A single microorganism is far too small to see. So how do scientists study them? The trick is to let them grow. When a single bacterium or a single fungus cell is given warmth, moisture and food, it divides in two. Then each of those divides again, and again, and again. In only a day or two, one invisible cell becomes a colony of millions of cells — and a colony is big enough to see with your naked eye, as a small spot or patch.

In a laboratory, scientists grow colonies on a special jelly called agar jelly, poured into a shallow round dish with a lid called a Petri dish. The agar jelly contains nutrients — the food the microorganisms need. Before use, both the dish and the jelly must be sterile, which means every living thing on them has already been killed. If the dish were not sterile, unwanted microorganisms would already be growing there and would spoil the experiment. When the dish is left open to the air for a few minutes, microorganisms floating in the air settle onto the jelly, and after a few days each one has grown into a visible colony.

You can even tell the two main groups apart by looking. Colonies of bacteria usually have smooth, shiny edges, while colonies of fungi are usually fuzzy or furry with rough edges, because the fungus grows as fine threads. In the Experiments file you will grow your own colonies safely at home, using nothing more than a slice of bread — no laboratory needed.
concept-2-growing-microorganisms-into-co.example: Did You Know? The word 'sterile' means totally free of all living things. Doctors sterilise their instruments so that no harmful microorganisms are passed to a patient. This is exactly why a nurse boils water or uses very hot steam to clean equipment — heat kills microorganisms.

concept-3-useful-and-harmful-microorgani.explanation:
Because a few microorganisms cause serious disease, people often fear all of them. But the truth is more interesting and more balanced: microorganisms are among the most useful living things we have, and human life would be impossible without them.

Think of your own kitchen. Bacteria turn fresh milk into yoghurt and into the sour fermented camel milk that many families drink. They do this by changing the sugar in the milk into acid, which is what gives yoghurt its sharp, pleasant taste and its thick texture. Yeast, a fungus, makes dough rise so that bread and canjeero become soft and light instead of hard and flat. In the wider world, decomposer bacteria and fungi in the savanna soil break down dead plants and animal dung and release their nutrients back into the ground, so that fresh grass and acacia trees can grow — which in turn feeds the goats, camels and wild animals. Inside your own body, friendly bacteria in your gut help you digest food and keep harmful microbes out.

Some microorganisms, though, are harmful. When bacteria or mould grow on food we meant to eat, they spoil it and can make us ill if we eat it. This is why food left out in the heat goes bad so quickly, and why we must be careful with meat, milk and cooked rice in a hot climate. A small number of microorganisms cause disease directly. The protozoan that causes malaria is spread by mosquito bites and remains one of the most serious health problems in East Africa, especially for young children. Dirty water can carry bacteria that cause cholera and typhoid, and other bacteria cause tuberculosis. Viruses cause the flu, measles and many other illnesses.

The good news is that simple actions protect us. Boiling drinking water kills the microorganisms in it. Washing hands with soap before eating and after using the toilet stops harmful microbes spreading from hands to food. Cooking food thoroughly and keeping it covered and cool slows down spoilage. Sleeping under a bed net and clearing away still water where mosquitoes breed reduces the risk of malaria. In Islam, keeping clean is highly valued — Muslims wash carefully before each prayer, and cleanliness is described as part of faith. Science shows us exactly why this care with cleanliness and clean water keeps whole communities healthy.

concept-4-food-chains-how-energy-flows.explanation:
To understand where microorganisms fit into the natural world, you first need to understand how energy flows through all living things. Every living thing needs energy — to move, to grow, to stay warm, to reproduce. When Hassan eats a plate of bariis (rice) with goat meat, that food gives him energy for the day. But where did that energy come from in the first place?

The answer is the Sun. Almost all the energy used by living things on Earth begins as sunlight. Green plants — and algae — can capture the energy in sunlight and use it to make their own food. Because they produce food from sunlight, plants are called producers. Some of the energy from the sunlight becomes stored in the plant's roots, stems, leaves, grains and fruits.

When an animal eats the plant, it takes in that stored food and so takes in the energy too. This passing of energy from one living thing to the next is called energy transfer. Animals cannot make their own food, so they must eat ready-made food. For this reason all animals are called consumers. We can show the path of the energy by drawing a food chain, using arrows to show the direction the energy flows.

For example, here is a simple food chain from the savanna:

Read the arrows as 'is eaten by' or, better, as 'energy flows to'. The grass is the producer; it captured energy from the Sun. The goat eats the grass and gains that energy. The lion eats the goat and gains the energy in turn. Notice that the arrows always point in the direction the energy travels — from the food to the eater — never backwards. A very common mistake is to draw the arrow the wrong way, from the eater to its food. Always ask yourself: which way is the energy flowing?

Scientists use special words to describe each organism's role:

Producer — the first organism in the chain; it makes its own food from sunlight. Grass and acacia trees are producers.

Consumer — any organism that eats others. Every animal is a consumer.

Herbivore — a consumer that eats only plants, such as a camel, a goat or a springbok.

Carnivore — a consumer that eats only other animals, such as a lion or a cheetah.

Predator — an animal that catches, kills and eats other animals.

Prey — an animal that is caught and eaten by a predator.

The same animal can have more than one label. A leopard is a consumer, a carnivore and a predator all at once. A zebra it hunts is a consumer, a herbivore, and also prey. Learning to apply these labels correctly is an important skill in this unit.

Did You Know? Every food chain starts with a producer, because producers are the only living things that can capture new energy from the Sun. Along the Indian Ocean coast near Mombasa and Kismaayo, tiny floating algae are the producers that begin nearly every ocean food chain, feeding the small fish that feed the larger fish that people catch.

In the real world, very few animals eat only one kind of food, and very few plants are eaten by only one kind of animal. A cheetah might eat a springbok or a young zebra. A springbok might be eaten by a cheetah, a leopard or a hyena. When we join many food chains together to show all these connections, we get a food web. A food web is a much more realistic picture of a habitat than a single food chain.

Imagine a savanna food web near Garissa. Grass and acacia trees are the producers. Springbok and zebra eat the grass and the acacia leaves — they are herbivores. Termites also eat grass, and aardvarks eat the termites. Cheetahs, leopards and hyenas hunt the springbok and zebra. From one such diagram you can trace many different food chains, each one starting at a producer and following the arrows up to a top predator.
concept-4-food-chains-how-energy-flows.example: A food web is a model — a simplified picture that scientists use to represent something complicated. Like any model, it is useful but not perfect. A real savanna has thousands of species, and no drawing could ever show every single feeding relationship. Still, a food web helps us understand how the living things in one place depend on one another. If one link is removed — say, disease kills most of the zebra — every animal connected to them in the web is affected.

concept-5-microorganisms-and-decay.explanation:
Now we can bring microorganisms into the story of energy and food. Think of a mango that has been left on the table for a week. It becomes soft, then brown, then covered in fuzzy patches. Each patch is a colony of millions of cells of microscopic fungi — this is mould, and we say the mango has become mouldy. The microorganisms have changed the mango; they have made it decay, or rot.

Organisms that make things decay are called decomposers. The most important decomposers are certain bacteria and fungi. A decomposer feeds on dead material by breaking it down, and as it feeds, the material rots. The mango is made of material that was produced by a living plant. Any substance made by a living thing — fruit, bread, wood, leather, paper, dead leaves, dead animals — is called organic matter. Decomposers can break down organic matter, but they cannot break down things that were never alive, such as rock, glass, plastic or metal.

At first, decay seems like nothing but a nuisance. No one wants to eat a rotten mango, and food spoiling in the heat is a real problem in a warm climate. But decay is one of the most important processes on the whole planet, and without it life could not continue.

Think about what would happen if nothing ever decayed. Every leaf that ever fell, every animal that ever died, every pile of dung dropped by a camel or an elephant would simply stay there forever. The savanna would be buried metres deep in dead plants, dead animals and waste. Instead, decomposers get to work. As bacteria and fungi break down dead bodies and dung, they release the valuable nutrients locked inside back into the soil. Plants then take up these nutrients through their roots and use them to grow. More plant growth means more food for the herbivores, which means more food for the carnivores. In this way, decomposers return nutrients to the soil and keep the whole web of life going.

You can see this yourself. Where a camel or a cow has left dung in a field, fungi grow on the dung, break it down, and the grass nearby grows greener and taller than the grass further away. The dung, broken down by decomposers, has fed the soil. This is exactly the idea behind composting: when a family collects fruit peelings, vegetable scraps and dead leaves into a pit or heap and lets decomposers break them down, the result is rich compost that makes garden soil fertile — turning waste into food for plants.

Did You Know? Almost all decomposers are microorganisms. Fungi and bacteria are the most important of all. In caring for the earth and not wasting what it provides, a Muslim acts as a khalifah, a steward or caretaker of the land. Composting kitchen waste instead of throwing it away is one small, practical way of doing this.

How Temperature and Moisture Affect Decay

Decomposers are living things, so the speed at which they work depends on the conditions around them. Two conditions matter most: warmth and moisture (water). Like most living things, decomposers grow and feed faster when it is warm and there is plenty of water. That is why food goes bad far more quickly on a hot day than on a cool one, and why bread kept in a refrigerator stays fresh much longer than bread left on the counter. It is also why moist bread grows mould faster than dry bread.

This everyday science is the reason for many of the ways people keep food safe. Drying meat and fish in the sun removes the water that decomposers need, so the food lasts longer. Keeping milk and cooked food cool slows the microorganisms down. Salting and smoking food make it harder for microorganisms to grow. In the Experiments file you will test these ideas for yourself by comparing how quickly bread decays in a warm place and in a cool place, and in moist and dry conditions.
concept-5-microorganisms-and-decay.example: [*] Remember! Decomposers (mostly bacteria and fungi) break down dead organic matter and cause decay. Decay returns nutrients to the soil so that plants can grow — this keeps all life going. Decomposers work faster in warm, moist conditions and slower in cold, dry conditions. We slow down harmful decay of our food by keeping it cool, dry, covered and clean.

concept-6-placing-decomposers-into-food-.explanation:
You have learned that food webs show how energy flows from producers to consumers. But those webs left something out: what happens to the energy and nutrients when a plant or animal dies? This is where decomposers complete the picture.

Decomposers feed on almost every organism after it dies, and on the waste that living animals leave behind. When they do this, energy from the dead organism is transferred into the decomposer — just as energy was transferred when a goat ate grass. So decomposers are a special kind of consumer: they consume dead organisms and waste rather than living food. They are never producers, because they do not make their own food from sunlight.

To add decomposers to a food web properly, you would need to draw an arrow from every single plant and animal in the web to the decomposers, because eventually every organism dies and is broken down. That would make the diagram very crowded, which is why decomposers are often left off simple food webs. But they are always there, doing the vital work of recycling.
