sci-g07-u08.unitOverview: Look around you right now. A piece of charcoal glows red under the pot as your mother cooks bariis (rice). A steel gate on the coast near Berbera is slowly turning orange with rust. A cup of warm milk left overnight has thickened into yoghurt. A slice of mango turns brown after you cut it. Every one of these is a change to a material — the substance you started with has become something new, or has simply changed its form. In this unit you will learn to tell these two kinds of change apart and to explain, like a real scientist, exactly what is happening.
outcomes: By the end of this unit you will be able to:
Describe the difference between a physical change and a chemical change, with your own examples.
Explain what happens to substances in a chemical reaction, using the words reactant and product.
Recognise the signs that tell you a chemical reaction has taken place (gas, colour change, heat, a new solid, a change in pH, a substance being used up).
Explain burning (combustion) as a reaction between a fuel and the oxygen in the air.
Describe oxidation and rusting, and explain why iron rusts faster in damp, salty coastal air.
Explain what happens when an acid reacts with an alkali, and describe neutralisation as a change to pH 7.
Give real-life examples of neutralisation, such as antacids for a sour stomach, toothpaste, and lime added to acidic soil.
State the law of conservation of mass — that no atoms are lost or made in a reaction.
Carry out safe household investigations and record your observations like a scientist.

concept-1-physical-changes-and-chemical-.explanation:
Every material has two kinds of properties. Its physical properties are the things you can see or measure without changing what the substance is: its colour, whether it is a solid, liquid or gas, whether it is heavy or light, and the temperature at which it melts or boils. For example, iron is a grey, heavy solid that melts at a very high temperature. Its chemical properties describe how it reacts with other substances — for example, iron combines with oxygen to form rust, and it combines with sulfur when strongly heated. Physical properties tell you what a substance is like; chemical properties tell you how it behaves when it meets others.

Now here is the key difference between the two kinds of change. In a physical change no new substance is made. When you melt a lump of animal fat to make cooking oil, or freeze water into ice for a hot Mogadishu afternoon, or dissolve sugar into your tea, the material only changes its state or its form. The sugar is still sugar even after it disappears into the tea — taste it and you will know. If you could cool the melted fat or evaporate the tea, you would get your original substance back. Physical changes can usually be reversed.

In a chemical change, one or more new substances are formed, and these new substances have different properties from what you started with. When your mother bakes cake or canjeero, the soft runny batter turns into something firm, golden and spongy that can never become batter again. When firewood burns, it turns into grey ash and smoke — the ash weighs less, looks different, and will not burn again the way the wood did. When you fry an egg, the clear runny part turns solid and white forever. These are all chemical changes, because brand-new substances have been made and the change cannot easily be undone.

[Did You Know] Did You Know? The browning of a cut mango, avocado or banana is a real chemical reaction called oxidation. The fruit reacts with oxygen in the air. Squeezing a little lemon juice on the surface slows it down, which is why cooks add lemon to fruit salad to keep it looking fresh.

concept-2-reactants-and-products.explanation:
When a chemical reaction happens, scientists have special words for the substances involved. The reactants are the substances you start with — the ones that react together. The products are the new substances that are made. We can show a reaction with a word equation, where an arrow means 'turns into' or 'reacts to make'. The reactants go on the left and the products go on the right, like this:

Read that as: iron reacts with sulfur to make a new substance called iron sulfide. The iron and the sulfur are the reactants; the iron sulfide is the single product. The tiny particles called atoms in the iron have combined and joined tightly with the atoms in the sulfur to build a completely new material with its own properties. Iron is magnetic and grey; sulfur is a yellow powder; but iron sulfide is a dark solid that is not magnetic at all. New substance, new properties — that is the signature of a chemical reaction.

Sometimes a reaction goes the other way, and one substance breaks apart to make two or more new substances. For example, water can be split into the two gases it is made from:

Reactions are happening around you and inside you every second. They happen when a seed sprouts and a mango tree grows, when fallen leaves rot into the soil, and inside your own body when you digest your breakfast of canjeero and turn it into the energy you need to walk to school. Life itself is a vast, well-ordered set of chemical reactions.
concept-2-reactants-and-products.example: [Did You Know] Did You Know? Turning fresh camel or cow milk into yoghurt is a chemical reaction carried out by tiny living microbes called bacteria. They feed on the sugar in the milk and produce a mild acid. That acid makes the milk proteins clump together, thickening the liquid into yoghurt — a new substance with a new taste and texture that will not turn back into fresh milk.

concept-3-the-signs-that-a-reaction-has-.explanation:
Because a chemical reaction always makes something new, it usually leaves clues behind. A good scientist learns to spot these clues. Here are the six main signs that a chemical reaction has taken place:

A gas is given off. You see bubbles or fizzing, even though you did not heat a liquid to boiling. When you drop bicarbonate of soda into vinegar or lemon juice, it froths wildly — a gas called carbon dioxide is being made.

A colour change that will not reverse. A shiny grey nail slowly turns orange-brown as it rusts; a green mango ripens and a cut apple browns.

Heat or light is given off (or taken in). Burning charcoal gives out heat and a red glow. Some reactions instead feel cold as they take heat in.

A new solid appears in a liquid, called a precipitate. Clear limewater turns cloudy and milky when you breathe carbon dioxide into it, because a new white solid forms.

A change in pH. When an acid meets an alkali, the acidity changes — this is a neutralisation reaction, which you will study soon.

A reactant is used up or 'disappears'. A strip of metal placed in acid slowly vanishes as it turns into a new dissolved substance.
concept-3-the-signs-that-a-reaction-has-.example: One of the most useful clues is a gas being given off. But bubbles alone only tell you that *a* gas is being made — they do not tell you *which* gas. Scientists have simple tests to identify three common gases. Carbon dioxide turns limewater cloudy and can put out a burning splint. Oxygen will relight a glowing splint — a splint that has stopped flaming but is still glowing red will burst back into flame in oxygen. Hydrogen burns with a quick, high 'squeaky pop' when a flame is brought near it. These three tests are like fingerprints that let you name the invisible gas.

concept-4-burning-and-combustion.explanation:
Burning, which scientists call combustion, is one of the most important chemical reactions in daily life. Every time your family lights charcoal in the jiko or burns firewood to cook, a chemical reaction is taking place. In combustion, a fuel reacts with the oxygen in the air and releases energy as heat and light. The fuel and the oxygen are the reactants; new substances called oxides are the products, and some of them leave the scene as smoke and gas while others stay behind as ash.

Charcoal is mostly the element carbon. When carbon burns, it combines with oxygen from the air to make an invisible gas called carbon dioxide:

This is why a fire needs air. If you cover glowing charcoal tightly so that no fresh air can reach it, the flames die — without oxygen, the reaction stops. It is also why blowing gently on embers, or fanning them, makes them glow brighter and hotter: you are giving the reaction more of the oxygen it needs. Cooks all along the coast, from Kismaayo to Lamu, know this trick even if they never called it chemistry.

When the metal magnesium burns, it burns with a blinding white light and leaves behind a white powder called magnesium oxide. The magnesium has combined with oxygen to make a new substance:

Notice how different the product is from the reactants. Magnesium is a soft, shiny grey metal that carries electricity and melts at about 651 degrees Celsius. Oxygen is a colourless gas with no smell. But magnesium oxide is a white powder that does not carry electricity and only melts at about 2800 degrees Celsius. The reaction has made something with completely new properties — the surest sign of a true chemical change.

[Did You Know] Did You Know? Charcoal is made by heating wood in a pit or mound with very little air, so it does not burn away. This drives off water and gases and leaves behind almost pure carbon. That is why a lump of charcoal is so light for its size, and why it burns hotter and cleaner than the raw wood it came from.

There is an important safety lesson hidden inside the chemistry of burning. Charcoal only burns cleanly to carbon dioxide when there is plenty of fresh air. If a charcoal fire or a jiko is burning in a closed room with too little air, the carbon cannot combine fully with oxygen, and it makes a different, dangerous gas called carbon monoxide instead. Carbon monoxide has no colour and no smell, so you cannot tell it is there, yet it is poisonous. This is exactly why you should never leave a charcoal jiko burning inside a small, closed room overnight, and why cooking fires need good ventilation. The same reaction that cooks your food safely outdoors can be harmful indoors without enough air — understanding the chemistry helps keep your family safe.

concept-5-oxidation-and-rusting.explanation:
Combining with oxygen does not always need a flame. When a substance combines with oxygen, scientists call it oxidation. Burning is fast oxidation, with lots of heat and light. But oxidation can also happen slowly and quietly, with no flame at all. The most familiar slow oxidation of all is rusting.

Rusting happens to iron and to steel, which is mostly iron. When iron is left where it can reach both oxygen and water, the iron slowly combines with the oxygen to make a flaky, orange-brown substance called rust, which is a kind of iron oxide. Both water and oxygen must be present — iron kept perfectly dry does not rust, and iron kept completely away from air does not rust either. It is the combination of damp air and oxygen that does it.

This is why iron objects rust so much faster near the sea. On the humid Indian Ocean coast around Mombasa, Berbera and Dar es Salaam, the air is warm, wet and full of tiny salt droplets carried off the ocean, and salt speeds rusting up even more. A steel gate, a car body, a corrugated-iron roof or a box of nails will grow orange and crumbly there far quicker than the same objects kept in the dry, inland air of Garissa or the Rift Valley highlands. Rust is a serious and costly problem: it eats away at roofs, tools, ships and bridges.

concept-6-acids-alkalis-and-neutralisati.explanation:
You may already know that substances can be acids, alkalis, or neutral. An acid has a pH below 7 and often tastes sour, like the lemon or vinegar in the kitchen. An alkali has a pH above 7 and feels soapy, like bicarbonate of soda or soap. A neutral substance, such as pure water, sits right in the middle at pH 7. We measure acidity on the pH scale, a number line running from 0 (strongly acidic) up to 14 (strongly alkaline).

Here is something wonderful: acids and alkalis are chemical opposites, and they can cancel each other out. When you mix an acid and an alkali in the right amounts, they react together and make a neutral solution at pH 7. This reaction is called neutralisation, and it is a true chemical change — new substances are formed. When the strong acid hydrochloric acid reacts with the alkali sodium hydroxide, the products are ordinary table salt (sodium chloride) and water:

hydrochloric acid + sodium hydroxide -> sodium chloride + water

It helps to know that acids and alkalis come in different strengths. A weak, mild acid like the vinegar or lemon juice in your kitchen is safe to handle and even to eat, while a strong acid can burn skin and clothes. In the same way, bicarbonate of soda is a gentle alkali you can touch, but oven cleaner is a strong alkali that is dangerous. So it is not true that acids are always dangerous and alkalis always safe — what matters is how strong the substance is. Whatever the strength, an acid and an alkali will still react together and move towards neutral when you mix them.

If you add too little acid to an alkali, the mixture stays alkaline. If you add too much acid, the mixture becomes acidic. To hit pH 7 exactly, scientists add the acid slowly, a few drops at a time, watching carefully. To *see* the change, they add an indicator — a substance that changes colour with pH. In your own kitchen you can make an indicator by boiling purple red cabbage or soaking dark hibiscus flowers; the coloured water turns reddish/pink in acid and greenish/blue in alkali, so it shows you exactly when a mixture becomes neutral.

[Did You Know] Did You Know? The fizzing you see when vinegar meets bicarbonate of soda is partly neutralisation and partly a gas-making reaction: the acid and the alkali react, and carbon dioxide gas bubbles out. This same reaction is what makes cakes and canjeero rise — the trapped bubbles of gas puff up the batter as it cooks.

Neutralisation is not just a classroom trick — it quietly solves real problems every day:

A sour stomach. Your stomach makes hydrochloric acid to help digest food. Too much of it causes the burning pain of indigestion. Antacid medicines are alkalis that neutralise the extra acid and bring relief — some contain the same bicarbonate of soda found in the kitchen.

Toothpaste. Bacteria in your mouth make acid that attacks and decays your teeth. Toothpaste contains a mild alkali that neutralises this acid, protecting your teeth — one scientific reason the Prophet (peace be upon him) encouraged keeping the mouth clean.

A bee or insect sting. A bee sting is acidic. Dabbing on a paste of bicarbonate of soda (an alkali) helps neutralise the acid and ease the sting. (A wasp sting is alkaline, so a dab of vinegar helps instead.)

we01.solution:
Problem: Amina heats 24 grams of magnesium in the air until it fully burns. It combines with 16 grams of oxygen from the air to make magnesium oxide. What mass of magnesium oxide is formed?

Step 1 — Name the reactants and product. Reactants: magnesium (24 g) and oxygen (16 g). Product: magnesium oxide.

Step 2 — Apply conservation of mass. Total mass of products equals total mass of reactants, because atoms are only rearranged.

Step 3 — Add the reactant masses. 24 g + 16 g = 40 g.

sci-g08-u02.unitOverview: Every human being who has ever lived — your parents, your grandparents, the scholars and travellers of long ago, and you yourself — began life in the same remarkable way: as a single, tiny cell smaller than a grain of sand on the beach at Berbera. From that one cell grew a whole person, with a beating heart, a thinking brain, and hands able to write and to give. In this unit you will study, with care and respect, how new human life begins and grows. This is one of the great wonders of creation, and studying it is a way of reflecting on how carefully we have been made.

concept-1-why-living-things-reproduce.explanation:
Every living thing eventually grows old and dies. If living things could not make new individuals to take their place, every kind of animal and plant would disappear from the Earth. Reproduction is the process by which living things produce new members of their own kind, and it is one of the seven signs that something is alive (you may remember these from your work on living things). A camel gives birth to a young camel; a mango tree grows seeds that become new mango trees; and human parents have children. In this way each kind of living thing continues, generation after generation.

There are two main kinds of reproduction. In asexual reproduction, a single parent produces offspring on its own, and the offspring are identical to the parent — this is how bacteria multiply and how some plants grow new shoots. In sexual reproduction, which is how humans and nearly all animals reproduce, two parents are needed: a male and a female. Each parent provides a special cell called a sex cell (also called a gamete). When these two cells join, they form the first cell of a new individual. Because the new individual receives instructions from both parents, it is not identical to either one — it is a unique blend. This is why children resemble their parents and relatives, yet are never exactly the same as anyone else. Even brothers and sisters from the same parents are each unique.

concept-2-the-human-reproductive-systems.explanation:
To understand how new life begins, we must first learn the parts of the body responsible for reproduction, and the job each part does. We will study the male system and the female system in turn, using the correct medical names. Learn these calmly and respectfully, as you would learn the parts of the heart or the digestive system. Knowing the names helps you understand your own body and speak about health clearly with a parent or a doctor.

The main job of the male reproductive system is to make sperm cells and to deliver them so that fertilisation can happen. Its main parts are:

Testes (singular: testis) — the two organs that produce sperm cells and the male hormone testosterone. They are held outside the main body in a bag of skin called the scrotum, which keeps them slightly cooler than the rest of the body, because sperm cells form best at a slightly lower temperature.

Scrotum — the protective bag of skin that holds and supports the testes.

Sperm ducts (also called the vas deferens) — the tubes that carry sperm cells away from the testes.

Glands — these add a fluid to the sperm cells. Together the fluid and sperm cells are called semen. The fluid nourishes the sperm cells and helps them to move.

Urethra — the tube that runs through the penis. It can carry either urine or semen at different times, but never both at once.

Penis — the organ through which sperm cells leave the male body so that they can reach an egg cell inside the female body.

Notice how each part has a clear purpose, working together as a system, just like the parts of the digestive or circulatory systems you have already studied. From about the time of puberty onwards, the testes are able to make sperm cells continuously.

The female reproductive system has a larger task: not only to make egg cells, but also to hold and nourish a developing baby for around nine months, and finally to give birth. Because of this, most of the female reproductive system is inside the body, well protected. Its main parts are:

Ovaries — the two organs that store and release egg cells and make the female hormone oestrogen. A girl is born with all her egg cells already stored in her ovaries. From puberty, usually one egg cell matures and is released about once a month.

Oviducts (also called the fallopian tubes or egg tubes) — the two tubes that carry an egg cell from an ovary towards the uterus. Fertilisation, if it happens, takes place inside an oviduct.

Uterus (womb) — a strong, muscular, pear-shaped organ where a baby develops during pregnancy. It has a soft inner lining that thickens each month, ready to nourish a developing baby.

Cervix — the ring of muscle at the lower end of the uterus that acts like a doorway; it keeps the developing baby safely inside and stretches open during birth.

Vagina — the muscular passage that connects the uterus to the outside of the body. It is the passage through which a baby is born.

Study how wonderfully the female system is designed to protect and feed a new life. The egg cell is released from the ovary, travels along the oviduct, and if it is fertilised it settles into the thick, blood-rich lining of the uterus, where it can grow safely for many months. Every part has its role in this careful process.

Did You Know? A baby girl is born with around one to two million immature egg cells already stored inside her ovaries — all the egg cells she will ever have. A boy, by contrast, does not make any sperm cells until puberty, but then his body can make many millions of them every single day. The male and female bodies each contribute in their own remarkable way to the beginning of a new life.

concept-3-puberty-and-adolescence.explanation:
Between about the ages of eleven and sixteen, every young person goes through puberty — the stage when the body changes from a child's body into an adult body that is able to reproduce. The period of life during which these changes happen is called adolescence. This is a natural, healthy and universal part of growing up. Every adult you know — your parents, teachers and elders — passed through it. It does not happen all at once but gradually, over several years, and it begins and finishes at slightly different ages for different people. If your changes come a little earlier or later than a friend's, there is nothing wrong: bodies simply follow their own timing.

Puberty is controlled by hormones, the chemical messengers made by the body. In boys, the testes begin to make more testosterone; in girls, the ovaries begin to make more oestrogen. These hormones travel in the blood and switch on the many changes of puberty. Some changes happen to both boys and girls, while others are specific to one or the other. Let us look at them clearly.

A growth spurt — the body grows taller quite quickly, and hands and feet may grow first.

Body hair grows in new places, such as under the arms.

The sweat glands become more active, so the body sweats more and body odour can develop — this is why daily washing becomes so important.

The skin may become oilier, and some young people get spots or pimples (acne) for a time.

Emotional changes — stronger and sometimes changing feelings, new interests, and a wish for more independence and privacy.

The ovaries begin to release egg cells, and menstruation (monthly periods) begins — we will study this in the next section.

The voice deepens (sometimes 'breaking' or cracking for a while as it changes).

The shoulders broaden and the muscles develop.

Alongside these physical changes come emotional changes, and these matter just as much. During adolescence young people often feel their emotions more strongly, may feel happy and low within the same day, and begin to think more deeply about who they are and about their place in the family and community. This is completely normal — it is the mind maturing just as the body is. In these years, the support of a loving family, honest conversation with a trusted parent or elder, prayer and patience all help a great deal. If you ever feel worried or confused about the changes happening to you, speaking to a parent, an older relative or a teacher is a sign of wisdom, not weakness.
concept-3-puberty-and-adolescence.example: Did You Know? During the growth spurt of puberty, some young people can grow as much as 8 to 10 centimetres taller in a single year — faster than at any time since they were a small baby. This is why you may suddenly need larger shoes and longer clothes, and why growing bodies need plenty of good food and rest.

concept-4-the-menstrual-cycle.explanation:
One of the most important changes that begins at puberty in girls is the menstrual cycle. This is a natural monthly cycle in the female body that prepares the uterus, month by month, in case a baby begins to develop. Understanding it helps every young person — girls and boys alike — to understand how the female body works and to treat it with respect and care. The cycle takes about 28 days on average, though it is perfectly normal for it to be a little shorter or longer, and it is often irregular for the first year or two after it begins.

Let us follow one cycle from its beginning. We count Day 1 as the first day of menstruation (a period). Here is what happens across the cycle:

Days 1 to about 5 — Menstruation. The soft lining of the uterus, which had thickened during the previous cycle, is not needed because no baby is developing. So it gently breaks down and leaves the body through the vagina as a small flow of blood and tissue. This is menstruation, or a 'period'. It is a normal, healthy sign that the body is working well.

About Days 6 to 13 — Rebuilding. After the period, the lining of the uterus begins to build up again, becoming thick, soft and rich with blood — preparing a comfortable place in case a fertilised egg needs to settle there. At the same time, an egg cell is ripening inside an ovary.

About Day 14 — Ovulation. A mature egg cell is released from one of the ovaries. This release is called ovulation. The egg cell then travels slowly into the oviduct, moving towards the uterus. This is the time in the cycle when fertilisation is most likely if a sperm cell is present.

About Days 15 to 28 — Waiting. The egg cell travels along the oviduct. If it is not fertilised, it simply breaks down and is reabsorbed by the body. Because no baby is developing, the thick uterus lining is no longer needed, so towards the end of the cycle it begins to break down — and menstruation begins again on Day 1 of the next cycle.

So the cycle turns, month after month: the lining builds up, an egg is released, and if there is no fertilisation the lining is shed and the cycle starts again. If a fertilisation does happen, the cycle stops, the lining stays in place to nourish the developing baby, and menstruation pauses for the length of the pregnancy. This is one way a woman may first realise she is expecting a baby: her monthly periods stop.

During menstruation it is especially important to keep clean and comfortable. Girls use clean sanitary pads or cloths, changed regularly, and wash carefully — we will return to this in the section on hygiene. A period is nothing to be ashamed of; it is a healthy and natural part of a woman's body. Some girls feel a little tired or have mild cramps at this time; gentle rest, warmth, drinking water and eating well all help.
concept-4-the-menstrual-cycle.example: Did You Know? The word 'menstruation' comes from a Latin word meaning 'monthly', which is related to the word for 'moon', because the cycle takes roughly the same length of time as one cycle of the moon — about a month. Just as the lunar calendar guides the months of Ramadan and the seasons of the year, the female body follows its own gentle monthly rhythm.

concept-5-fertilisation-how-a-new-life-b.explanation:
We now reach the moment at which a new human life begins. Recall that the male body makes sperm cells and the female body releases an egg cell. Fertilisation is the joining, or fusion, of the nucleus of a single sperm cell with the nucleus of the egg cell. This is the scientific heart of this whole unit, so learn it precisely.

When sperm cells are present inside the female body, they swim, using their tails, up through the uterus and into the oviducts, searching for an egg cell. Although many sperm cells begin the journey, usually only one reaches and enters the egg cell. At the instant the nucleus of that sperm cell joins with the nucleus of the egg cell, fertilisation is complete. The single new cell that forms is called a zygote. This one cell carries a complete set of instructions — half from the mother's egg cell and half from the father's sperm cell — and from it a whole new person will grow.

The zygote does not stay a single cell for long. As it travels down the oviduct towards the uterus, it begins to divide: one cell becomes two, two become four, four become eight, and so on, forming a tiny ball of cells. This growing ball is now called an embryo. After about a week, the embryo reaches the uterus and sinks into its thick, soft, blood-rich lining — a step called implantation. Safely settled in the lining, the embryo can now grow and be nourished. Pregnancy has begun.
concept-5-fertilisation-how-a-new-life-b.example: It is worth pausing to reflect on how much is carried in that first single cell. Everything about the new person — whether their eyes will be like their mother's, whether they will be tall like an uncle, the shape of their hands — is written in the instructions gathered from both parents at fertilisation. From something far too small to see grows a complete human being. Studying this carefully is a way of appreciating how wonderfully living things are made.

concept-6-pregnancy-and-the-development-.explanation:
The time during which a baby develops inside the uterus is called pregnancy, or gestation. In humans it lasts about 40 weeks, which is roughly nine months. During this time the tiny embryo grows into a fully formed baby, ready to be born. Let us follow this remarkable journey.

For the first eight weeks or so, the developing baby is called an embryo. During these early weeks the main body parts begin to form: a tiny heart starts to beat, and the beginnings of the brain, spine, arms and legs take shape. From about eight weeks until birth, the developing baby is called a fetus. By now it looks clearly like a tiny human being, and over the following months it grows larger and stronger, its organs mature, it begins to move, and it can even hiccup, suck its thumb and respond to sounds from outside.

How is the developing baby fed and kept alive inside the uterus, when it cannot yet eat or breathe for itself? The answer is a special organ that grows during pregnancy called the placenta. The placenta is joined to the baby by a cord called the umbilical cord. Through the placenta and umbilical cord, the mother's blood passes oxygen and dissolved food (nutrients) to the baby, and carries away the baby's waste substances, such as carbon dioxide, to be removed by the mother's body. The mother's blood and the baby's blood flow very close together in the placenta but do not actually mix; useful substances pass across from one to the other. In this way the mother's body breathes, eats and cleans the blood on behalf of her developing baby.

The baby is also cushioned and protected. It floats in a bag of watery liquid called amniotic fluid, held in a thin sac. This fluid acts like a soft, protective cushion, guarding the baby against bumps and knocks and letting it move and grow freely, while keeping it at a steady, warm temperature. Everything the growing baby needs — food, oxygen, protection, warmth and cleaning — is provided through the careful design of the placenta, the cord and the fluid.

Because the mother is now nourishing two bodies with one, what she does matters greatly for the baby. A pregnant mother needs plenty of good, balanced food, clean water, rest and gentle care. Harmful things that a mother takes in — such as tobacco smoke or unclean food and water — can pass across the placenta and harm the baby, which is why looking after a pregnant mother well is so important for the whole family. Caring for a mother and her unborn child is a duty and a kindness that brings the family together.

Did You Know? Around the middle of pregnancy the mother begins to feel her baby moving inside her — gentle flutters at first, then clear kicks and turns. Many babies become more active at night when the mother is resting. By the later months a baby can hear muffled sounds from outside the uterus, including its mother's voice and heartbeat, which it will recognise after it is born.

The table below shows the main stages of development during pregnancy. Times are approximate, because every baby grows at its own pace.

Main organs begin to form; the heart starts to beat; arms and legs begin to appear.

Clearly human in shape; fingers and toes form; the fetus begins to move (too small to feel yet).

Grows quickly; the mother feels movement; the fetus can hear sounds; hair and eyebrows form.

we01.solution:
Problem: Maryam's menstrual cycle is a regular 28 days. Her most recent period began on the 3rd day of the month. (a) On about which day of the month is she likely to release an egg cell (ovulate)? (b) On about which day of the month would her next period be expected to begin?

Step 1 — Recall the pattern of the cycle. Day 1 of the cycle is the first day of the period. In a 28-day cycle, ovulation happens at roughly the middle — about Day 14. The next period begins when the whole cycle of 28 days is complete, that is, on Day 1 of the next cycle.

Step 2 — Fix Day 1. Maryam's period began on the 3rd of the month, so the 3rd is Day 1 of her cycle.

Step 3 — Find ovulation (part a). Ovulation is about Day 14. Counting 14 days from the 3rd: the 3rd is Day 1, so Day 14 falls on the 16th of the month (3 + 13 = 16). So Maryam is likely to ovulate around the 16th of the month.

sci-g08-u04.unitOverview: Look carefully at the world around you. The iron in a farmer's hoe near the Jubba River, the gold dug from mines in the East African highlands, the carbon in a bag of charcoal, the oxygen you are breathing in this very moment, the salt on your family's table, and the calcium in your own bones and in the limestone rocks along the coast — every single one of these is built from tiny building blocks called atoms. In this unit you will discover that the entire universe, from the smallest grain of sand to the largest star, is made from just over one hundred basic substances called elements.

concept-1-atoms-the-building-blocks-of-e.explanation:
Imagine you take a small piece of pure gold — perhaps a tiny nugget from a mine in the East African highlands — and you cut it in half. Then you cut one of those halves in half again. Suppose you had a magical knife and could keep cutting, again and again, into smaller and smaller pieces. Would you ever reach a piece so small that it could not be cut any further and still be gold? The answer is yes. That smallest possible piece of gold is called an atom of gold.

An atom is the smallest particle of a substance that still behaves as that substance. Atoms are unimaginably tiny. If you lined up ordinary atoms side by side, it would take around ten million of them just to stretch across the width of a single human hair. They are far too small to see with any ordinary microscope. Yet every object you have ever touched — the camel's leather saddle, the metal cup, the water you drink, your own body — is built from countless billions upon billions of these tiny atoms.

Here is the wonderful part. There are not billions of different kinds of atom. There are only about one hundred and eighteen different kinds. Each different kind of atom makes a different element. Just as the twenty-something letters of an alphabet can be arranged to write every word in a whole language, these hundred or so kinds of atom combine in different ways to build every material in the entire universe. That is a breathtaking economy of design.

Did You Know? The word 'atom' comes from an ancient Greek word, atomos, which means 'cannot be cut'. The idea that everything is made of tiny uncuttable pieces was first suggested more than two thousand years ago, long before anyone could prove it. It took until the last two hundred years for science to show the ancient thinkers were right.

An element is a pure substance that is made of only one type of atom. Because it contains just one kind of atom, an element cannot be broken down into any simpler substance by ordinary chemistry. This is what makes elements the true building blocks of chemistry.

Think about the oxygen you are breathing right now. Oxygen is an element: it is made entirely of oxygen atoms and nothing else. Iron, the metal in a farmer's hoe or a cooking pot, is an element: it is made entirely of iron atoms. Carbon, the black material in the charcoal your family may use for cooking, is an element made only of carbon atoms. Gold, copper, sodium, calcium — each of these is a pure element with its own single type of atom.
concept-1-atoms-the-building-blocks-of-e.example: Scientists have found around ninety elements occurring naturally on Earth and in the stars, and have made a further two dozen or so in special laboratories. That gives the total of about 118 elements. Some, like oxygen, carbon and iron, are extremely common. Others are so rare that only a few atoms have ever been made. Every element has its own name and its own personality — some are soft, some hard, some are gases, some are shiny metals, and a few are so reactive they burst into flame in water.

concept-2-chemical-symbols-a-language-fo.explanation:
Scientists live and work in every country on Earth, speaking hundreds of different languages. A scientist in Mogadishu, one in Nairobi and one in far-away Japan all need to write about the same elements without confusion. To make this possible, every element is given a short code called a chemical symbol. These symbols are the same in every country and every language, so they act as a shared scientific language for the whole world.

A chemical symbol is made of one or two letters. There is a strict and important rule about how the letters are written: the first letter is always a capital (uppercase) letter, and the second letter, if there is one, is always small (lowercase). This rule is not just for neatness — it can completely change the meaning. For example, Co means the element cobalt, but CO (two capitals) means carbon and oxygen joined together as carbon monoxide. One is a shiny metal; the other is a poisonous gas. The way you write the letters really matters.

Many symbols are easy because they come straight from the English name. O is oxygen, H is hydrogen, C is carbon, N is nitrogen, Ca is calcium, and Al is aluminium. But some symbols look strange at first, because they come from the old Latin names that scientists used hundreds of years ago. This is why the symbol for iron is Fe (from the Latin *ferrum*), the symbol for gold is Au (from *aurum*), the symbol for sodium is Na (from *natrium*), and the symbol for lead is Pb (from *plumbum*).

Here are some of the most useful symbols to know. Notice how many of these elements appear in everyday East African life. Learn this table well, because we will use these symbols constantly for the rest of the unit.

The lightest element; joins with oxygen to make water.

Found in charcoal, diamonds, and all living things.

The gas we need to live; about one fifth of the air.

Half of common table salt; from Latin natrium.

The other half of table salt; a green, choking gas on its own.

In bones, teeth, limestone and seashells.

In tools, cooking pots and your own blood; from Latin ferrum.

A reddish metal used in wires and cooking pans; from cuprum.

A precious, shiny metal mined in the region; from aurum.

A light metal used in cooking pots and drink cans.

Needed by plants and by your body; from Latin kalium.
concept-2-chemical-symbols-a-language-fo.example: Did You Know? Your own red blood carries oxygen around your body using iron. Each red blood cell contains millions of tiny iron-carrying parts. This is one reason doctors tell people to eat iron-rich foods like meat, beans and dark green leaves — the same element that makes a hoe strong also keeps your blood healthy.

concept-3-the-periodic-table-order-out-o.explanation:
With over a hundred elements to keep track of, scientists needed a sensible way to organise them. Imagine a shopkeeper in the Bakaara market with a hundred different goods thrown together in one heap — finding anything would be impossible. A good shopkeeper arranges goods in neat rows and shelves, grouping similar things together. Scientists did exactly the same thing with the elements, and the result is the Periodic Table.

The Periodic Table is a chart in which every element has its own box. The elements are placed in order of how heavy their atoms are, from the lightest (hydrogen) to the heaviest. But they are not just in one long line. They are arranged in rows and columns so that elements with similar properties end up near each other. This arrangement is so useful that it is one of the most important tools in all of science.

The man most remembered for creating it is Dmitri Mendeleev, a Russian scientist who published his table in 1869. What made him brilliant was that when the pattern left a gap, he did not force an element into it. Instead he said, 'there must be an element here that nobody has discovered yet,' and he even predicted what it would be like. Years later, those missing elements were found, and they matched his predictions almost exactly. A good pattern in science does not just organise what we know — it can predict what we do not yet know.

There are two directions to read the Periodic Table, and each has its own special name. This is one of the most important ideas in the whole unit, so read carefully.

A group is a vertical column — one that runs from top to bottom. There are eight main groups, numbered 1 to 8 (the last group is often called Group 0). The wonderful thing about groups is that all the elements in the same group behave in a similar way, because their atoms are built in a similar way. This means if you know how one member of a group behaves, you can make a very good guess about the others. Group 1, for example, contains sodium and potassium, which are both soft, reactive metals.

A period is a horizontal row — one that runs from left to right. As you move across a period, the elements change gradually from metals on the left, through some in-between elements, to non-metals on the right. A helpful way to remember the difference: groups go down (like a group of camels walking in a line down a path), and periods go across (like reading a period, or sentence, from left to right).

It also helps to know that the Periodic Table is split roughly into three regions. On the left and middle are the metals — and this is by far the largest part, since most elements are metals. On the right-hand side are the non-metals. And squeezed along the staircase-shaped line between them are a few in-between elements that share some properties of both. So just by knowing where an element sits, you can already predict a great deal about how it will behave. The position tells the story.

concept-4-metals-and-non-metals.explanation:
The biggest and most useful division among the elements is between metals and non-metals. You already know many metals from daily life: the iron in a cooking pot, the copper in an electrical wire, the aluminium in a drink can, the gold in jewellery. You also know many non-metals: the oxygen and nitrogen in the air, the carbon in charcoal, the sulfur sometimes used in matches. Metals and non-metals behave in almost opposite ways, and learning their properties lets you predict how a material will act.

Metals share a set of properties that make them extremely useful. Let us go through the most important ones, with examples you can find at home.

Shiny when polished. A clean metal spoon or a gold ring gleams in the light. Scientists call this a lustrous surface.

Good conductors of heat. A metal pot heats up quickly on the fire, which is exactly why we cook with metal and not with wood or clay for boiling.

Good conductors of electricity. This is why electrical wires are made from copper — electricity flows through metals easily.

Malleable, meaning they can be hammered into new shapes without shattering. A blacksmith beats hot iron into a blade or a hoe.

Ductile, meaning they can be pulled into long thin wires. Copper can be drawn out into the thin wires inside a phone charger.

Strong and hard, and most have high melting points, so they stay solid even when very hot. This is why tools and machines are made of metal.

Sonorous, meaning they make a ringing sound when struck — think of a metal bell or two spoons tapped together.

Because of this powerful combination of properties, metals are the materials we reach for whenever we need something strong, long-lasting, able to be shaped, or able to carry heat or electricity. Almost every tool, vehicle, wire and machine depends on them.

Non-metals are, in most ways, the opposite of metals. There are fewer of them, but they are just as important — after all, the air you breathe and the charcoal you cook with are non-metals.

Dull, not shiny (with a few exceptions). A lump of charcoal or a piece of sulfur has no gleam.

Poor conductors of heat and electricity. They are called insulators. This is why the handle of a good cooking pot is often plastic or wood — non-metal materials that do not carry the heat to your hand.

Brittle when solid, meaning they crack or shatter if you hit them, instead of bending. Charcoal crumbles rather than flattens.

Low melting points, and many are gases at ordinary temperatures, such as oxygen, nitrogen and chlorine.

Not sonorous — they make a dull thud, not a ring, when struck.

Lower density, so a piece of a non-metal usually feels lighter than a piece of metal of the same size.

There is one famous exception worth remembering. Carbon in the form of graphite (the 'lead' in a pencil) is a non-metal, yet it does conduct electricity. Nature always keeps a few surprises, and good scientists watch out for exceptions rather than ignoring them.

Did You Know? Mercury is the only metal that is a liquid at room temperature — it flows like shiny silver water. And bromine is one of the very few non-metals that is a liquid too. Most metals are hard solids and most non-metals are gases or brittle solids, but these two break the usual pattern. Mercury is poisonous, so it must never be touched.

Because elements in the same group behave alike, chemists have given special names to some of the most important groups. You do not need to memorise every detail, but knowing these makes the Periodic Table come alive.

Group 1 — the alkali metals. These are soft, light metals such as sodium and potassium. They are so reactive that they must be kept under oil, because they burst into flame if they touch water. This may surprise you, because you eat sodium every day — but only after it has safely joined with chlorine to make harmless table salt. On its own, pure sodium is dangerous.

Group 7 — the halogens. These are colourful, reactive non-metals such as chlorine and iodine. Chlorine is a green, choking gas that is poisonous on its own, yet in tiny amounts it is added to drinking water to kill germs and keep people healthy. Iodine is added to salt in many countries to prevent illness. The same element can be dangerous or life-saving depending on how it is used.
concept-4-metals-and-non-metals.example: Group 0 (or Group 8) — the noble gases. These are gases such as helium, neon and argon. They are famous for being extremely unreactive — they hardly ever join with anything else. Because helium is lighter than air and does not catch fire, it is used to fill balloons and airships. Because neon glows brightly when electricity passes through it, it is used in the bright signs of city shops.

concept-5-compounds-mixtures-and-formula.explanation:
So far we have talked about pure elements. But most of the materials around you are not pure elements at all — they are elements joined together. When atoms of different elements join chemically, they make a brand new substance called a compound. This is one of the most important ideas in chemistry, so let us build it up slowly and carefully.

The clearest example is water. Water is not an element. It is a compound made from two elements: hydrogen and oxygen, chemically joined. On their own, hydrogen and oxygen are both invisible gases — and hydrogen even burns fiercely. Yet when their atoms join in the right way, they make water, a cool liquid that puts out fire. This is the astonishing thing about compounds: the compound is completely different from the elements that made it.

Another example is right on your dinner table. Common salt is a compound called sodium chloride, made from the element sodium (a dangerous, reactive metal) joined with the element chlorine (a poisonous green gas). Neither is safe to eat on its own, yet joined together they make the harmless salt that flavours your food and that the sea leaves behind when it dries on the coast. The calcium in limestone and seashells is likewise joined with carbon and oxygen to make a compound called calcium carbonate.

It is very important not to confuse a compound with a mixture. In a compound, the elements are chemically joined, and it takes a chemical reaction to separate them. The compound has new properties, quite unlike its ingredients. In a mixture, the substances are simply mixed together without joining chemically, so each one keeps its own properties and they can usually be separated easily.

For example, air is a mixture of oxygen, nitrogen and other gases — they are jumbled together but not joined, and each keeps its own nature. Sea water is a mixture of water and salt; when the sun dries it on the coast, the salt is left behind, showing the two were never chemically joined. But water itself is a compound, because its hydrogen and oxygen are truly joined and cannot be separated just by drying or filtering.

Scientists describe a compound using a formula — a short code made of chemical symbols and small numbers. Once you learn to read a formula, it tells you exactly which atoms are inside and how many of each. This is one of the most useful skills in chemistry.

The symbols tell you which elements are present. The small number written just after and below a symbol tells you how many atoms of that element there are. If a symbol has no number, it means there is just one atom. Look carefully at these examples:

H2O (water) means 2 atoms of hydrogen and 1 atom of oxygen joined together.

CO2 (carbon dioxide) means 1 atom of carbon and 2 atoms of oxygen. This is the gas you breathe out.

NaCl (common salt) means 1 atom of sodium (Na) and 1 atom of chlorine (Cl).

CaCO3 (calcium carbonate, in limestone) means 1 calcium, 1 carbon and 3 oxygen atoms.
concept-5-compounds-mixtures-and-formula.example: So a formula is like a recipe written in code. Just as a recipe for canjeero tells you how much of each ingredient to use, a formula tells you exactly how many atoms of each element are combined in the compound. Reading formulae carefully — noticing exactly where each small number sits — is a skill worth practising until it feels natural.

concept-6-an-introduction-to-chemical-re.explanation:
How do compounds get made in the first place? And how does iron turn to rust, or charcoal turn to ash and heat? The answer is a chemical reaction. A chemical reaction is a change in which one or more substances are turned into one or more new substances. This is different from simply mixing or melting, because in a chemical reaction the atoms rearrange themselves to make something genuinely new.

Scientists use two special words to describe a reaction. The substances you start with are called the reactants. The new substances you end with are called the products. We can show a reaction as a kind of sentence, with an arrow that means 'turns into':

Let us look at a reaction you have almost certainly seen: rusting. When a farmer leaves an iron hoe out in the damp air, it slowly turns orange-brown and crumbly. This is a chemical reaction. The iron joins with oxygen from the air to make a new substance, iron oxide, which we call rust. We can write it like this:

Here iron and oxygen are the reactants, and rust is the product. Notice that rust is completely different from the shiny, strong iron we started with — it is weak, flaky and orange. That is the sign of a chemical reaction: a new substance with new properties has appeared, and you cannot simply turn it back by drying or cooling it.

Another everyday example is burning charcoal. When your family lights charcoal to cook, the carbon in the charcoal joins with oxygen in the air to make carbon dioxide gas, and releases heat and light in the process. We write it as carbon + oxygen -> carbon dioxide. The carbon and oxygen are the reactants; the carbon dioxide is the product. The heat that cooks your food is the energy released by this reaction.
concept-6-an-introduction-to-chemical-re.example: Did You Know? When you cook bread or canjeero, chemical reactions are hard at work. Heat causes reactions that make new substances, giving cooked food its brown colour and delicious smell. The raw batter and the finished bread are chemically different — which is why you cannot un-cook a loaf. Cooking is one of the oldest kinds of chemistry humans ever practised.

sci-g08-u05.unitOverview: Think about the water your family drinks. If it comes from a well, a river like the Jubba, or a rain barrel, it is almost never truly clean. It carries bits of sand, mud, tiny living germs, and sometimes dissolved salt you cannot even see. Now think about the salt your mother sprinkles into a pot of bariis, or the sugar that sweetens a glass of shaah. Both of these were once locked inside something else — salt inside sea water, sugar inside a sugar-cane plant — and clever people used science to pull them out. In this unit you will learn the science of mixtures and how to separate them. It is one of the most practical, life-saving topics in all of chemistry.
outcomes: By the end of this unit you will be able to:

Study this table carefully. These words are the tools of a chemist who works with mixtures. Notice how the example column ties each word to something you already know from home.

concept-1-pure-substances-and-mixtures.explanation:
The first big idea in this unit is the difference between something that is pure and something that is a mixture. In everyday speech, 'pure' can mean clean or natural. In science it has a much more exact meaning.

A pure substance is made of only one type of particle, with nothing else mixed in. Pure water contains only water particles. Pure salt contains only salt particles. Pure sugar contains only sugar particles. Because a pure substance is always the same all the way through, it behaves in a fixed, predictable way. For example, pure water always boils at exactly 100 degrees Celsius and always freezes at exactly 0 degrees Celsius at sea level. This fixed behaviour is actually a test for purity — if a scientist wants to check whether a sample of water is pure, one thing they can do is measure its boiling point.

A mixture is made of two or more substances that are simply mixed together and not chemically joined. This is the key point: in a mixture, each substance keeps its own properties and can be separated out again. When you stir salt into water, the salt does not turn into a new substance — it is still salt, just spread out among the water. If you remove the water, the salt comes back exactly as it was. This is why almost every method in this whole unit works: because the parts of a mixture keep their own properties, we can use the differences between those properties to pull the mixture apart.

Mixtures do not have a fixed boiling or melting point. Salty water, for example, boils at a slightly higher temperature than pure water, and the exact temperature depends on how much salt is dissolved in it. So a substance that boils over a range of temperatures, rather than at one exact temperature, is probably a mixture.

Look around and you will see that mixtures are everywhere, and pure substances are actually quite rare in nature. The air is a mixture of nitrogen, oxygen, carbon dioxide and other gases. Sea water is a mixture of water and many dissolved salts. Soil is a mixture of sand, clay, small stones and decayed plants. Camel milk is a mixture of water, fats, sugars and proteins. Even the smoke rising from a charcoal fire is a mixture of gases and tiny solid specks.
concept-1-pure-substances-and-mixtures.example: Did You Know? The salt we buy in shops is often not perfectly pure — it may have tiny amounts of other minerals mixed in, which is why some salt is slightly grey or pink. Rainwater is one of the purest natural waters, because it forms when water evaporates into the sky and leaves its dissolved salts and dirt behind — a natural distillation carried out by the sun.

concept-2-solutions-solvents-and-solutes.explanation:
One of the most important kinds of mixture is a solution. You make solutions every single day, probably without thinking about it. When your family makes shaah and stirs in sugar, the sugar seems to vanish. It has not disappeared — it has dissolved, and you have made a solution. Let us learn the proper words for what is going on.

Whenever something dissolves, three words describe what is happening:

The solvent is the liquid that does the dissolving. In a glass of sweet shaah, the water is the solvent.

The solute is the substance that dissolves into the solvent. In sweet shaah, the sugar is the solute.

The solution is the clear mixture you get at the end — the solvent with the solute spread evenly through it.

A simple sentence links them all together: solute + solvent = solution. So sugar (the solute) plus water (the solvent) makes sugary water (the solution). Salt (the solute) plus water (the solvent) makes salty water (the solution). Water is by far the most common solvent in the world — it dissolves so many things that scientists sometimes call it the 'universal solvent'.

When a solid dissolves, its tiny particles break away from each other and spread out to fill the gaps between the particles of the liquid. Picture a spoonful of salt dropped into water. At first you can see the white grains. As they dissolve, the salt particles separate one by one and slip in among the water particles, spreading out until they are shared evenly through the whole glass. That is why a solution looks clear — the particles are far too small to see — and why the salt is now in every part of the water, not just at the bottom. Very importantly, the salt is not destroyed. Its particles are still there, hidden among the water. This is exactly why we can get the salt back later by evaporating the water.
concept-2-solutions-solvents-and-solutes.example: Not everything dissolves. A substance that can dissolve in a particular liquid is called soluble; a substance that cannot is called insoluble. Salt and sugar are soluble in water. Sand, charcoal, chalk and cooking oil are insoluble in water — stir sand into water and, however long you wait, it just sinks to the bottom. This difference is enormously useful. If a solid is insoluble, we can catch it with a filter; if it is soluble, we cannot filter it out, and we must use evaporation or distillation instead. Knowing whether something is soluble is the first question a scientist asks when planning how to separate a mixture.

concept-3-solubility-and-saturation.explanation:
Now we go a step deeper. It is not enough to know whether something dissolves — a good scientist also asks how much dissolves, and how fast. This is the idea of solubility.

Solubility tells us how much of a solute will dissolve in a certain amount of solvent at a given temperature. Some solutes are very soluble — you can dissolve a great deal of sugar in a cup of water. Others are only slightly soluble. Solubility is not a fixed, single number, because it depends strongly on the temperature of the solvent, as you will now see.

If you have ever waited for sugar to dissolve in cold water, you know it can be slow. Three things speed up dissolving, and you can feel each of them in your own kitchen:

Heating the solvent. Sugar and salt dissolve much faster in hot shaah than in cold water. Warmer particles move faster and pull the solute apart more quickly. Hot water also holds *more* solute in total.

Stirring. Stirring keeps fresh solvent moving past the solid, carrying dissolved particles away so more can dissolve. This is why you stir sugar into your tea.

Crushing the solid into smaller pieces. A powder dissolves faster than a big lump because more of its surface is touching the water. A block of rock salt dissolves slowly; ground salt dissolves quickly.

Notice that stirring and crushing make the solute dissolve faster, but they do not let you dissolve more in total. Only heating does both — it speeds things up and increases how much can dissolve.

Did You Know? Hot water can hold far more dissolved sugar than cold water. This is the secret behind making sweets and toffee: sugar is dissolved in very hot water and then, as it cools, the water can no longer hold it all and the sugar sets solid. Gases behave the opposite way to solids: a cold fizzy drink holds its gas better than a warm one, which is why a warm soda goes flat and foams over quickly.

There is a limit to how much you can dissolve. Keep adding salt to a glass of water and stirring, and at first it all disappears. But eventually you reach a point where no more salt will dissolve — the extra salt just sinks to the bottom and stays there, no matter how long you stir. When a solution is holding as much dissolved solute as it possibly can, we say it is a saturated solution.

concept-4-separation-methods.explanation:
Now we come to the heart of the unit: how to separate a mixture back into its parts. The golden rule is always the same — find a property that is different between the substances, and use that difference to separate them. A different particle size, whether something dissolves, a different boiling point, or how strongly a dye sticks to paper — each difference gives us a method. Let us take the five main methods in turn.

Filtration separates an insoluble solid from a liquid. You pour the mixture through a filter — filter paper in a laboratory, or a clean cloth or a fine sieve at home. The liquid passes through the tiny holes, but the solid bits are too big to fit through, so they are trapped. The two parts even have proper names: the solid trapped on the filter is called the residue, and the clear liquid that drips through is called the filtrate.

Filtration is one of the most useful skills in daily life. When your grandmother pours a pot of shaah through a strainer, the tea leaves (residue) stay behind and the clear tea (filtrate) flows into the cup. When a family in a village near Garissa pours muddy well water through a folded cloth, the mud and sand are caught and clearer water passes through. Remember one vital point, though: filtration removes only the solid bits you can catch. It does not remove dissolved salt, and it does not kill germs. Filtered water may look clear but can still make you very ill, so it must always be boiled before drinking to be truly safe.

Did You Know? A traditional cloth filter can remove the tiny water creatures that carry some diseases, which is why folding a clean cloth several times over a water pot has protected families for generations — but boiling is still needed to kill the smallest germs.

Evaporation does the opposite job to filtration — it separates a soluble solid from the liquid it is dissolved in. You cannot filter salt out of salty water, because the salt is dissolved and slips straight through the filter. Instead, you gently warm the solution so that the water turns into a gas (water vapour) and escapes into the air, leaving the solid behind. The solute stays because it does not evaporate at that temperature — only the water does.

This is exactly how sea salt is harvested along the Indian Ocean coast near Berbera and Kismaayo. Sea water is let into shallow pans, and the hot sun slowly evaporates the water. Day by day the water disappears into the air, and the salt is left behind in the pan, ready to be scooped up, dried and sold. It is powered by nothing but sunshine — a free and clever use of evaporation that has fed and preserved food for thousands of years.

Crystallisation is a gentler, more careful cousin of evaporation. It is used when you want to collect the solute as beautiful, well-formed crystals rather than a rough powder. You warm the solution to evaporate some — but not all — of the water, until the solution is saturated. Then you stop heating and let it cool slowly. As it cools, the solubility drops, the solution can no longer hold all its solute, and the solute comes out slowly as solid crystals. The slower it cools, the larger and neater the crystals grow.

You have almost certainly seen crystallisation without naming it. Rock sugar (sometimes called sugar crystals) is made this way, and so are the large flat crystals of sea salt. The difference between evaporation and crystallisation is subtle but real: evaporation drives off *all* the water quickly and leaves a dry solid, while crystallisation removes only *some* water and then cools the solution to grow clean, pure crystals. If a chemist wants a pure, well-shaped product, they choose crystallisation.

Sometimes it is not the solid you want — it is the pure liquid. If you have salty water and you want to drink the water, evaporation is no use, because it lets the precious water escape into the air and keeps only the salt. Distillation solves this problem cleverly by catching the escaping vapour and cooling it back into a liquid.

Here is how it works, step by step. You boil the salty water. The water turns to steam and rises, but the salt cannot turn to a gas at that temperature, so the salt stays behind in the container. The steam then travels to a cool surface, where it condenses — cools and turns back into liquid water. Because only the water evaporated and then condensed, the liquid you collect is pure water, with the salt left behind. In a laboratory the cooling is done in a tube called a condenser; at home, steam condenses on a cool pot lid and drips off.

Distillation is how ships at sea and desert towns turn salty sea water into fresh drinking water, and it is one of the most important technologies for regions that face drought. It also explains a natural wonder: the sun distils the ocean every single day. Water evaporates from the sea, rises, cools high in the sky, condenses into clouds, and falls as clean rain — leaving all the sea salt behind. Rain is nature's distilled water.

Did You Know? Distillation uses two changes of state you already know: boiling (liquid to gas) and condensing (gas back to liquid). No new substance is made — the water is just taken apart from the salt and put back together, pure. A large desalination plant on the coast can distil millions of litres of sea water into fresh water every day to supply a whole city.

The last method looks almost like magic. Chromatography separates different coloured dyes that are mixed together in a liquid, such as the many colours hidden inside a single ink or food dye. You put a small spot of the coloured mixture near the bottom of a strip of paper, then stand the paper so its bottom edge just touches a shallow pool of water (the solvent), without the spot itself touching the water.

The water slowly soaks up the paper, and as it rises it carries the dyes with it. Here is the clever part: different dyes are carried at different speeds. A dye that dissolves easily and does not stick to the paper is carried far and fast. A dye that sticks tightly to the paper and dissolves less easily is left behind, low down. So a single black spot may separate into several bands of colour spread up the paper — perhaps blue, red and yellow all hiding inside one 'black' ink. Each dye is separated because of a difference in how strongly it holds to the paper versus how well it dissolves in the moving solvent.

concept-5-choosing-the-right-method.explanation:
A real scientist does not just know the methods — they know which one to choose for a given mixture. This is where all your learning comes together. To choose correctly, ask yourself a short chain of questions about the mixture:

Is it a solid mixed with a liquid? If the solid is insoluble (like sand or mud), use filtration. If the solid is dissolved (soluble), filtration will not work.

Do I want to keep the dissolved solid? If yes, use evaporation (for a quick dry solid) or crystallisation (for pure, well-formed crystals).

Do I want to keep the liquid itself, pure? Then use distillation, which catches and cools the vapour.

Am I separating coloured dyes in a liquid? Then use chromatography.

concept-6-a-worked-real-life-example-cle.explanation:
Imagine a family during a drought has only muddy water that is also slightly salty, and they want clean drinking water. No single method does it all — you must combine them in the right order:

Filter first. Pour the muddy water through a clean cloth to catch the mud and sand (the insoluble residue). Now the water is clear but still salty and may still hold germs.

Distil next, if salt must be removed. Boil the clear water and catch and cool the steam to collect pure water, leaving the dissolved salt behind.

If there is no salt to remove, simply boil the filtered water. Boiling kills the germs that filtration cannot remove. Filtered water that has been boiled is safe to drink.

method-5.example: To collect pure water from salty water by boiling it gently and catching the steam on a cool lid — a simple, safe model of distillation.
steps: An adult pours the salty water into the pot to a shallow depth, and stands the empty clean cup in the middle so its rim is above the water.
Put the lid on the pot UPSIDE DOWN (so the dome points inwards, guiding drips towards the cup).
An adult heats the pot gently so the salty water simmers — not a violent boil.
Steam rises, touches the cool lid and condenses into drops that run down and drip into the clean cup.
After several minutes, the adult turns off the heat and lets everything cool before removing the cup.

we01.solution:
Worked Example 1

Question: Halima has a bowl of bariis (rice) with small stones mixed in. How should she separate them, and what property is she using?

Step 1 — Find the difference. The stones and the rice grains are different sizes and colours, and both are solids that are easy to see.

Step 2 — Choose the method. Because the difference is in size and appearance, she can separate them by hand — hand-sorting or sieving the smaller grains from the larger stones.

we02.solution:
Step 1 — Find the difference. The stones and the rice grains are different sizes and colours, and both are solids that are easy to see.

Step 2 — Choose the method. Because the difference is in size and appearance, she can separate them by hand — hand-sorting or sieving the smaller grains from the larger stones.

Answer: She hand-sorts or sieves them, using the difference in size between the stones and the rice. No dissolving is involved, so no filter or heat is needed.

Worked Example 2

we03.solution:
Step 1 — Find the difference. The salt is dissolved (soluble), so it cannot be filtered. But salt does not evaporate at the temperatures water does.

Step 2 — Choose the method. Since he wants the solid and not the water, he uses evaporation: gently warm the salty water so the water turns to vapour and escapes.

Answer: He uses evaporation. The water escapes into the air as water vapour, and the salt is left behind — exactly as sea-salt farmers do with sunshine.

Worked Example 3

we04.solution:
Step 1 — Find the difference. Water boils and turns to steam at 100 degrees Celsius, but the salt stays behind because it does not turn to gas at that temperature.

Step 2 — Choose the method. Because she wants to keep the water, she must catch the escaping steam and cool it back into a liquid — this is distillation.

Answer: She uses distillation. She boils the salty water, and the steam condenses on a cool lid into pure water, leaving the salt behind. Unlike evaporation, distillation saves the water instead of losing it.

Reading Comprehension — Clean Water in the Dry Season

concept-2-reflection-and-the-law-of-refl.explanation:
When light hits a surface and bounces off, we call it reflection. Every surface reflects at least some light, which is why you can see it at all. A very smooth, shiny surface like a mirror or the calm surface of the Indian Ocean at dawn reflects light in an orderly way, so it can form a clear image. A rough surface like a wall or a dusty road reflects light in all directions and scatters it, so it shows no image. Both are reflection; the difference is only how smooth the surface is.

To describe reflection precisely, scientists do not measure angles from the mirror itself. Instead they draw an imaginary line straight out of the surface, at exactly 90 degrees to it, at the point where the ray hits. This line is called the normal. It is your reference line. You measure every angle from the normal, never from the mirror.

The ray arriving at the mirror is the incident ray.

The ray bouncing away is the reflected ray.

The angle of incidence (often written as the letter i) is between the incident ray and the normal.

The angle of reflection (written as r) is between the reflected ray and the normal.

Now here is one of the most reliable rules in all of science, the law of reflection: the angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection. In short, i = r. If light strikes a mirror at 30 degrees from the normal, it leaves at exactly 30 degrees from the normal on the other side. It never changes. This law is always true for every flat mirror, every time, everywhere.

Worked Example: using the law of reflection

Let us work through a problem step by step, the way you should in your notebook. Hassan shines a torch at a flat mirror. The incident ray hits the mirror so that it makes an angle of 50 degrees with the mirror surface. What is the angle of reflection, measured from the normal?

Find the angle of incidence first. The angle is given from the mirror surface, but we must measure from the normal. The normal is at 90 degrees to the mirror. So the angle of incidence = 90 — 50 = 40 degrees.

Apply the law of reflection. The law says angle of incidence = angle of reflection, so i = r.

State the answer. Since i = 40 degrees, the angle of reflection r = 40 degrees (measured from the normal).

Check it makes sense. The reflected ray also makes 90 — 40 = 50 degrees with the mirror surface, mirroring the incident ray perfectly. That is exactly what we expect from a flat mirror.

Let us try a second one. A ray strikes a mirror with an angle of incidence of 25 degrees. What is the angle of reflection, and what is the total angle between the incident ray and the reflected ray? By the law of reflection, the angle of reflection is also 25 degrees. The two rays sit on opposite sides of the normal, so the total angle between them is 25 + 25 = 50 degrees. Notice the pattern: the angle between the two rays is always double the angle of incidence.

When Khadija looks into a flat mirror, she sees an image of herself that is the same size as she is, standing the same distance behind the mirror as she is in front of it, and the right way up. But the image is laterally inverted, which means left and right are swapped. Raise your right hand in front of a mirror and your image raises what looks like its left hand. This is why the word on the front of an ambulance is often printed backwards, so that a driver ahead sees it the right way round in their rear-view mirror.
