outcomes: By the end of this unit, you will be able to:
Name the main food groups and nutrients — carbohydrates, proteins, fats (lipids), vitamins, minerals, water and fibre — and give a local food example of each.
Explain the job of each nutrient in the body and describe what happens when a nutrient is missing (deficiency).
Describe a balanced diet and explain why different people (a farmer, a baby, a pregnant mother, a person fasting) need different amounts of food.
Name the organs of the digestive system in order and state the function of each: mouth, oesophagus, stomach, small intestine, large intestine, and the helper organs (liver, pancreas).
Explain the difference between mechanical and chemical digestion and give an example of each.
Describe what enzymes are and explain how they break large food molecules into small, soluble ones.
Explain absorption — how digested food passes into the blood through the wall of the small intestine.
Carry out simple food tests for starch, sugar and fat, and interpret the results.
Apply your knowledge to plan a healthy, balanced meal from foods available in your community.

concept-1-why-does-your-body-need-food.explanation:
Think about a car or a lorry travelling on the road from Hargeisa to Berbera. It cannot move without fuel. Your body is far more wonderful than any machine, but it too needs fuel and building materials. Food does three great jobs in your body:

It gives you energy. Every movement — running, breathing, even blinking — uses energy. Your body also uses energy just to stay warm and keep your heart beating. This energy comes mainly from carbohydrates and fats.

It helps you grow and repair. You are still growing! Your body builds new cells and heals wounds using proteins and minerals. When Amina cuts her finger, her body repairs the skin using material from the food she eats.

It keeps you healthy and protected. Vitamins and minerals keep your eyes, skin, bones and blood working well and help you fight off illness such as malaria or infections.

Because food does so many different jobs, no single food can do everything. Rice alone gives energy but cannot build strong muscles. Meat alone builds muscle but gives little quick energy. This is exactly why we need a balanced diet — a mixture of many foods.
concept-1-why-does-your-body-need-food.example: Did You Know? An active 12-year-old needs roughly 2000 to 2200 kilojoules of energy from food per day — and even more if you walk long distances to school or help herd goats. When you are asleep, your body still uses about one-fifth of its daytime energy just to keep you alive.

concept-2-the-nutrients-in-your-food.explanation:
Scientists group the substances in food into seven types of nutrient. Let us look at each one, its job, and where you can find it in the foods around you.

Carbohydrates are your body's main and fastest source of energy. There are two kinds: starch and sugars. Starchy foods release their energy slowly and steadily, which is why a plate of bariis or canjeero keeps you going for hours. Sugars release energy very quickly but do not last long. A date gives you a quick burst of energy — which is one reason the Prophet (peace be upon him) recommended breaking the fast with dates at iftar. Good sources include rice, canjeero, pasta, potatoes, sweet potatoes, bread, dates and honey.

Proteins are the building blocks of your body. Your muscles, skin, hair and even your blood are made largely of protein. Growing children, pregnant mothers and people healing from illness need plenty of protein. Proteins come from two places: animal sources such as fish from the Indian Ocean, goat meat, camel milk, eggs and cheese; and plant sources such as beans, lentils and groundnuts. A meal of beans (digir) is an excellent and affordable way to get protein.

Fats and oils (lipids) — the energy stores

Fats give more energy per gram than any other nutrient — more than twice as much as carbohydrate. Your body stores extra fat under the skin, where it also keeps you warm. Fats are found in cooking oil, ghee (subag), the fat on meat, milk, nuts and avocado. You need some fat, but too much — especially from fried and oily foods — can be harmful over time, so eat fats in moderation.

Vitamins are needed only in very small amounts, but without them the body cannot work properly. For example, vitamin C (found in mango, lime, guava and tomatoes) keeps your gums and skin healthy and helps wounds heal. Vitamin A (found in liver, milk, and orange vegetables like carrots and pumpkin) keeps your eyes healthy, especially your ability to see in dim light. Vitamin D, which your skin makes in sunlight, helps build strong bones — and in sunny East Africa, that vitamin is a daily gift.

Minerals are simple substances the body needs in small amounts. Calcium (in milk, cheese and small fish eaten with bones) builds strong bones and teeth. Iron (in red meat, liver, beans and dark green leaves) is needed to make healthy red blood. A person who lacks iron becomes tired and pale — a condition called anaemia, which is common and can be prevented by eating iron-rich foods.

More than half of your body is water. You need water for your blood, for digestion, for sweating to keep cool in the heat, and for removing waste in urine. In a hot, sometimes dry climate, and especially when you are fasting, drinking enough clean water is very important. Always drink water that is safe — from a protected well, or boiled and cooled — to avoid diseases like cholera and diarrhoea.

Fibre is the tough part of plant foods that your body cannot digest, such as the skins of beans and vegetables and the outer part of whole grains. Even though it is not absorbed, fibre is very important: it gives the muscles of your gut something to push against, keeping food moving smoothly and preventing constipation. Vegetables, fruit, beans and whole grains are all rich in fibre.

concept-3-a-balanced-diet.explanation:
A balanced diet contains all seven nutrients in the correct amounts. Picture a plate. Roughly, a healthy plate should have a good portion of carbohydrate (rice, canjeero or potato) for energy, a portion of protein (fish, meat or beans) for growth, plenty of vegetables and fruit for vitamins, minerals and fibre, a small amount of fat, and always a drink of clean water. A meal of bariis with fish, a spoon of vegetables, and a mango afterwards is close to a perfectly balanced plate.

Not everyone needs the same amount of food. The amount depends on several things:

Age: A growing teenager needs more protein for building than an elderly person. A baby needs milk above all.

Activity: A fisherman rowing all day, or a boy herding goats across the savanna, needs far more energy than someone sitting most of the day.

Body size: A larger body needs more food to run it.

Special conditions: A pregnant mother eats for herself and her growing baby, so she needs extra protein, iron and calcium.

Too little food of the right kind leads to malnutrition — the body becomes weak, growth slows, and illness comes easily. Too much food, especially too much sugar and fat, can lead to being overweight and to health problems later in life. Balance is the goal in all things.

Did You Know? Eating too much sugar does not only cause tooth decay. Over many years, a diet very high in sugar can lead to a serious illness called type 2 diabetes, where the body can no longer control the sugar level in the blood. Choosing fruit and dates for sweetness, instead of many sweets and sugary drinks, protects your future health.
concept-3-a-balanced-diet.example: During Ramadan, when many Muslims fast from dawn to sunset, a balanced diet becomes even more important. At suhoor (the meal before dawn), foods that release energy slowly — like whole grains, beans, and canjeero — help you feel full and strong through the day. Plenty of water at suhoor helps you stay hydrated. At iftar, breaking the fast gently with dates and water, then eating a balanced meal, is both a beautiful tradition and wise nutrition. Eating well during Ramadan lets you worship and study with strength.

concept-4-the-journey-through-your-diges.explanation:
Now for the amazing journey. The food you eat is far too big and complex to enter your blood as it is. A grain of rice cannot simply slip into your bloodstream! It must first be broken down into tiny, soluble molecules. This breaking-down process is called digestion, and it happens along a long muscular tube called the digestive system (or alimentary canal). If you could stretch this tube out straight, it would be several metres long — longer than you are tall, coiled neatly inside you.

Let us follow a piece of canjeero on its journey, organ by organ. Imagine the path as a long, winding road, and each organ is a station where a different job is done.

Digestion begins the moment you take a bite. Your teeth cut and grind the food into smaller pieces. This is mechanical digestion — physically breaking food apart, like using a pestle and mortar. At the same time, glands in your mouth release saliva. Saliva makes the food soft and slippery, and it contains an enzyme called amylase that begins chemical digestion by starting to break starch down into sugar. This is why, if you chew a piece of plain canjeero or bread for a long time, it slowly begins to taste slightly sweet — the amylase is turning starch into sugar right there in your mouth. Your tongue then rolls the food into a soft ball and pushes it to the back of your throat to be swallowed.

When you swallow, the ball of food enters the oesophagus (the gullet), a muscular tube that connects your mouth to your stomach. Food does not simply fall down by gravity — if it did, you could not eat lying down or drink while bending over. Instead, the muscles in the wall of the oesophagus squeeze in waves behind the food, pushing it along. This wave-like squeezing is called peristalsis, and it happens all the way along your gut.

The oesophagus leads to the stomach, a stretchy, muscular bag. Here the food stays for a few hours. The stomach walls churn and squeeze the food, mixing it thoroughly — more mechanical digestion. The stomach also releases gastric juice, which contains a strong acid (hydrochloric acid) and enzymes that begin to digest proteins. The acid has a second important job: it kills most of the harmful germs (bacteria) that may have come in with the food, protecting you from illness. After a few hours, the food has become a thick, souplike liquid.

4. The small intestine — where most digestion and absorption happen

The soupy food now passes into the small intestine, a long, narrow, coiled tube where the most important work happens. It is called 'small' because it is narrow, but it is actually the longest part of the gut — about six metres in an adult. Here, digestive juices from the pancreas and liver pour in and mix with the food. Enzymes finish breaking down carbohydrates, proteins and fats into their smallest molecules: carbohydrates into glucose (a simple sugar), proteins into amino acids, and fats into fatty acids. The liver makes a green-yellow liquid called bile, stored in the gall bladder, which breaks large drops of fat into tiny droplets so the enzymes can work on them more easily.

Once the food is fully digested into these tiny soluble molecules, they are ready to be absorbed — to pass through the wall of the small intestine and into the blood. The inside wall of the small intestine is not smooth; it is covered with millions of tiny finger-like folds called villi (one is a villus). These villi give the wall a huge surface area, like the many tiny loops of a towel that soak up much more water than a flat cloth. Because of this enormous surface, digested food is absorbed quickly and efficiently into the blood, which carries the nutrients to every cell in your body.
concept-4-the-journey-through-your-diges.example: By now, almost all the useful nutrients have been absorbed. What remains is the material the body cannot digest — mainly fibre and water. This passes into the large intestine. Here, most of the water is absorbed back into the body, so the body does not waste it. This is why drinking enough water matters: some of the water your gut uses is reclaimed here. The remaining solid waste, called faeces, is stored until it leaves the body through the anus. If a person has diarrhoea, water is not properly reabsorbed and is lost from the body, which is why diarrhoea can cause dangerous dehydration — and why drinking clean water and salts to replace the loss is so important.

concept-5-mechanical-and-chemical-digest.explanation:
Digestion happens in two ways that work together, and it is important to tell them apart.

Mechanical digestion is the physical breaking of food into smaller pieces without changing what it is made of. Your teeth grinding food and your stomach churning it are both mechanical. Think of breaking a large loaf into crumbs — the crumbs are still bread. Mechanical digestion is helpful because it creates many smaller pieces, giving the enzymes a much larger surface to work on.

Chemical digestion is the breaking of large food molecules into small ones using enzymes and other chemicals like acid and bile. This actually changes the food into different, simpler substances — starch becomes sugar, protein becomes amino acids. Chemical digestion happens in the mouth (starch), the stomach (protein), and the small intestine (all nutrients).

The two work as a team. Mechanical digestion breaks the food into small pieces so that chemical digestion, using enzymes, can act on a large surface and finish the job quickly. If you swallowed food without chewing, the enzymes would have far less surface to work on and digestion would be slow and difficult. This is also why we are taught to eat calmly and chew our food well.

Breaking large molecules into small ones.
concept-5-mechanical-and-chemical-digest.example: Yes — it becomes a new, simpler substance.

concept-6-enzymes-the-tiny-workers.explanation:
Enzymes are one of the most wonderful discoveries in biology. An enzyme is a special kind of protein that speeds up a chemical reaction without being used up itself. Because they speed things up, we call them biological catalysts. Without enzymes, digesting a single meal might take days or even weeks. With them, it takes only hours.

A useful way to picture an enzyme is a key and lock. Each enzyme has a special shape that fits only one type of food molecule, just as one key fits only one lock. When the food molecule fits into the enzyme, the enzyme snips it apart into smaller pieces. Then the enzyme is free to grab the next molecule and do it again, and again, thousands of times.

There are three main groups of digestive enzymes you should know:

Carbohydrase (for example, amylase) breaks carbohydrates (starch) into sugars (glucose). It works in the mouth and small intestine.

Protease breaks proteins into amino acids. It works in the stomach and small intestine.

Lipase breaks fats (lipids) into fatty acids and glycerol. It works in the small intestine.

Enzymes are fussy about their conditions. They work best at your body temperature, about 37 degrees Celsius — which is one reason your body keeps itself warm. They also each need the right level of acid: the protease in your stomach likes acidic conditions, while the enzymes in the small intestine prefer conditions that are slightly alkaline. If an enzyme gets too hot, its special shape is destroyed forever — we say it is denatured — and it can no longer work, like a key that has been melted out of shape.

explore-3.answer: Which dissolved faster — the whole lump or the crushed sugar? Why? The crushed sugar has a larger total surface area touching the water. How does this connect to why we chew our food? Explain how this experiment models the teamwork between mechanical and chemical digestion in your mouth.

we01.solution:
Step 1 — Start with energy (carbohydrate). Maryam is active, so she needs good energy. We choose a portion of bariis (rice). This supplies starch for steady energy.

Step 2 — Add growth food (protein). She is still growing, so she needs protein. We add a piece of grilled fish from the coast, or a serving of beans if fish is not available.

Step 3 — Add vitamins, minerals and fibre. We add a spoonful of cooked vegetables (such as spinach or carrots) and a fresh mango for vitamin C and fibre.

Step 4 — Include a little fat. The fish is cooked with a small amount of oil, which supplies fat — but we keep it modest.

outcomes: By the end of this unit you will be able to:
Explain the difference between a rock and a mineral, with everyday examples.
Describe the three main types of rock — igneous, sedimentary and metamorphic — and how each one forms.
Explain how weathering breaks rock down and how erosion carries the pieces away.
Describe how loose pieces (sediment) are transported by rivers and settle into layers that harden into sedimentary rock.
Explain how fossils form and why they are almost always found in sedimentary rock.

Give examples of how people use rocks and minerals in building, farming, trade and daily life.
Carry out simple tests, such as a scratch-hardness test, and interpret the results.

concept-1-rocks-and-minerals-what-is-the.explanation:
Before we can talk about the three types of rock, we must be clear about two words that people often mix up: rock and mineral. They are not the same thing, and knowing the difference is the first step to thinking like a geologist.

A mineral is a natural solid substance with a fixed chemical make-up. Each mineral is always built from the same ingredients arranged in the same way, so it has the same properties wherever you find it. Salt is a mineral — it is always made of the same particles, whether it comes from a salt pan near Berbera or from under the ground. Quartz, the hard, glassy mineral that makes up much of ordinary sand, is another. Gold, iron, gypsum and the colourful crystals of feldspar and mica are all minerals. A mineral is a single, pure kind of material.

A rock is a natural solid that is usually made of a mixture of minerals stuck together. Think of it this way: if a mineral is a single ingredient, a rock is the finished dish made from several ingredients. Granite, for example, is a hard rock made of at least three minerals mixed together — the pale grains of quartz and feldspar and the dark flecks of mica. If you look closely at a piece of granite, perhaps in a polished floor or a grinding stone, you can often see these different coloured grains with your own eyes.

So a useful way to remember it is: minerals are the building blocks, and rocks are what you get when the blocks are joined together. A few rocks are made of just one mineral — pure limestone is mostly a single mineral called calcite — but most rocks are mixtures. This matters because the minerals in a rock decide how hard it is, what colour it is, whether water can soak through it, and how useful it is to people.
concept-1-rocks-and-minerals-what-is-the.example: Did You Know? The sand on an Indian Ocean beach is mostly tiny grains of the mineral quartz, which is so hard and long-lasting that it survives being tumbled by waves for thousands of years after the rock it came from has crumbled away. Some beautiful minerals are prized as gemstones — East Africa is famous for tanzanite, rubies and garnets, all of which grow inside rock deep underground.

concept-2-igneous-rock-born-from-fire.explanation:
The first great family of rock is igneous rock. The word 'igneous' comes from an old word for fire, and that is a perfect name, because igneous rock is born from heat. Deep inside the Earth it is so hot that rock is molten — a thick, glowing liquid called magma. When this molten rock cools down and hardens, it becomes solid igneous rock.

There are two closely related words to learn. While the molten rock is still beneath the surface, we call it magma. When a volcano erupts and the molten rock pours out onto the surface, we call it lava. It is the same hot liquid rock — the only difference is whether it is still underground (magma) or has come out into the open (lava). Both cool and harden into igneous rock.

Here is a beautiful piece of science. The speed at which the molten rock cools decides what the igneous rock looks like, especially the size of its crystals.

Fast cooling at the surface makes rock with tiny crystals. When lava pours out of a volcano into the open air or the sea, it cools quickly. The mineral crystals have no time to grow, so they stay very small. Basalt, the dark, fine, heavy rock that makes up the black lava fields of the Great Rift Valley, formed this way.

Slow cooling deep underground makes rock with large crystals. When magma is trapped far below the surface, it cools very slowly over thousands of years. The crystals have plenty of time to grow big, so you can see them clearly. Granite, with its visible grains of quartz, feldspar and mica, formed this way.

So if you find an igneous rock with large, easy-to-see crystals, you know it cooled slowly, deep underground. If it is smooth and fine with crystals too small to see, you know it cooled quickly, at or near the surface. The rock itself carries the memory of how it was born.

East Africa is one of the best places on Earth to see igneous rock, because the Great Rift Valley runs right through it. The Rift Valley is a giant crack where the Earth's surface is slowly pulling apart, and along it stand many volcanoes. Over millions of years these volcanoes have poured out huge sheets of lava that hardened into dark basalt. The same volcanic activity has produced hot springs, rich volcanic soil and even natural glass called obsidian, which people once used to make sharp tools.
concept-2-igneous-rock-born-from-fire.example: Did You Know? Basalt is one of the most common rocks on Earth — it makes up most of the floor of the oceans, hidden beneath the water. The rich, dark soil found near old volcanoes is famous for growing crops well, because as volcanic rock weathers it releases minerals that plants need.

concept-3-sedimentary-rock-built-in-laye.explanation:
The second great family is sedimentary rock. If igneous rock is born from fire, sedimentary rock is built slowly, layer by layer, from broken pieces of older rock and the remains of living things. Sedimentary rock is where we find almost all fossils, and it is the rock most useful for building. Understanding how it forms means understanding a chain of four steps.

Step 1 — Weathering breaks rock into pieces

It all begins when older rock is broken into small loose pieces by weathering. Weathering is the wearing down of rock where it stands, by the weather and by living things. In the strong sun of the dry season a rock heats up and expands by day, then cools and shrinks at night; done over and over, this stress cracks the rock. In the wet season, rain water seeps into the cracks; the roots of an acacia tree push in and widen them. Little by little, solid rock is broken into gravel, sand and mud. You will study weathering in more detail in Part 6.

The loose broken pieces are called sediment. Erosion is the carrying away of this sediment by moving water, wind, ice or simply gravity pulling it downhill. In East Africa the great movers of sediment are the rivers. When the Jubba and Shabelle rivers run high in the wet season, their brown, muddy water is thick with sediment — sand, silt and mud scraped from the land upstream and carried far downstream toward the sea.

Step 3 — Deposition drops the sediment in layers

Moving water can only carry sediment while it is flowing fast. When a river slows down — where it spreads out over flat land, or where it meets a lake or the ocean — it can no longer hold its load, and it drops the sediment. This dropping is called deposition. The heaviest pieces (gravel and sand) settle first, and the lightest (fine mud) settle last and furthest out. Over many, many years, layer settles upon layer, building up thick beds of sediment on river beds, lake bottoms and the sea floor. These layers are called strata.

Step 4 — Compaction and cementation harden the layers into rock

As more and more layers pile up, the weight of the upper layers squeezes the lower ones. This squeezing is called compaction, and it presses the grains tightly together and forces out the water. At the same time, minerals dissolved in the water crystallise between the grains and glue them together, like a natural cement. This gluing is called cementation. Together, compaction and cementation turn loose sediment into solid sedimentary rock — a process that takes thousands to millions of years.

Different sediments make different sedimentary rocks. Cemented sand becomes sandstone. Cemented mud becomes mudstone. The crushed shells and skeletons of tiny sea creatures build up into limestone. Along the East African coast, ancient coral reefs have hardened into coral limestone, a soft, pale stone that people in Lamu, Mombasa and Berbera have quarried and cut into blocks to build houses and mosques for centuries. When you see the old stone town of Lamu, you are looking at sedimentary rock made from the skeletons of sea creatures that lived long ago.

concept-4-metamorphic-rock-changed-by-he.explanation:
The third great family is metamorphic rock. The word 'metamorphic' means 'changed in form', and that is exactly what these rocks are: older rocks that have been changed into something new by enormous heat and pressure, deep inside the Earth — but without melting completely. If they melted fully, they would become magma and later igneous rock. Metamorphic rock is what you get when a rock is cooked and squeezed almost to melting, so that its minerals rearrange into a new, usually harder form.

Two forces do the work. Heat comes from deep inside the Earth or from nearby magma. Pressure comes from the crushing weight of rock above, or from the mighty forces that push up mountains and pull apart the Rift Valley. When a rock is buried very deep and left under this heat and pressure for a long time, its minerals slowly change. New, often denser minerals grow, and the rock becomes harder and sometimes takes on a striped or banded pattern.

The best way to understand metamorphic rock is through before-and-after pairs:

Limestone becomes marble. Soft, dull limestone, when heated and squeezed, changes into hard, smooth marble, which can be polished to a shine. Marble is prized for floors, tabletops and the beautiful decoration of grand buildings and mosques.

Mudstone becomes slate. Soft mud rock, under pressure, changes into slate, a hard rock that splits into flat sheets. These flat sheets have been used for roofing tiles and writing boards.

Sandstone becomes quartzite. Sandstone, when cooked and squeezed, changes into quartzite, an extremely hard rock that resists weathering and often stands up as rugged hills.

Notice the pattern: in every case a softer rock is changed into a harder one. That is why metamorphic rocks are often the toughest of all, and why they form the cores of many ancient mountains. Much of the very old, hard rock deep beneath East Africa is metamorphic, formed long ago when the land was squeezed and heated during the building of ancient mountains.
concept-4-metamorphic-rock-changed-by-he.example: Did You Know? The word for these three rock families gives a neat memory aid: Igneous = made by fire; Sedimentary = settled in layers; Metamorphic = changed in form. Marble and limestone are chemically almost the same, yet marble is far harder and can be polished — all because of the heat and pressure it went through.

concept-5-the-rock-cycle-nature-s-great-.explanation:
Now comes the idea that ties the whole unit together: the rock cycle. So far you have met three families of rock as if they were separate. But they are not separate at all. Over immense stretches of time, any type of rock can be changed into any other type. Rock is constantly being destroyed and rebuilt in a never-ending loop. This loop is the rock cycle, and it is one of the grandest ideas in all of Earth science.

Let us follow a single piece of rock around the cycle. Imagine it starts as black basalt, an igneous rock, on a lava field in the Rift Valley:

Weathering and erosion attack the basalt. Sun, rain and roots break it into small pieces of sediment, and a river carries the pieces away.

Deposition drops the sediment in layers on a river bed or the sea floor. Over long ages, compaction and cementation harden the layers into sedimentary rock, such as sandstone.

Heat and pressure bury the sedimentary rock deep underground and change it into metamorphic rock, such as quartzite.

Melting deep inside the Earth turns the metamorphic rock into magma.

Cooling of the magma hardens it back into igneous rock — and the whole journey can begin again.

The cycle does not always run in that exact order, though. A rock can take shortcuts. Igneous rock can be buried and turned straight into metamorphic rock without ever becoming sediment. Sedimentary rock can be weathered back into new sediment. Any rock can be melted and reborn as igneous rock. The key idea is that there is no beginning and no end — the rock beneath your feet has almost certainly been many different rocks before, and will become many more long after we are gone.
concept-5-the-rock-cycle-nature-s-great-.example: Two great sources of energy drive the whole cycle. Heat from deep inside the Earth melts rock, pushes up mountains and powers volcanoes — these forces build rock up. Energy from the Sun drives the wind and the rain that weather and erode rock, wearing it down. The building-up and the wearing-down are in a slow, endless balance, and between them they keep the rock cycle turning forever.

concept-6-weathering-and-erosion-in-deta.explanation:
You have already met weathering and erosion as the first steps in making sedimentary rock. They are so important that they deserve a closer look. The two words are often confused, so hold on to this simple rule: weathering breaks rock; erosion carries it away. Weathering happens on the spot; erosion is the transport.

Physical weathering (also called mechanical weathering) breaks rock into smaller pieces without changing what it is made of. The pieces are still the same rock, just smaller. In the climate of East Africa the biggest cause is the daily swing of temperature. In the dry season the surface of a rock is scorched by the sun each day and cools sharply each night. The outer layer expands when hot and shrinks when cold, again and again, until it cracks and flakes off — a bit like the way a road surface cracks over years. Plant roots add to the work: a seed lands in a crack, grows, and its roots push the crack wider until the rock splits.

Chemical weathering changes the minerals in the rock into new substances, usually by reacting with water and gases in the air. Rain water is very slightly acidic, and over long times it can slowly dissolve certain rocks. Limestone is especially affected — slightly acidic rain water eats away at it, which is why limestone landscapes often have caves and hollows. In the wet season, when rain is plentiful, chemical weathering speeds up. Warm, wet places weather rock faster than cold, dry ones, which is one reason tropical soils can be very deep.

Biological weathering is the breaking of rock by living things. Tree roots widen cracks; burrowing animals loosen stones; even tiny lichens growing on a rock face slowly eat into its surface. In truth, physical, chemical and biological weathering usually work together on the same rock at the same time.

Once weathering has broken rock into loose pieces, erosion carries them away. The movers are water, wind, ice and gravity:

Water is the greatest mover of all. Rivers like the Jubba and Shabelle carry huge amounts of sand and mud, especially in the wet season when they run fast and full. Waves erode the coast, and rain washes soil down slopes.

Wind is a powerful mover in dry, semi-arid places. It lifts fine sand and dust and carries it far — the dust storms of the dry season are wind erosion in action, and wind piles sand into dunes.

Gravity pulls loose rock straight downhill, causing rockfalls and landslides, especially after heavy rain loosens a slope.

Erosion has a serious human side. When land is stripped of its plants — by overgrazing, cutting too many trees, or farming badly — the bare soil is easily eroded by wind and rain. The precious topsoil that grows crops is washed or blown away, leaving hard, barren ground behind. This is soil erosion, and it is one of the biggest threats to farming in the region. Protecting the soil — by keeping plant cover, planting trees, and farming gently — is part of our duty as khalifah, careful guardians of the land.
concept-6-weathering-and-erosion-in-deta.example: Did You Know? The muddy brown colour of a river in flood is the colour of the land itself, dissolved and carried in the water — a river in flood can move millions of tonnes of sediment toward the sea. The Grand Canyon in another part of the world is a giant river carving a valley over millions of years — proof of just how much even a single river can erode, given enough time.

we01.solution:
Worked Example 1 — Naming a rock type from clues

Question: Amina finds a pale, layered rock in a cliff. When she looks closely she can see the shapes of tiny shells in it, arranged in flat bands. What type of rock is it, and how do you know?

Step 1 — Look for clues. It is in layers (strata), and it contains the shells of living things.

Step 2 — Match the clues to a rock family. Layers and fossils are the fingerprints of sedimentary rock, which forms from settled sediment and the remains of living things.

we02.solution:
Step 1 — Look for clues. It is in layers (strata), and it contains the shells of living things.

Step 2 — Match the clues to a rock family. Layers and fossils are the fingerprints of sedimentary rock, which forms from settled sediment and the remains of living things.

Answer: It is a sedimentary rock (a limestone). We know because sedimentary rock is the only family that forms gently in layers and preserves fossils.

Worked Example 2 — Reasoning about crystal size

we03.solution:
Step 1 — Recall the rule. Slow cooling gives crystals time to grow large; fast cooling gives small crystals.

Step 2 — Apply it. Rock A (large crystals) must have cooled slowly, deep underground, like granite. Rock B (tiny crystals) must have cooled quickly, at the surface, like basalt from a lava flow.

Answer: Rock A cooled slowly underground; Rock B cooled quickly at the surface. The crystal size is the clue.

Worked Example 3 — Reading the order of layers

we04.solution:
Step 1 — Recall the rule. Each new layer settles on top of the older ones, so the oldest layer is at the bottom.

Step 2 — Apply it. The bottom layer is the sandstone, so it was laid down first, before the mudstone and limestone above it.

Answer: The sandstone at the bottom formed first. Reading strata from bottom to top reads them from oldest to youngest.

Worked Example 4 — A hardness test

we05.solution:
Step 1 — Recall the idea. A harder mineral can scratch a softer one, but a softer mineral cannot scratch a harder one.

Step 2 — Apply it. Mineral X scratches everything and is scratched by nothing, so it is the hardest. Mineral Z is scratched by both others, so it is the softest.

Answer: Mineral X is the hardest and Mineral Z is the softest. This scratch test is exactly how geologists compare hardness, using a scale that runs from soft talc up to hard diamond.

rule-1.text: Rocks come in three families: igneous (made by fire), sedimentary (settled in layers) and metamorphic (changed by heat and pressure). Weathering breaks rock; erosion carries it away. The rock cycle has no start and no end — any rock can become any other rock over time. Fossils are found in sedimentary rock; soil is weathered rock plus humus.

rule-2.text: Igneous rock is made by fire (cooling magma or lava); sedimentary rock settles in layers; metamorphic rock is changed by heat and pressure. Weathering breaks rock; erosion carries it away; deposition drops it in layers. The rock cycle never stops — any rock can become any other, given enough time. Soil is weathered rock plus humus, and caring for it is part of being a khalifah.

sci-g08-u09.unitOverview: Think about the last time the electricity in your home flickered on after dark. A single small bulb, or the glow of a phone screen, suddenly pushes back the night. In many homes across East Africa that light does not come from a distant power station at all — it comes from a solar panel on the roof charging a battery, which then powers lamps, a radio, and the charger for a mobile phone. Every one of those things works because of two invisible partners in nature that you will study in this unit: electricity and magnetism. They are so closely linked that scientists give them a single joined name, electromagnetism, and together they run almost every machine humans have ever built.

concept-1-what-is-electric-current.explanation:
Everything around you is made of tiny particles called atoms, and inside every atom are even smaller particles. Some of these carry a tiny amount of electric charge. In metals, some of these charged particles are free to move about, and when they all drift in the same direction along a wire, we have an electric current. So an electric current is simply the flow of electric charge. It is a little like water flowing through a pipe, except that instead of water it is charge that flows, and instead of a pipe it flows along a wire.

Current can only flow when there is a complete circuit — an unbroken loop of conductor leading from one end of a cell, through the wires and components, and back to the other end of the cell. If there is any gap in the loop, the current stops everywhere at once, just as water stops flowing if you cut the pipe. This is exactly why a switch works. A switch is nothing more than a controlled gap: when it is closed, the loop is complete and current flows; when it is open, there is a gap and the current stops. Turn off the switch on a solar lamp and the light dies instantly, because you have broken the loop.

Not every material lets current pass. A conductor is a material that current flows through easily, because it has charged particles that are free to move. Metals such as copper, aluminium and iron are excellent conductors, which is why wires are made of metal. An insulator is a material that current cannot flow through, because its charged particles are locked in place. Plastic, rubber, dry wood, glass and dry cloth are insulators. This difference is used everywhere for safety: the copper inside a wire carries the current, and the plastic coating around it stops the current escaping into your hand. Notice that the human body is a conductor — this is exactly why electricity is dangerous to touch.

By an old agreement that scientists still use, we draw conventional current as flowing from the positive end of the cell, round the circuit, and back to the negative end. You do not need to worry about the deep details yet; what matters is that the current flows in a loop, always in the same direction, driven by the cell. Every cell has a positive end (marked +) and a negative end (marked -), and connecting them the correct way round is part of making a circuit work.
concept-1-what-is-electric-current.example: Did You Know? A current of just one ampere means an enormous number of charged particles — roughly six billion billion of them — passing a point every single second. Copper is used for almost all wiring because it conducts electricity extremely well and can be pulled into thin, bendy wires without breaking.

concept-2-voltage-the-push-behind-the-cu.explanation:
If current is the flow of charge, something must push that charge around the loop. That push is called voltage, and it comes from the cell or battery. The proper scientific name for voltage is potential difference, but in everyday use we simply say voltage. Voltage is measured in volts (V).

Think of the cell as a pump and the current as water flowing round a loop of pipe. The pump does not create the water — it pushes it round. In the same way, the cell does not create charge — it provides the energy that pushes the charge around the circuit. The bigger the voltage, the stronger the push, and (for the same components) the bigger the current that flows. A single dry cell of the kind used in a torch gives about 1.5 V. When you stack cells together to make a battery, their voltages add up: two 1.5 V cells in a line give 3 V, and four give 6 V. That is why a torch that needs more power holds several cells stacked end to end.
concept-2-voltage-the-push-behind-the-cu.example: Inside a cell, stored chemical energy is turned into electrical energy that pushes the current. This is why batteries eventually go flat — the chemicals are used up, the voltage falls, and the push gets weaker until the bulb dims and dies. A solar panel does the same job in a different way: instead of chemicals, it uses the energy of sunlight to provide the voltage that pushes the current. During the day the panel pushes current to charge a battery; at night the battery takes over and pushes the current itself. Understanding voltage as a push, and the cell or panel as the source of energy, is one of the most important ideas in this whole unit.

concept-3-resistance-slowing-the-current.explanation:
The third big idea is resistance. Resistance is how much a component slows down the current that tries to pass through it. Everything in a circuit has some resistance, even the wires, but some components resist much more than others. Resistance is measured in ohms.

As the charged particles drift along, they keep bumping into the fixed particles of the material and are slowed down. A material or component that makes this harder has a high resistance; one that lets charge slip through easily has a low resistance. Several things change how much resistance a wire has:

A longer wire has more resistance than a short one, because the charge has further to travel and more particles to bump into.

A thinner wire has more resistance than a thick one, because there is less room for the charge to move through.

Some materials naturally resist more than others. Copper resists very little, which is why we use it for wires; the special thin wire inside a bulb resists a lot, which is why it heats up and glows.

These three ideas are joined by one simple rule. For a fixed voltage, more resistance means less current, and less resistance means more current. Picture squeezing a pipe: pinch it (more resistance) and less water flows; open it wide (less resistance) and more water flows. In the same way, if you add more resistance to a circuit while the battery stays the same, the current drops. And if you raise the voltage while the resistance stays the same, the current rises. Scientists write this relationship as a neat word equation:

This means that if you know any two of the three quantities, you can work out the third. You can rearrange it to find current (current = voltage / resistance) or to find resistance (resistance = voltage / current). You will practise using this rule in the Worked Examples below — it is one of the most useful relationships in all of physics.

concept-4-circuits-series-and-parallel.explanation:
Now that you know about current, voltage and resistance, you can understand how components are joined together. There are two main ways to build a circuit, and they behave very differently. Learning to tell them apart is a key skill of this unit.

Scientists do not draw pictures of real bulbs and batteries every time — it would take too long and look untidy. Instead they use a set of agreed symbols to draw a neat circuit diagram. You should learn these common symbols:

A cell is drawn as one long thin line and one short thick line side by side (the long line is the positive end).

A battery is two or more cells drawn in a row.

A bulb (lamp) is drawn as a circle with a cross inside it.

A switch is drawn as a small gap with a line that can close it like a lever.

An ammeter is a circle with a letter A inside it; a voltmeter is a circle with a letter V inside it.

Wires are drawn as straight lines joining everything into a loop.

A series circuit has just one loop. All the components are joined end to end, one after another, so the current has only one path to follow. This gives series circuits two important behaviours that you must remember:

The current is the same everywhere in a series circuit. Because there is only one path, the same current flows through every component — the cell, each bulb and the wires.

The voltage is shared between the components. If a 3 V battery drives two identical bulbs in series, each bulb gets about 1.5 V. The bulbs are dimmer than a single bulb would be on its own.

A series circuit has a big weakness. Because it is a single loop, if one component breaks, the whole circuit breaks. Take out one bulb, or let one bulb burn out, and every bulb goes dark, because the loop now has a gap. Old strings of decorative lights worked this way, which is why one dead bulb could switch off the whole string.

A parallel circuit gives the current more than one path by splitting it into separate branches. Each bulb sits on its own branch, like separate side-roads leaving and rejoining a main road. Parallel circuits behave in the opposite way to series circuits in two important ways:

Each branch gets the full voltage. If a 3 V battery drives two bulbs in parallel, each bulb gets the full 3 V, so the bulbs are bright, as bright as a single bulb on its own.

Each branch can work on its own. If one bulb breaks, the others stay lit, because each has its own complete loop back to the battery. The current simply keeps flowing through the branches that are still whole.

This is exactly why the lights and sockets in a house are wired in parallel. If your home were wired in series, switching off one lamp would plunge every room into darkness, and a single blown bulb would kill all the power. Because the house is wired in parallel, each light and socket has its own branch: you can switch one on or off, and a fault in one does not stop the rest. The same is true of a solar-powered home — each lamp and each phone charger is on its own branch so one can fail without darkening the others.
concept-4-circuits-series-and-parallel.example: Did You Know? Every room in a house shares the same voltage from the mains because the rooms are wired in parallel — that is why a lamp is just as bright whether it is the only thing switched on or one of many. In a series circuit, adding more bulbs makes them all dimmer, because the same voltage has to be shared among more of them.

concept-5-measuring-current-and-voltage.explanation:
A real scientist does not just guess how much current flows — they measure it. There are two instruments you must know, and each is connected in its own special way.

An ammeter measures the current in amps. Because the current has to pass through it to be counted, an ammeter is always connected in series — it becomes part of the single loop, so that all the current flows through it, like a gate that counts everything passing along the road. If you break the loop and slot the ammeter into the gap, it will read the current flowing at that point.

A voltmeter measures the voltage across a component in volts. Voltage is a difference in push between two points, so a voltmeter is connected in parallel — across the component, touching the wire on each side of it, like measuring the height of a step by standing beside it rather than walking through it. Connect a voltmeter across a bulb and it tells you how many volts are being used up pushing current through that bulb.
concept-5-measuring-current-and-voltage.example: A simple way to remember the difference: the Ammeter goes Along the circuit (in series), while the Voltmeter goes aVer, or across, the component (in parallel). Getting these connections right is a real practical skill, and using them lets you check the rules you learned in Part 4 — for example, that current is the same everywhere in a series circuit, and that each branch of a parallel circuit gets the full voltage.

concept-6-magnets-and-magnetic-fields.explanation:
We now turn to the second half of the unit: magnetism. At first it may seem completely separate from electricity, but you will soon see that the two are deeply connected. Let us start with what a magnet is.

A magnet is an object that can attract certain metals and that always has two poles, called the north pole and the south pole. The force of a magnet is strongest at its poles. There is one golden rule of magnets that you must know by heart:

This means two north poles push each other away, and two south poles push each other away, but a north pole and a south pole pull together. You can feel this yourself with two fridge magnets: turn them one way and they snap together, turn one around and they push apart so strongly you can hardly force them to meet.

Only a few materials are magnetic — that is, attracted to a magnet. The main ones are iron, steel (which is mostly iron), nickel and cobalt. Most other materials, including copper, aluminium, plastic, wood and glass, are not magnetic and are not pulled by a magnet at all. This is why a magnet will pick up an iron nail or a steel spoon but ignore a copper coin or a plastic ruler. Note the difference from electricity here: copper is a brilliant electrical conductor but is not magnetic, while iron is magnetic — so 'metal' does not automatically mean 'magnetic'.

Around every magnet there is an invisible region where its force can be felt, called the magnetic field. We cannot see it, but we can map its shape. If you scatter tiny iron filings on a sheet of paper over a bar magnet, they line up in curved lines running from the north pole to the south pole, showing the shape of the field. These lines are called field lines. They are closest together near the poles, where the field is strongest, and spread further apart away from the magnet, where the field is weaker. A compass is simply a tiny magnet that is free to turn, and it lines itself up with whatever magnetic field it is in.

Here is one of the most wonderful facts in science: the Earth itself behaves like a giant magnet, with a magnetic field stretching all around it. This is why a compass works. The compass needle is a small magnet that lines up with the Earth's field, so one end always swings round to point roughly north. Travellers have used this for hundreds of years to find their way across deserts and oceans. For a Muslim family far from home, a compass helps find the qibla — the direction of the Kaaba in Makkah — so they can face the right way for prayer. A simple magnet, and the invisible field of the whole planet, guides them.
concept-6-magnets-and-magnetic-fields.example: Did You Know? The Earth's magnetic field also protects all life on the planet by turning away much of the harmful particles that stream out from the Sun. The needle of a compass does not point to the exact geographic North Pole, but to a slightly different magnetic pole — sailors and pilots have to allow for this small difference.

we01.solution:
Worked Example 1 — Finding the current

Question: Khadija connects a bulb of resistance 3 ohms to a battery giving 6 V. What current flows through the bulb?

Step 1 — Choose the right form of the rule. We want the current, so use current = voltage / resistance.

Step 2 — Put in the numbers. current = 6 V / 3 ohms = 2. So the current is 2 A.

we02.solution:
Step 1 — Choose the right form of the rule. We want the current, so use current = voltage / resistance.

Step 2 — Put in the numbers. current = 6 V / 3 ohms = 2. So the current is 2 A.

Answer: A current of 2 amps flows through the bulb. Notice that if the resistance were larger, the same 6 V would push a smaller current.

Worked Example 2 — Finding the voltage

we03.solution:
Step 1 — Choose the right form of the rule. We want the voltage, so use voltage = current x resistance.

Step 2 — Put in the numbers. voltage = 0.5 A x 4 ohms = 2. So the voltage is 2 V.

Answer: The voltage across the component is 2 V. This is the push being used up driving the current through that component.

Worked Example 3 — Series circuit voltage sharing

we04.solution:
Step 1 — Voltage. In a series circuit the voltage is shared between the components. Two identical bulbs share the 3 V equally, so each gets about 1.5 V.

Step 2 — Current. In a series circuit the current is the same everywhere, so exactly the same current flows through both bulbs.

Answer: Each bulb gets about 1.5 V, and the same current flows through both. Because each bulb has only half the battery's voltage, the two bulbs are dimmer than a single bulb would be.

Worked Example 4 — Parallel circuit voltage

we05.solution:
Step 1 — Voltage. In a parallel circuit each branch gets the full battery voltage, so each bulb gets the whole 3 V and shines brightly.

Step 2 — One bulb breaks. Each bulb has its own complete loop, so if one breaks, the other keeps its full voltage and stays lit.

Answer: Each bulb gets the full 3 V and is bright, and if one bulb breaks the other still works. This is why homes are wired in parallel.

connection-1.text: Energy (next unit) — a solar panel charging a battery that lights a lamp is a chain of energy changes.

connection-5.text: Geography / navigation — the Earth's magnetic field, compasses and finding the qibla.

capstone-cap-u05-q1.explanation: a pure substance — it is made of only one type of particle.

capstone-cap-u05-q2.explanation: sugar — salt and sugar are soluble; sand, charcoal and oil are not.

capstone-cap-u05-q3.explanation: residue — the solid trapped on the filter is the residue; the liquid through it is the filtrate.

capstone-cap-u07-q1.explanation: carbohydrate — carbohydrates give the fastest, main energy supply.

capstone-cap-u07-q2.explanation: amylase — amylase (a carbohydrase) breaks starch into sugar.

capstone-cap-u07-q3.explanation: fibre — fibre is not digested but keeps the gut moving.

capstone-cap-u08-q1.explanation: rock — a rock is a natural solid usually made of a mixture of minerals.

capstone-cap-u08-q2.explanation: slowly deep underground — slow cooling gives crystals time to grow large.

capstone-cap-u08-q3.explanation: metamorphic — it is changed by heat and pressure without melting.

capstone-cap-u09-q1.explanation: the flow of electric charge — that is the definition of a current.

capstone-cap-u09-q2.explanation: copper — metals conduct well; plastic, rubber and glass are insulators.

capstone-cap-u09-q3.explanation: iron — iron, steel, nickel and cobalt are magnetic; copper, aluminium and gold are not.
